News.title: 'I'd rather die than ring the police': Distrust and fear in Middlesbrough after A66 crash
News.content:
All but one of the residents who speak to us do so on the condition of anonymity. They are worried that showing their faces could place them or their homes at risk.

What message do the attacks send to people on this street, I ask one.

"Well, they should be scared, shouldn't they, that something's going to happen to their property if they say anything or get involved. So we don't."

Victoria, who moved here several years ago, says the escalating violence cannot be separated from the wider condition of the town.

"This is a social problem, especially in this area. Teesside has been massively neglected and ignored," she says.

The attack in Acklam is far from Middlesbrough's only recent case of a vehicle being used as a weapon. Back in May, a tractor was driven into a house on Priory Road, and since the A66 crash Cleveland Police has investigated at least two further rammings.

Detectives have also linked their wider investigation to a caravan fire on Attlee Road in Grangetown.

"It's getting worse," a nearby resident says. "They're always balaclava-ed up as well, do you know what I mean?"

He blames drugs.

"It can't be anything else. Why would you be like you are unless it was drugs?" he says.

Whether every incident is part of a single feud has not been established. But taken together, the rammings, fires and arrests have created a powerful sense that violence is being used to intimidate, punish and send messages.

What is most unsettling for these residents is the sense that nobody is fully in control.

Grangetown and South Bank are communities still living with the void left by the decline of heavy industry. Both now rank among England's most deprived neighbourhoods.

In South Bank, we see a group of teenagers tend three ponies tethered on the grass. Two perform wheelies on electric scooters while another uses a long stick to scatter rubbish.

On the adjoining estate, more than a dozen homes have boarded-up windows.

On a wall are the words "RIP 2UZZI", said locally to have been the nickname of Jakub Matusiak, who lived one street away.

One 17-year-old boy tells us he knew him. "He was my best mate," he says. "It's sad."

Elsewhere, three letters are repeated: "FTP" - an expletive directed at the police.

I ask the teenager if he would call the police if another young person approached him carrying a knife.

"No," he says. Before adding: "I've never needed the police in my life. I'd rather die than ring the police."

Again and again, the young people we speak to express a profound distrust of the police.

Cleveland's Chief Constable Victoria Fuller said what we'd heard was "horrifying".

"Yes, there are a small minority of people in the Grangetown area who blight those communities. But we will continue relentlessly to serve our communities."

The scale of the challenge facing the force and the community it serves is not new.

The area has some of the highest police-recorded crime rates in England and Wales.

Its leaders have been warning for years that its resources did not match the demands placed upon it.

But recent inspections show Cleveland is one of the most improved forces in England and Wales, with performance levels also judged to be some of the best in the country.

The force has recently arrested 87 people for offences linked to organised crime gangs and over the past two years 16 people have been jailed for such crimes.

Since the crash, more than 200 additional officers have been deployed in Middlesbrough and surrounding communities. Their immediate task is to suppress the violence and identify those directing it.

There is also the question of restoring order and rebuilding trust and confidence.

News.title: Cleveland police chief proud of force but being 'let down' by funding
News.content:
Cleveland Police's Chief Constable has said she is proud of her "brave" force but that it was being "let down" by the way it was funded, following a fatal crash which killed seven people including two police officers.

In her first sit-down interview since the A66 crash, speaking exclusively to the BBC, Victoria Fuller said the force needed to become part of a larger force with greater resources.

She said her officers are dealing with some of the highest crime levels in the country akin to those faced by metropolitan forces, but with less than half the number of officers.

Multiple people have since been arrested as part of a wider police operation against organised crime following the crash.

A Volkswagen Passat carrying five young men drove the wrong way down the motorway near Middlesbrough in the early hours of the morning before colliding with a marked police car.

Officers had been pursuing the car for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when the Passat turned on to the dual carriageway, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said.

Fuller, whose force covers an area of north-east England that includes Middlesbrough and Teesside, recalled being asleep when the duty commander rang her with the news.

"No matter how tragic and devastated you feel, we swing into action and we do what we need to do," she said.

The home secretary announced this week that Cleveland Police would be given an extra Â£2m to deal with the fallout from the crash, with 200 officers drafted in from elsewhere.

Fuller told the BBC on Friday that she was grateful for the support the force had been given, but added: "I need that all the time."

Cleveland's Labour police and crime commissioner has previously said the force needed an extra Â£20m a year to hire more officers and crack down on organised crime.

Cleveland Police is grappling with the highest recorded crime rate of anywhere in England and Wales, Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures for the year to March show.

At the same time, Fuller said Cleveland Police had experienced the largest decrease in the number of officers since 2010 and was staffed as if it were a rural force.

"It absolutely needs to change," she said.

Fuller expressed hope that reform to policing across the country was on the horizon, and that Cleveland Police would become one of the "big, strategic forces that have the resource, the flex and the capability to surge when they need to surge".

She added: "In the meantime, we need additional funding... to take us to that point."

Fuller denied that gangs had control over parts of Middlesbrough, describing it as a "complex" area to police, with high rates of school absence, drug addiction and mental health issues.

"We're doing the very, very best with what we've got - and we absolutely do need more."

Authorities say high deprivation and unemployment in the area are fueling organised crime.

"When young people have little aspiration or hope, who don't have confidence in the state, then unfortunately criminals exploit these people," Fuller said.

"They give confidence, and they give them hope, and they give them aspiration. And sadly what that means is young people doing things without thought of consequences."

News.title: Farage threatens to overhaul Lords and judges to meet his pledges
News.content:
In his speech, which was light on new policy announcements, Farage said the country needed a government "that actually delivers on its promises" and "we're the only people capable of doing it".

He argued the Tories "had 14 years in power and failed absolutely miserably", while Labour's new Prime Minister Andy Burnham "says he needs 10 years", a reference to the PM's promise to set out a 10-year plan for the country later this year.

If Reform wins the next general election, Farage pledged to sack ministers who fail to deliver on their promises in their first 100 days in the job "and replace them with somebody else with the courage to do it".

Setting out his plans to call a "national emergency" if Reform wins power, Farage said: "Parliament will sit, if necessary, for 24 hours a day, for six days a week until we pass the necessary legislation."

He said he expected the House of Lords to "honour" Reform's policy pledges but if they refused to do so threatened to appoint hundreds of new peers so the party had a majority in the upper chamber.

"And if that proves difficult, we will hold a referendum on the current composition of the House of Lords, and they would be swept away by a British public appalled by them," he added.

Identifying the judiciary as another possible "obstacle", Farage promised to remove the ability of judges to rely on conventions like the European Convention of Human Rights (ECHR), which critics blame for hindering some deportations.

"We don't want the courts striking down, do we, the will of the people," he said.

"Parliament makes the law, judges interpret the law. We will do whatever it takes, and perhaps have to consider how judicial appointments work in the future."

Meanwhile, he said civil servants who "try to obstruct us" would be removed from their posts and replaced by people from the world of business.

"I'm tired of being told what can't be done," the Reform leader said.

"That is not what the public want. The public want action, the public want genuine change, the public do not want any more of the same. And our attitude is can do, and will do."

Predicting that Burnham would call an early general election in spring 2027, Farage attempted to use his speech to convince the public Reform was ready to govern.

Stressing he now had a team of spokespeople with "frontline experience", he said the party was planning to broaden its expertise.

"There are more big jobs to fill, and I'm looking and working on defence, health, and the other areas," he added.

In his speech, Farage also hailed a "historic agreement" on small boat returns, signed earlier between Reform and France's hard-right National Rally party.

The deal sets out how a Reform government would intercept boats in the English Channel and return them to France using the Navy, with France "ordinarily" accepting those on board.

It was signed by the National Rally President Jordan Bardella, whose party is currently leading in opinion polls ahead of French presidential elections in April next year, after he gave a speech to the main conference hall.

Farage took to the stage after a long delay, which he told delegates was due to a "security alert".

He took the opportunity to walk through the crowd and greet delegates during the delay.

His speech was also interrupted several times by protesters, including two women who held up a banner reading "Reform works for billionaires".

They were booed by audience members who shouted "out", as they were removed by security.

Farage laughed off the disruption, chanting "boring, boring, boring".

Reform is no longer consistently topping national opinion polls, after more than a year of enjoying a comfortable lead.

Meanwhile, Labour's ratings have risen since Burnham entered Downing Street, and Reform has lost some support to Restore Britain, the new right-wing party founded by former Reform MP Rupert Lowe.

News.title: UN votes to adopt new world map to reflect Africa's true size
News.content:
The Mercator map was designed in 1569 by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator to help European explorers navigate across the world.

The distortion of his map is a result of the fact that it is impossible to accurately represent the surface of a globe on a two-dimensional chart.

Whenever a map of the world is drawn, compromises need to be made.

The Mercator map shows the curvature of the Earth by making countries near the equator seem smaller than they are, with countries nearer the poles appearing bigger.

In an effort to correct this, a team of cartographers in 2018 created an equal area map they called the Equal Earth projection.

In February, the AU's 54 member states adopted it, and said it "more accurately represents the sizes of all continents, particularly Africa".

Online campaign group #CorrectTheMap said: "You could fit the United States, China, India, Japan, Mexico and much of Europe into Africa and still have land to spare."

Ahead of Friday's vote, Togolese Foreign Minister Robert Dussey told the Reuters news agency: "A fair world begins with a fair map."

Earlier he had told a UN briefing: "A map is never neutral. It shapes perceptions, influences how the place of peoples and continents in the world is understood."

He had the backing of the French Foreign Minister Jean-NoÃ«l Barrot, who said his ministry was going to stop using the Mercator map, external.

"Changing the map obviously doesn't change the world. But correcting a representation that distorts it is already an act of truth," he said.

But Yaryna Ferencevych, a US representative at the UN, said the resolution mocked the work and purpose of the UN General Assembly, external.

"Instead of focusing on genuine problems of international peace, prosperity, or good relations, this body is debating map projects from the 16th Century, and their role in promoting reparations and 'cognitive justice'," she said.

In March, the US was also critical when a resolution was adopted declaring the transatlantic slave trade "the gravest crime against humanity".

News.title: Cambridge launches review into support for Jason Arday before death
News.content:
The University of Cambridge has launched an independent review into its "decision-making and actions" in the period leading up to former professor Jason Arday's death.

The review will examine the support available to Arday before his death, as well as the wider context of his time at the university.

Arday, 41, was found dead at his home in London on 14 August, the week after resigning from his position as professor of sociology of education amid intense scrutiny over allegations of plagiarism. He had denied the claims.

Announcing the review on Friday, Vice-Chancellor Prof Deborah Prentice said the time since his death had been a "period of profound sadness and reflection for the university".

"We worked very hard to support Professor Arday during an appalling period of external criticism and focus, but given the devastating outcome, we are still asking ourselves whether we could have and should have done more," she said.

"This review will help us answer that question."

In a post on social media, the University of Cambridge said: "University Council took the necessary steps to launch an independent review into the university's decision-making and actions, with a focus on identifying shortcomings and areas for improvement."

The first part of the review will look at the "support, interventions and protections" available to Arday in the period before his death.

Those findings will be reported within three months, allowing recommendations for "urgent action" to be considered and implemented "without delay".

It will be led by Nazir Afzal, chancellor of the University of Manchester and former chief crown prosecutor for the North West of England.

Afzal said in a statement that "it is important that we approach this work with both rigour and humanity", adding "we must be willing to ask difficult questions".

The second part of the review will examine the wider circumstances of Arday's time at Cambridge, including the recruitment of senior academic staff, mentoring and support arrangements.

It will also look at the university's response to allegations of research misconduct and the support available to academics facing "extraordinary public and media scrutiny".

An independent external chair will be appointed to lead the second part of the review, with an expert panel "including individuals with lived experience" advising it.

It is expected to conclude within six months of the panel being established.

In a video message, Prentice said: "I am conscious that Professor Arday's death has deeply affected black staff and students, as well as our neurodiverse community.

"There has also been an unacceptable rise in racist, hateful, and abusive attacks on our staff and students in online forums and on social media."

In 2023, the sociologist, then 37, became the youngest ever black professor at Cambridge.

Arday had faced allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements. He denied the claims, but admitted errors in his work.

Arday said some errors arose because of his autism, as he relied on using mimicry to make sense of information. He said similar scrutiny would find comparable errors in the work of other academics.

The allegations emerged after another academic - self-defined "race realist" Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 - said he found numerous instances of plagiarism in the professor's work.

Arday said the criticism had gone "far beyond scholarly disagreement".

Resigning from his post in August, he added: "The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and those I love."

Following his death, his family said they were "in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son".

They added: "The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone."

A vigil held in Trafalgar Square was attended by thousands, according to its organisers.

There have been calls for a public inquiry into media coverage of Arday before his death.

News.title: Nepal bet nearly everything on hydropower - the floods show why that's a problem
News.content:
Hydropower continues to dominate large-scale investments in Nepal, and some climate activists say the funding has continued despite known disaster risks.

The Upper Trishuli-1 project, which has been all but destroyed after last week's floods, was one of Nepal's largest foreign direct investment ventures, valued at about $647m. Its backers include the Asian Development Bank and the International Finance Corporation.

The Upper Trishuli 3A, which has also been severely hit, was funded by China's Export-Import Bank.

Himanshu Thakkar, coordinator of the South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers & People, says international lenders were "acutely aware of the extreme danger to which they were exposing thousands of labourers, officials, residents, rivers, infrastructure and landscape".

"Their own reports repeatedly highlighted it. But they did not take any preventive steps, did not demand stringent checks and balances, nor were they prepared for a calamity they knew could occur," he says.

History has already shown the Trishuli River basin to be volatile, Thakkar says, pointing to how it had been hit by floods in the last two years. In September 2024, an unprecedented cloudburst over the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi river basins sparked flash floods in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading - settlements by the river that are also among the hardest hit from last week's floods.

Then in July 2025, a glacial lake in Tibet's Gyirong county burst and swept down this very same stretch of river into Nepal, killing at least 11 people. That flood damaged critical infrastructure and halted trade along the busy Nepal-China corridor. The border crossing was shut for nearly six months and had only reopened on 1 January this year.

Dhakal from the Nepal Electricity Authority admits that even if climate risk assessments were carried out correctly, "the designing of the plants may not have been done accordingly".

"Clearly we will need to improve in the way we build and operate our hydropower plants," he adds.

Private operators are already feeling the financial impact. Insurers have paid out around $40m for flood-related damage to more than 20 privately owned plants over the past three years, according to Uttam Bhlon Lama from the Independent Power Producers' Association of Nepal.

He warns insurance premiums are rising significantly and making the cost of doing business "unfeasible".

News.title: Oasis fans say cryptic codes in chip shop video point to Glasgow gigs next year
News.content:
Oasis fans have uncovered a set of cryptic clues in a promo video from the band, suggesting that they will stage gigs at Celtic Park in Glasgow next year.

The Manchester rockers released the 23-second teaser on their social media accounts, showing two boys in what appears to be a Scottish chip shop.

Internet sleuths spotted sets of numbers in posters around the chippy which they worked out to be the map co-ordinates for Celtic's Parkhead stadium.

It has fuelled speculation that the band will be playing at the venue next year- possibly as the first date of a new tour.

It follows the Gallagher brothers' hugely successful reunion tour which saw them perform at 41 sold-out stadium shows in 14 countries.

This included three dates at Murrayfield Stadium, Edinburgh, in August 2025, when they played to 200,000 fans.

News.title: How the hunger for a new weight loss drug is feeding an industry of fakes
News.content:
Excitement around the creation of a new drug, especially one showing early promise in clinical trials, is often celebrated by those developing it.

But new weight-loss drug retatrutide has become a headache not only for Eli Lilly, the pharmaceutical company behind it, but for regulators in the UK and around the world.

The jab has not yet been approved for human use by any regulatory body.

But illicit, counterfeit dupes of retatrutide are currently flooding the black market.

Experts have told the BBC this is one of the first times they have seen copycat versions of an experimental drug, still in the throes of being tested, become so widely available.

Vials purporting to be "reta" as it's become known, are being sold in the UK in gyms, nail and beauty salons, hairdressers, on social media and even by flower sellers on the street.

"The world has gone mad," pharmacist and director of 24 HR Pharmacy, Sehar Shahid says. "People are effectively injecting an illegal drug and thinking it's safe.

"It's become so normalised people openly talk about their dealers, where's best to get it from and post all over social media."

One quick flick through my socials and I can order a batch of a drug billed as retatrutide in minutes - although I would have no proof what it's actually made of, what its effects would be and where it's come from.

Keen users are posting before and after "reta" pics on their TikTok feeds, describing how it has silenced food noise, helped them shed pounds and lose inches, with some saying it's completely transformed their lives.

The problem? Despite positive results in its most recent clinical trials, real retatrutide is still being tested for its safety and efficacy.

Only 50% of drugs in this Phase III stage of testing in the US are eventually approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), so there is no guarantee retatrutide will ever hit the market. The high rate of failure is primarily down to drugs not working as well in large, diverse human populations as they do in smaller early tests, or because they reveal unexpected safety hazards.

And the current, fake versions available may not resemble what's being developed in the safe confines of the laboratory.

News.title: Woman whose XL bully dog killed her cousin given suspended prison sentence
News.content:
A woman has been given a suspended prison sentence after her XL bully dog attacked and killed her cousin.

Kelcie Reed, 24, of Bristol, previously admitted being in charge of a dog dangerously out control, causing the death of Morgan Dorsett.

The 19-year-old, from Shrewsbury, died from neck injuries caused by the attack, which happened at Reed's flat in south Bristol in February 2025.

At Bristol Crown Court, Judge Anna Richardson sentenced Reed to 18 weeks in prison, suspended for 18 months. She will also be required to undergo mental health treatment.

Emergency services were called to the dog attack at a flat in Cobhorn Drive, Bishopsworth, but despite their best efforts, Morgan died from bites to her neck and face, a post-mortem examination ruled.

The dog, named Prince, which belonged to Reed and her boyfriend, was sedated at the scene and later "humanely destroyed", police said.

News.title: Stock up on food to prepare for extreme weather, minister says
News.content:
Households should stock up on food to prepare for extreme weather as the strongest El NiÃ±o event in a generation develops over the Pacific Ocean, a government minister has said.

Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle told the Guardian the powerful natural climate phenomenon will lead to "more extreme storms in this country".

Her comments came as the National Audit Office (NAO) warned Britain's food supply chain is at risk given the growing threat of cyber-attacks and the climate crisis.

The NAO said the government was too reliant on the private sector to deal with food supply disruption. The government is due to unveil a strategy about preparing for national emergencies later this year.

Dame Angela said, external: "We're about to experience probably the largest El NiÃ±o that has ever been seen, and that will lead to drier summers, wetter winters, with more extreme storms in this country.

"It will do a lot more damage in Asia with flooding, and therefore I think that we need to take it seriously.

"If you've got a store of a bit of food that can keep you going for a while before the emergency services can get to you, you're going to be a lot better off than if you haven't.

"So some of it is that kind of preparation for just being a bit more resilient."

Her comments came as an NAO report warned Britain's food supply chain is vulnerable to plant or human disease outbreaks, cyber-attacks and extreme weather.

It also cited climate change as a longer-term chronic risk which could leave Britain's food supply at risk.

The disruptions could push up prices and leave vulnerable people struggling to buy food, it said.

The NAO said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) was too reliant on private companies to handle disruptions to food supply.

It added the department had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience.

UK households are less prepared for emergencies than those in several other countries such as Finland, Sweden and European Union nations, the NAO added.

It said ministers should encourage households to prepare for supply chain disruptions and learn from the approaches taken by other countries.

News.title: The Grand Tour's new presenters: 'I hope we prove the critics wrong'
News.content:
For more than two decades, Top Gear and The Grand Tour were defined as much by the three men presenting them as by the cars they drove.

Jeremy Clarkson, Richard Hammond and James May built one of television's most recognisable partnerships, meaning anyone taking over The Grand Tour was always going to face a daunting task.

Now YouTubers James Engelsman and Thomas Holland and, perhaps most unexpectedly, train enthusiast-turned-internet star Francis Bourgeois are stepping into their shoes for the new series.

And, with initial reviews generally mixed, they knew they had some convincing to do.

"They literally changed the car world," Holland says of the previous trio.

He understands why some fans have questions about whether the show should continue with anyone else.

"They're completely justified to feel that, because they did the same thing that we did - which is grow up watching Clarkson, Hammond and May.

"The show was a very important part of our lives as car enthusiasts."

News.title: Rock stars gather on tiny island for Scotland's quirkiest sporting challenge
News.content:
Contenders from around the world are converging on a tiny Scottish island for one of the country's most unlikely international sporting events - the world stone skimming championships.

The annual contest on the isle of Easdale, in the Inner Hebrides, has attracted a record number of international entries, representing more than 30 nations, with some flying in from New Zealand and Canada.

Last year's competition was rocked by a cheating scandal after some contestants were accused of stone tampering.

Toss Master Kyle Mathews, co-organiser of the event, said an official tournament geologist had been appointed this year, leaving no stone unturned in keeping the 400 challengers in order.

The contest was first held in 1983, inspired by an alcohol-fuelled conversation in a pub, and has been held every year since 1997 apart from an interlude during Covid.

Traditionally a male-dominated sport, efforts have been made to make it more inclusive, with this year's event attracting a record number of women and under-16s.

News.title: Clock starts ticking on race to buy Scotland's 'forgotten Einstein' church
News.content:
The move follows a meeting in the village earlier this week where it was decided to push ahead with the plans.

A steering group has been set up along with a fundraising page.

Community council chairman Paul Hodson said they were optimistic that they could gather the funds needed to meet the deadline agreed with the Church of Scotland.

"Several individuals and families in the village have already pledged to donate," he said.

"So we are hopeful that with wider help we will be able to meet our target, hovever the deadline of 1 November gives us less than 60 days to do so."

He said that if they were successful in their plans it could have a major impact on the area.

"If we do manage to secure the building this will give us hope that the project to celebrate the life and work of this great scientist can become a vibrant centre and help reverse the slow rural decline of communities like ours and provide a boost for the whole region," he added.

News.title: Transgender surgery halted over concerns patients were not properly assessed
News.content:
Gender-affirming surgery was halted because of concerns from an NHS committee over whether patients had been "appropriately assessed".

After meeting Welsh government ministers on Friday the NHS Wales Joint Commissioning Committee (NWJCC) said data showed the rate of surgery referrals made by the Welsh Gender Service was "significantly higher" than in England.

It also said the proportion of Welsh patients progressing from referral for some types of surgery was "significantly lower" than across the border.

The NWJCC is the body which instructed Cardiff and Vale University Health Board to halt new referrals and planned surgeries.

The health board is responsible for the running of the NHS gender identity clinic which provides specialist care and support for adults in Wales.

It confirmed on Tuesday that some patients who had been awaiting gender-affirming surgery were already in hospital for their procedures when they were told of the suspension.

The Welsh Gender Service provides referrals for patients living in Wales, but all NHS surgeries are carried out in England.

Gender-affirming surgery includes both masculinising and feminising procedures. They are not reversible.

News.title: Controversial Jackdaw gas field set to be approved in weeks, sources say
News.content:
The UK government is set to give the go-ahead for a controversial new gas field off the coast of Aberdeen, the BBC understands.

Approval for the Jackdaw project could come in mid-September, just before Parliament breaks for party conference season, according to government and industry sources.

The gas field was approved by the former Conservative government in 2022 but was delayed by a legal ruling from a Scottish court, after environmental groups argued consent was given without fully considering the climate impact.

Jackdaw's owner says it will account for 6% of UK gas output when at peak production but environmental groups say it will provide only 2% of UK use when imports are included.

Campaigners launched legal challenges after Jackdaw was approved in 2022 and when the Rosebank oil field off Shetland was given the green light in 2023.

The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that Rosebank and Jackdaw had been unlawfully approved because the government had failed to take into account the climate impact of burning extracted oil and gas from the sites.

A judge ruled that more detailed climate assessments had to be published, and further estimates were put out for consultation in July.

News.title: Man who died near Notting Hill Carnival is named
News.content:
A man who died after jumping into a canal while fleeing from police near Notting Hill Carnival has been named.

Karnell Kelly, 25, died in hospital after entering the Grand Union Canal off Kensal Road, west London, while being pursued by police officers.

He had fled on foot after the officers attempted to stop him near Harrow Road as he approached the carnival wearing a face covering at about 15:20 BST on Monday, the Metropolitan Police said.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), which is investigating, said it was reviewing body-worn video from officers who had chased Kelly down Hormead Road.

Officers and members of the public entered the canal to pull him from the water and he was rushed to a central London hospital, where he was pronounced dead at about 16:40.

News.content:

Four people were killed and two were critically injured in an auto wreck when a car veered off a mountain road near Wrightwood, California, early on Friday.

"For unknown reasons, the vehicle swerved away from the roadway, struck a telephone pole and rolled down an embankment. At that time, four parties were ejected from the vehicle," California Highway Patrol Officer Thaniel Ong told ABC 7.

The crash, which was called in around 1:30am, occurred on Highway 2, between Big Pines and Wrightwood, near the LA-San Bernardino County line.

Most of those inside the 2016 Hyundai Veloster were not wearing seat belts and alcohol is thought to be a contributing factor to the crash, according to officials.

According to CHP, all six people involved in the crash are from Wrightwood, a town of about 5,000 people in the mountains north of Los Angeles.

Four people were killed and two were seriously injured in a rollover crash in the mountains north of Los Angeles early Friday morning ( ABC7 screengrab )

The dead include two women and two men.

Responding to the scene involved a complicated rescue process because most of the occupants were scattered outside the car and responders didn’t know how many people had been inside, Chris Prater, a public information officer for the San Bernardino County Fire Department, told The Los Angeles Times.

Upon searching the scene, responders found five people had been ejected from the car, and a sixth person, who had been wearing a seat belt, took it off and exited the vehicle.

Four people were confirmed dead on the scene, while two were flown by air ambulances to Arrowhead Regional Medical Center in Colton in critical condition.

“The CHP reminds all motorists and passengers that seat belts save lives,” the agency told the paper. “Wearing a seat belt is the single most effective action a person can take to protect themselves in the event of a traffic collision.”

“Impaired driving is illegal, dangerous, and entirely preventable,” the statement added. “If you plan to consume alcohol, designate a sober driver, use a rideshare service, or contact a friend or family member.”

The closely watched case of the Massachusetts mother who killed her three young children was on the verge of being declared a mistrial Friday — but there was still one more dramatic moment to come.

After weeks of grueling testimony, the jury could not get beyond an impasse on the seventh day of deliberations on murder charges against Lindsay Clancy. An audible gasp was heard in the courtroom as Judge William F. Sullivan said he was going to to end their deliberations without reaching a verdict.

But just as the jurors were about to come back to the courtroom, Lindsay Clancy’s lawyer asked to make a last-minute request for a higher court to stave off the mistrial. That kicked off a tense wait while a judge on the state’s top court considered the ask.

The whiplash moment was one last piece of courtroom drama in a livestreamed trial that captivated and divided many across the nation. And now prosecutors must decide whether to do it all over again with a second trial.

Ultimately on Friday, the high court denied the defense attorney's appeal and the judge formally declared a mistrial later in the afternoon. Clancy's attorney, Kevin Reddington, blamed a lone juror for the impasse. Defense attorneys argued in their written petition that the person had revealed a possible bias against those dealing with mental illness.

Clancy, a 36-year-old former labor and delivery nurse, never disputed that she killed her children, but her attorney said she was experiencing a rare condition called postpartum psychosis when she strangled her kids, the youngest just 8 months old, and then tried to take her own life in 2023. Prosecutors said Clancy knew what she was doing and should be held criminally responsible.

The jury foreperson had previously told Sullivan that a single juror wouldn’t follow the court’s instruction about reasonable doubt, according to Reddington.

In their last-minute appeal, Clancy’s lawyers had argued the juror should, at minimum, be questioned more thoroughly by the judge, or even dismissed outright before a mistrial was declared. Prosecutors responded that there was nothing in the jury’s notes indicating the juror in question had “a lack of impartiality, bias, extraneous influence, or inability to deliberate.”

Jurors had heard competing expert testimony about Clancy’s mental health.

Massachusetts defense attorney Joseph Perullo, who was not involved in the case, said it was “clear cut” for him, but he acknowledged that jurors could have difficulties.

“It’s clear that Lindsay had a psychotic break, and the psychotic break led her to kill her children,” he said. “But the prosecution can tell you that she sent her husband off for errands and therefore she is criminally responsible.”

Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz said after the mistrial was declared there would not be an immediate decision on whether to go forward with a second trial.

Perullo said he is hopeful prosecutors will speak to Patrick Clancy, the children's father, and other family.

“It is a tremendous stress on them to do it again, and it's going to be an even bigger circus,” he said.

But Crystal Lyons, a former prosecutor in Massachusetts, believes prosecutors don't have the option not to retry Lindsay Clancy.

“At the end of the day, it was a tragedy where there were three young children who lost their lives,” she said.

The trial to decide if Lindsay Clancy was criminally responsible when she strangled her three children in 2023 ended in a mistrial Friday after jurors were unable to reach a consensus after weeks of conflicting testimony about her post-pregnancy mental health and seven days of deliberations.

What happens now?

Clancy, a 36-year-old former labor and delivery nurse, remains charged with murder and will continue to be held in a psychiatric hospital until the case is resolved. Attorneys on both sides have a few options when it comes to the next steps.

A hearing later this month could determine the path forward

Judge William Sullivan set a hearing for Sept. 29. During that proceeding, defense attorney Kevin Reddington will likely ask the judge to declare Clancy not guilty. It’s a long shot move and very unlikely to succeed.

That hearing could also reveal whether prosecutors will move to put Clancy on trial for a second time. They could also choose to seek a plea deal or even drop the case entirely, though that option is unlikely.

Sullivan suggested that everyone involved in the case, from attorneys to witnesses to court administrators, would need to look at their calendars to find a suitable time for a new trial, if one is held.

___

EDITOR’S NOTE: This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988.

___

Clancy doesn’t deny strangling her children at their home south of Boston, but says postpartum psychosis led to her actions. After the killings, her husband found her badly injured in the yard, where she landed after jumping from a second-story window. She was left paralyzed from the waist down.

Prosecutors argue she knew what she was doing.

Prosecutors will weigh many factors as they decide on a new trial

Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz said there would not be an immediate decision about a second trial, but he emphasized that his goal was always “getting justice for those three little babies.”

“This case was about Lindsay Clancy and what she did … the cruel and calculated killing of three innocents,” Cruz said shortly after court ended on Friday. He later continued, “Children were murdered and it’s our job to seek justice.”

Still, prosecutors typically consider a lot of things when determining whether to retry a case, said New York Law School Professor Heather Ellis Cucolo, including the potential expense and the likely outcome.

“I know the prosecutor stated openly that he would not allow public opinion to sway his decision, which is accurate, but the prosecution serves the public,” Cucolo said. “If it is believed that justice must be served by another trial, that is something the prosecutor’s office will take into account and weigh very heavily.”

A conviction could mean life in prison for Clancy, while an acquittal might lead to confinement in a mental health facility.

Clancy’s defense will likely push to drop the charges

Cucolo said the defense attorney will likely push for the charges to be dropped entirely, and might also be open to a plea deal.

“But if the prosecution chooses to move forward with a trial, there's no way to prevent that from happening,” Cucolo said.

Reddington said in court that he believed Clancy's constitutional rights were violated when the judge declined to remove one juror after the other jurors suggested that he was not following the judge's instructions on reasonable doubt. But a mistrial isn't subject to an appeal, Cucolo said, because it's not a final judgment.

The impact on family members is another consideration, said Randy Gioia, a Boston-based defense lawyer who formerly supervised public defenders across the state.

Gioia said prosecutors should not put Clancy through another trial. He said he accepts Reddington’s disclosure that Clancy was extremely close to an acquittal, based on a note presented to the judge by the jury foreperson.

“Why put everyone through the trauma again: 16 to 18 jurors, all the witnesses, Patrick Clancy,” Gioia said, referring to Lindsay Clancy’s former husband. “What’s to be served here when we’ve had a long trial and long deliberations? You don’t have a strong case. You almost lost the case.”

Attorneys on both sides could tweak their approach in a retrial

It's not clear exactly how the jury reached an impasse, but Reddington suggested that just one juror stood in the way of an acquittal, and said the other jurors were “robbed.”

“They know they were robbed by one man, for whatever his agenda was, who stole seven weeks of the life of these other jurors that were so attentive, so beautiful, so wonderful,” he said outside the courthouse. “You could see how defeated they were sitting there. I got a funny feeling they would have gone on for another week if they had to. So I hope that guy can sleep well at night.”

Jurors are under no obligation to speak to attorneys on either side of the case, but it's common for the attorneys to see if any are open to talking about their experience, Cucolo said. Prosecutors can then use any information they get to reassess and fine-tune their approach, she said, perhaps focusing more on specific evidence or witnesses.

A retrial would have rippling impacts

David Meier, a lawyer who represents Patrick Clancy in a lawsuit over her mental health treatment, released a statement about the emotional burden of the case, saying “there will never be closure” from the loss of the children.

“The prospect of reliving this tragedy through another trial is extraordinarily painful — for Patrick, for his family, and for all of us,” Meier said.

The statement didn’t indicate whether Patrick Clancy would support a second trial.

Lindsay Clancy has also filed a lawsuit over her mental health treatment. A retrial would likely force those civil cases to be put on hold, Cucolo said.

“They would not be able to move forward for now because of concerns of possible Fifth Amendment violations,” Cucolo said, because anything Clancy says in a civil case could potentially be used against her in the criminal case. That means the lawsuits could remain in legal limbo for a year or more, she said.

___ Associated Press reporters Dave Collins, Michael Casey, Ed White and Leah Willingham contributed.

Carlos Alcaraz covered his modesty as he cruised into the fourth round of the US Open.

The Spaniard’s baggy sleeveless top has been raising eyebrows this week as it occasionally revealed a nipple during matches.

The sight even prompted former player-turned-pundit Genie Bouchard to post on social media: “Love you Carlos but we’ve got to put the nip away.”

open image in gallery Alcaraz wore a vest to cover his modesty at Flushing Meadows (Kirsty Wigglesworth/AP) ( AP )

So Alcaraz fixed his malfunctioning wardrobe by wearing a skin-tight vest underneath as he beat China’s Wu Yibing 6-3 6-4 6-1 in a two hours and 19 minutes.

The 23-year-old said: “Well, I think I saw my nipple too much lately. I felt like, you know, I could hide it for at least once match.

“I feel really comfortable, you know, with another shirt. So I think I’m going to stay like that.

“Maybe, you know, the second round was, a little bit distracting for me, but not that much.”

Alcaraz, back to defend his title after four months out with a wrist injury, has surprised himself with how well he is playing.

“I think today was a really high rhythm, the way he played was unbelievable,” he added.

“I played aggressive, I played smart in the toughest moments which I’m really happy about. I did everything good. Could be better, but I’m proud of the performance today.

“To be honest I’m better than I thought. I thought I would be dead after the first match, but I’m recovering really well. Right now my level is really good.”

In the fourth round Alcaraz will play American Tommy Paul, the former Queen’s Club champion, who came through a titanic five-setter with Kazakhstan’s Alexander Bublik.

“He’s going to play at home which is going to be an advantage for him,” added Alcaraz. “But hopefully he will be a bit tired from today’s match.”

Russian seventh seed Daniil Medvedev beat France’s Arthur Rinderknech 6-4 6-4 6-4 while, in the women’s draw, third-seeded American Jessica Pegula recovered from a disastrous first set to knock out former runner-up Leylah Fernandez 1-6 6-4 6-3.

The United Nations General Assembly on Friday endorsed a new world map that represents Africa more accurately in its larger size, a culmination of a recent campaign led by African countries and advocacy groups.

Friday’s resolution, which was sponsored by Togo and backed by members of the African Union, was passed with 164 member states voting in favor. Only the U.S. voted against it while six other countries — Serbia, Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova and Ukraine — abstained.

The vote encourages governments and institutions around the world to replace the traditional Mercator map, commonly used since the 16th Century, with the Equal Earth projection that advocates and geographers say shows locations more accurately.

The Mercator projection shows Greenland and Africa as appearing to be about the same size whereas in the Equal Earth projection that shows continents in their true proportions, Africa is 14 times larger than Greenland.

Friday’s resolution does not ban the Mercator projection or impose a replacement, but only encourages the use of the Equal Earth projection, the U.N. said in its report.

“Maps shape our understanding of the world,” the global body quoted Togo’s Foreign Minister Robert Dussey as saying before the vote. “They guide education, nourish the imagination, and influence collective perceptions.”

Africa No Filter, one of the lead campaigners for the adoption of the new map, hailed the resolution, adding: “We want to see accurate maps in schools, textbooks, newsrooms, businesses and on the digital platforms billions of people use every day.”

Several countries hailed the adoption and urged the adoption of the Equal Earth map. “Changing the map obviously doesn’t change the world. But correcting a representation that distorts it is already an act of truth,” French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said on X after the vote.

The Mercator map was designed by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator to help European navigators at sea, but advocates say it distorted landmasses by enlarging regions near the poles such as North America and Greenland while shrinking Africa and South America.

The 2018 Equal Earth projection, on the other hand, follows the Earth’s curvature and shows continents in their true proportions.

Geographers say the traditional map is only useful for navigation.

“Outside of that very narrow navigation application, there is no point in using it,” according to Mark Monmonier, a Syracuse University professor of geography.

Simon Cowell’s recent back surgery was a “success”, according to his fellow America's Got Talent judge Howie Mandel.

Cowell, 66, has undergone a series of operations in recent years after he broke his back in an electric bike accident in 2020.

Speaking to E! News on Thursday, September 3, 70-year-old Mandel revealed that at that point Cowell was “just hours out of surgery”.

He added: “I heard that it was a success, everything’s okay.”

Kenan Thompson filled in for Cowell on the talent show this week, with Heidi Klum set to take his place next week.

'America's Got Talent' judges Simon Cowell and Howie Mandel together in 2022 ( Vivien Killilea/Getty Images for Cold Stone Creamery )

Mandel joked that he hadn’t yet spoken to Cowell because: “I don't know that, this close to surgery, if this is the first thing you need to see.”

The comedian added that he “can't wait to see him and visit him and give him my best wishes.”

Cowell’s injuries stopped him from appearing in the 2020 season of Britain’s Got Talent. He was temporarily replaced by the show’s previous winner Ashley Banjo.

After he recovered, Cowell said he was “lucky to survive” the ordeal. He told OK! magazine in 2022: “I didn’t talk about it too much at the time. I kept a lot back. It was a lot worse than people thought. I had a lot of long-term nerve damage as well.”

He admitted: “If there was one good thing about lockdown, it was that it gave me the time to heal because I wasn’t working on a TV show. I was able to walk a lot and strengthen my legs.”

In 2022, the TV personality had another e-bike crash that saw him hospitalized with a broken arm, badly bruised cheek and possible concussion. However, the injuries were not as serious as his first accident and he was released from the hospital that same day.

Cowell is known for his brutally honest judging style on reality competitions like AGT, The X Factor and American Idol. He is also hailed as a successful talent scout, having put together massive acts like One Direction and Fifth Harmony.

AGT’s current season 21 marks Cowell’s eleventh season as a judge on the show, although he has been an executive producer since the show’s creation in 2006.

Hosted by Terry Crews, the show usually features Cowell alongside fellow judges Sofía Vergara, Howie Mandel and Mel B.

The final competition and the finale episode will air September 22 and 23.

NFL career rushing leader Emmitt Smith is being sued by a Native American investment company over claims that the former Dallas Cowboys running back and his business partners misappropriated a $2.5 million loan that was supposed to fund a wind farm project in Texas.

Kituwah LLC claimed in a lawsuit filed this week in Delaware that 4 13 Solutions used the money to repay an investor from previous dealings with Smith's company. Kituwah seeks to invest in business opportunities for the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians.

Kituwah's attorneys said Smith and the Pro Football Hall of Famer's longtime business partner, David Mosley, misrepresented their efforts to secure a U.S. Department of Energy loan that would have triggered repayment to Kituwah.

Kituwah claims the loan has accrued about $600,000 in interest and is asking a jury to determine damages. A message sent to 4 13 Solutions wasn't immediately returned. There was no information on an attorney for Smith or his company in the filing.

According to the lawsuit, Darrel Wilson of Wilson Holdings of North America LLC told Kituwah that he accepted a $2.5 million payment from Smith's company and said he didn't know what triggered the payment. Kituwah's attorneys said it was, “Essentially, like a ponzi scheme.”

Kituwah claims Wilson Holdings was supposed to be repaid only after the wind farm project between Austin and San Antonio, called Project Exodus, secured permanent financing.

“Smith and Mosley knew this was improper,” the lawsuit said. “Instead of telling the truth, they represented to Kituwah that 4 13 Solutions had used the money to acquire Project Exodus as promised, but that the acquisition had been held up for one reason or another.”

The lawsuit claims Smith and his partners never met the requirements for securing government funding and repeatedly made excuses for why the project wasn't proceeding or stopped responding to requests.

Kituwah said it delivered the funds on Sept. 1, 2023, with the expectation of being paid back within months. The lawsuit said 4 13 Solutions promised the wind farm would be operational by December 2024, but Kituwah had seen no evidence the project even existed just a month before that date.

Kituwah said Smith and his partners claimed the wind farm project was valued at $396 million and would generate nearly $14 million in net income in its first year.

The 57-year-old Smith spent the first 13 of his 15 seasons with the Cowboys, won three championships and was the MVP of Super Bowl 28. He broke Walter Payton's rushing record in 2002 and finished with 18,355 yards.

Lawyers for Maria Bartiromo have rejected reports that the anchor has been terminated or has left Fox News Media, calling the claims inaccurate and threatening potential legal action.

Bryan Freedman, an attorney representing Bartiromo, told The Independent that his client remained with the company despite reports surrounding her status.

“For many years, Maria Bartiromo hosted three number-one-rated television shows on Fox channels,” Freedman said.

“She has been, without question, one of the hardest-working journalists throughout her award-winning career. The irresponsible reports that have been published stating that Maria Bartiromo was fired or is no longer an employee of Fox are absolutely and unequivocally false.

“Make no mistake, we have the receipts and witnesses and they will come out whether through the courthouse or otherwise. Those reporting her firing or the incredulous facts supporting that fiction have exhibited a complete and utter reckless disregard for the truth.”

open image in gallery An attorney for Maria Bartiromo pushed back on reports that she was fired or left Fox News Media, dismissing the claims as false and raising the prospect of legal action ( AFP/Getty )

Freedman, a high-profile media lawyer who previously handled high-stakes separations for figures including Megyn Kelly, Chris Cuomo, Tucker Carlson and Don Lemon, issued the statement following widespread coverage of Bartiromo’s abrupt absence from the network.

The dispute follows a brief announcement from Fox News Media stating that the network was parting ways with the long-time presenter after 12 and a half years, thanking her for her work, and wishing her the best in future endeavors.

Reporting by media watchdog Status subsequently alleged that Bartiromo was let go after sharing an internal company guidance with the Trump administration. The internal directive reportedly instructed network personnel to avoid amplifying unsubstantiated election claims made by Donald Trump during a speech.

Reports also indicated that Bartiromo’s top producer, Patrick Ignozzi, was no longer with the network.

The sudden shift led to swift reactions across political and media circles. Trump defended the host on Truth Social, calling her a “total professional” and a “true warrior.” Eric Trump praised her as “the hardest-working person in media” in a post on X, calling the departure a major loss for the network.

open image in gallery Donald Trump praised his long-time ally as a ‘true warrior’ while rumors circulated that she could be considered for a White House role ( Reuters )

Fox has already moved to adjust its program lineup. Mornings with Maria on Fox Business is being rebranded as Mornings with Fox Business with rotating anchors. Maria Bartiromo’s Wall Street has been renamed Fox Business Network’s Wall Street, hosted this week by Cheryl Casone, and Jason Chaffetz was tapped to host Sunday Morning Futures.

Speculation briefly linked Bartiromo to a potential role within the White House following the departure of former press secretary Karoline Leavitt. However, reporting from Vanity Fair indicated she was not pursuing a position in the administration.

Throughout her tenure, Bartiromo remained a prominent conservative media voice and frequent interviewer of Trump. During an April broadcast, Trump told her he was “very surprised” crude oil prices were at $92 a barrel, adding, “it’s going to come dropping down very big as soon as it's over.”

In another notable broadcast, Bartiromo mistakenly cited a parody post as authentic, telling former Representative Dan Crenshaw, “I love the way the president handled it because, congressman, he put out a tweet... The president had fun with that!”

News.title: Alexander Isak finally starts to justify £125m price tag with fine double
News.content:
Emersonn, Ipswich’s Brazilian striker, did not see the ball in the opening exchanges and, by the time he did, Liverpool had zoomed into the distance to such an extent that you felt it was going to be impossible for them to peg their visitors back.

“I hate having to talk about good performances when you do not get points,” O’Neil declared to a room full of raised eyebrows and you can only assume his message was to ensure that morale in the dressing room was not drooping.

What damage was inflicted with Liverpool’s first significant attack. Gakpo, the subject of an £80m bid from Manchester City, was never going to allow transfer speculation to disrupt his focus and he nudged a perfect little ball into Isak’s path in the sixth minute to show his wellbeing.

The next move announced the return of Isak. One touch gave him an avenue to shoot, the next was a shot with his right foot that was so hard from 16 yards, on an angle, it bent the wrists of Kjell Scherpen as it howled into the net. Critics will feel Ipswich’s keeper should have done better.

Your first thought was to think of the first goal Isak scored in English football in September 2022, a similarly venomous drive, against Liverpool at Anfield. He oozed quality that evening, his pace and skill had Jürgen Klopp’s defenders persistently fretting and this is what he was doing again.

It was no coincidence that three minutes later, he came up with another wonderful goal. This one owed much to the beautiful pass Gakpo presented to him, an inch-perfect through ball with the outside of his right foot, but Isak still showed great poise to bamboozle Scherpen.

News.title: Forced displacement in the West Bank could be ‘crime against humanity’, says UN report
News.content:
Israel’s forced displacement of more than 33,000 Palestinians in the West Bank could amount to a “crime against humanity” and involves “ethnic cleansing”, according to a report published by the UN.

A report by the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) said that Israeli actions in the area had sparked the “largest and longest displacement crisis in the West Bank since 1967” – the year in which Israel captured the territory.

The report said “large-scale, long-term and systematic displacement of over 33,000 Palestinians from refugee camps … during Israel’s Operation Iron Wall [which] raises serious concerns of the crime against humanity of forcible transfer”.

It added: “The documented use of airstrikes, armoured bulldozers and controlled detonations, to render entire camps uninhabitable, to force the displacement of their residents and to prevent their return, in the absence of imperative military necessity to justify such destruction and displacement, are not permissible under international law, appear to amount to collective punishment and raise concerns of ethnic cleansing.”

The 27-page report covers the period December 5, 2024 to January 31, 2026.

In January 2025, Israeli forces launched “Operation Iron Wall” in the northern West Bank in a bid to counter what they said were terrorist threats.

They destroyed hundreds of homes, cut off water and electricity, and barred humanitarian access to the Jenin, Nur Sham and Tulkarm refugee camps.

By October 2025, 52 per cent of structures in Jenin camp, 48 per cent in Nur Shams and 36 percent in Tulkarm had been destroyed or damaged.

The three camps are among 19 in the West Bank established to shelter Palestinians after the 1948 Nakba, and are administered by the UN Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA).

Although still referred to as refugee camps, they are in fact now densely packed towns.

News.title: When is Black Friday 2026? This year’s dates and what to expect
News.content:
Five tips for finding genuine Black Friday discounts and deals

Learning how to find the best Black Friday discounts can make a meaningful difference to your festive budget, especially if you’re a keen sale shopper. The following five tips are a good starting point.

1. Don’t over-fixate on Black Friday itself

Although the day of Black Friday brings some of the best discounts of the festive sale season, good deals are likely to be available both before and after it – and some items may sell out.

“When we look at our pricing data on a daily level, you have certain events such as Amazon’s October Prime sale [not yet confirmed for 2026] that are an earlier vector for change in prices,” says Vivek Pandya, a director at Adobe for Business.

“We typically see more significant discounts starting to emerge as we get into late October or early November, and these really kick up a notch as we get into Black Friday week.”

So, while interest in Black Friday deals will peak around the day itself, some of the best deals may have been available since the beginning of the week, or earlier.

2. Expand your search to everyday essentials

At Telegraph Recommended, we’ve picked up on a proliferation of discounts on everyday household items during recent Black Friday sales (and during other occasional events such as Prime Day). If you need a top-up of items such as cleaning products or pet supplies, this could be a thrifty time to buy them.

“These sales have become a spending spree on what retailers frame as ‘everyday essentials’, as well as bigger items and gifts,” says Pandya. Last year’s Cyber Weekend saw a 260 per cent spike in sales of “personal care” items including cosmetics, shampoos, fragrances and toothbrushes, according to Adobe.

3. Use a price tracker

Free price tracking tools such as camelcamelcamel can show you how the price of a product has changed over time. This allows you to identify when a Black Friday deal has actually brought a product’s price significantly lower than usual, or when the retailer’s pricing strategy has artificially made a deal appear to be generous.

Gabrielė Vitkė, product marketing team lead at data-gathering specialist Decodo, warns shoppers to watch out for “anchoring”, where a product’s price is set high prior to Black Friday, allowing the retailer then to reduce it sharply and advertise an eye-catching reduction.

“Discounts on items such as electronics and computing products can seem steep, sometimes exceeding 50 per cent against the list price,” says Vitkė. “However, our data shows that prices in this category rose in the run-up to Black Friday 2025, which is a sign of anchor pricing before the ‘discount’ is applied.”

News.title: Indonesia wildfires trigger 50,000 respiratory infections
News.content:
More than 50,000 people have contracted respiratory infections in Indonesia, as raging wild fires blanket huge swathes of the country in a thick, toxic smoke.

The vast archipelago is only a month into its fire season, but intense blazes have proven hard to control across Sumatra and Indonesian Borneo. There are fears the situation will only get worse, because the “Godzilla” El Niño is set to suppress rains that would normally have helped extinguish the flames.

“Our problems are not over. September is the peak of El Niño,” said Raja Juli Antoni, the forestry minister. “September is the main fight for us.”

Already the toxic haze has spread across Southeast Asia. On Friday Kuching, a city in Malaysian Borneo, was the most polluted city in the world on the IQ Air Index, followed by Jakarta and Singapore.

The wildfires have brought memories of record-breaking blazes in 2015. Then, the smoke was linked to roughly 100,000 excess deaths in Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore, according to one study. The World Bank said Indonesia alone saw economic losses of $16.1bn, or 2 per cent of GDP.

News.title: Global hunger is a threat to Britain’s national security, report says
News.content:
Global hunger poses a direct threat to Britain’s national security, and tackling it should be a government priority, a new report from the London School of Economics has warned.

It says hunger is a major driver of mass migration, extreme violence and war – events that threaten significant repercussions for Britain and Europe’s national security.

“Hunger prevention is an important part of national security policy, not an optional act of charity,” Stuart Gordon, professor of International Development at LSE and author of the report, told The Telegraph.

Recent hunger crises in places like Sudan, Afghanistan and across North Africa have contributed significantly to rising numbers of people moving to the West.

Between January and November 2025 alone, 12,684 migrants from Sudan – which is facing what has been described as the worst hunger crisis in Africa’s history – arrived in Europe, roughly three times as many as the previous year.

Last year, an estimated 155,000 African refugees arrived in Europe.

“Food insecurity tests one of the most basic expectations people have of government: that it will protect access to the essentials of life,” said Prof Gordon.

“Food price shocks can rapidly escalate into political instability when governments are perceived to have failed to protect access to basic subsistence goods,” he added.

News.title: Congo’s Ebola outbreak slows at epicentre but widens elsewhere, modelling suggests
News.content:
Congo’s Ebola outbreak shows signs of slowing at the epicentre of the flare-up, but is widening as the infection spreads further afield, modelling suggests.

The daily tally of new cases in Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) was falling at the end of August, but more cases were being found outside Ituri province, where the infection burst out.

Latest official figures say the outbreak has now killed more than 3,000 people out of over 6,100 confirmed cases, with the infection spreading faster than any previous epidemic of the viral haemorrhagic fever.

Modelling by Airfinity, a health analytics firm, suggests the true toll of cases could be more than four times higher than reported.

The outbreak remains on track to eclipse the 2014 West Africa outbreak later this month, to become the largest ever recorded.

Airfinity said that data from late August showed the seven-day averages of reported cases and reported deaths had fallen by 16 per cent and 18 per cent respectively.

The firm said it was “too early to confirm the decline will hold, and it may mask subnational variation: The outbreak has fluctuated before and a week of falling case and death counts does not rule out another surge.

“Even if the decline continues at this current pace, low case levels remain weeks away.”

News.title: Bank of England must raise interest rates, says chief economist
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. Government borrowing costs edged lower on Thursday as Andy Burnham continues to face scrutiny over the public finances.

The yield on 10-year US treasury bonds – considered a benchmark for what governments pay to borrow money – declined slightly to 4.78pc on Thursday after a drop in oil prices.

Pre-market trading of bonds in Britain, France and Germany suggested the market was poised to rally after a brutal first half of the week.

However, Mr Burnham and Chancellor John Healey remain under intense pressure, with analysts estimating that as much as half of the country’s fiscal headroom has been wiped out by the jump in bond yields.

Borrowing costs surged after a jump in oil prices caused by fresh strikes between the US and Iran.

The yield on 10-year gilts, as UK bonds are known, hit levels not seen since the global financial crisis in 2007, while longer-term debt costs hit their highest point since 1998.

It means the Chancellor will have less room for manoeuvre in the Budget next month, with some economists predicting the rise in borrowing costs has wiped out up to £14bn of breathing room.

The rise in bond yields across major economies had deepened concerns about deteriorating financial conditions.

Central banks in the US and Europe are increasingly expected to raise interest rates this month to combat inflation caused by the Iran war, although the Bank of England is expected to hold rates steady for now.

Gavin Friend, an analyst at NAB, said: “If this war ‌were to be ‌put to bed, then that ⁠would certainly be something very positive to bring yields back down again across the board.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

What happened overnight

Oil prices slipped, helping boost stocks and bonds.

Renewed fighting between the US and Iran pushed oil prices sharply higher earlier in the week.

However, Brent crude was trading near $94 a barrel after Donald Trump said he does not expect the US bombing campaign to last “much longer”.

Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 advanced 0.2pc to 64,455.83. Among major gainers, OpenAI investor SoftBank Group rose 2.9pc, memory chipmaker Kioxia rose 0.6pc, and chip equipment manufacturer Tokyo Electron gained 0.8pc.

South Korea’s Kospi rose 1.4pc to 6,656.81. Samsung was 1.3pc higher, while memory chipmaker SK Hynix was up 1.4pc.

In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng edged 0.1pc higher, to 25,344.80. The Shanghai Composite index climbed 0.4pc to 3,958.79.

Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.5pc to 9,025.10.

The Taiex in Taiwan rose 0.6pc, while India’s Sensex climbed 0.3pc.

It comes after Wall Street bounced back after its sharp sell-off at the start of September, as investors snapped up shares that had fallen in recent days.

The S&P 500 rose, with almost 350 companies ending higher. Dell was among the biggest winners, jumping 14pc after giving an upbeat outlook, while investors were also looking ahead to results from chipmaker Broadcom.

The recovery came despite continued concerns over inflation, with oil prices remaining high as fighting between the US and Iran escalated. Brent crude briefly climbed close to $97 a barrel before easing back after Donald Trump said he did not expect the renewed bombing campaign to last “too long”.

US government bond yields were little changed after surging to their highest levels in several years earlier in the week.

Investors also got a mixed picture from the Federal Reserve’s latest assessment of the US economy. Economic activity increased modestly over the past two months, helped by strong demand from data centres, while companies added jobs at a slower pace in August.

The figures come ahead of Friday’s closely watched US jobs report, which could influence expectations for the next move in interest rates.

News.title: Weapons and mercenaries from foreign states fuelling Sudan’s war, UN report finds
News.content:
The war in Sudan is being fuelled by weapons and mercenaries from external states including the United Arab Emirates, Colombia and Turkey, a United Nations report has found.

An investigation by a UN fact-finding mission published on Thursday found that the supply of drones in particular to both sides in the civil war was extending the fighting’s reach and contributing to war crimes.

“Increasingly sophisticated drone capabilities [has] enabled both parties to strike far beyond immediate front lines”, says the report.

“The [UN] mission calls on States to enforce the Darfur arms embargo and suspend transfers of weapons, drones, components, or military assistance where there is a substantial risk of their use in serious violations”.

Sudan’s civil war erupted in April 2023 following a power struggle between the head of the military and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) as part of a planned transition to civilian rule. Hundreds of thousands have died and some 14 million people have been displaced in what has become the world’s deadliest conflict.

In a previous report in February, following the capture of El Fasher in which at least 60,000 people were killed, the UN said the RSF’s mass killings of Black African ethnic groups, including Zaghawa and Fur, bore the “hallmarks of genocide”.

The latest report said “individuals and entities” in the UAE were part of a transnational network supplying weapons, logistics, training and foreign personnel to the RSF – including NORINCO AH-4 howitzers, FK-20000 air defence systems and Chinese-made CH-95 strike drones.

The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), meanwhile, separately obtained Turkish-manufactured drones, including Bayraktar Akıncı combat drones and Yiha III loitering munitions.

The Turkish embassy in London has been contacted for comment.
