World.title: Canadian 'banking' company linked to sanctioned money-laundering network
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Maple Digital Financial Solutions describes itself as a "revolutionary banking" company, with an address in a skyscraper in the heart of Vancouver's financial district.

On paper, the company is registered with Canada’s financial intelligence agency, and offers "fast and easy" global currency transfers and "convenient banking" with the click of a button.

In practice, however, it’s a shell company. Its website offers no option to open an account and provides no employee names, while phone calls go straight to voicemail and emails go unanswered.

A CBC News visual investigation, in collaboration with the Centre for Information Resilience (CIR), reveals this shell company is closely linked to the TGR network, accused by international law enforcement of laundering billions of dollars for ransomware gangs, drug cartels and wealthy Russians.

"Red lights are flashing, there are a number of red flags here," said Denis Meunier, former deputy director at the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC), who reviewed the findings.

Maple Finance’s web site markets a 'revolutionary approach to banking solutions.' (Maple Finance)

A report by CIR, a U.K.-based research organization, used digital clues to connect Maple Digital Financial Solutions with a series of companies called The OneGate and the TGR network.

CBC shared its findings with multiple legal and financial experts, and each had a similar takeaway: Maple Digital Financial Solutions, also known as Maple Finance, is at "high risk" for suspicious activity.

Unlike traditional banks, money services businesses (MSB) such as Maple Finance already pose a threat of laundering illicit funds due to a lack of transparency and the fact that they don’t require an operating licence in many provinces.

This, coupled with ties to a sanctioned network and individuals known for money laundering, should put authorities in Canada on alert, said Meunier.

This graphic shows the connections between Carenoks, Zvigulis, Maple Finance, The OneGate and TGR. (Illustration: Froilan Untalasco/CBC)

TGR network: transnational money-laundering

The CIR report and the experts CBC News spoke to acknowledge there's no definitive proof of money laundering. But there are substantial digital clues that connect Maple to TGR — primarily Andrejs Carenoks, a Latvian sanctioned by the U.S. in 2024 for his role in a sophisticated money-laundering operation allegedly led by Yury Maksakov, a Ukrainian national born in Russia.

Carenoks, according to corporate records, was a director at Maple Finance in 2021.

The current director is Janis Zvigulis. He is also director of The OneGate and a registered director of TGR Wealth Solutions in the U.K., which was sanctioned in 2024.

Zvigulis has not been sanctioned.

Andrejs Carenoks's name appears in BC Registry records for Maple Finance. Carenoks was sanctioned by the U.S. in 2024. (Illustration: Froilan Untalasco/Daniel Rofusz/CBC; LinkedIn)

Authorities in the U.S. and U.K. described TGR as a full-service shadow financial hub, offering unregistered crypto exchanges , prepaid credit cards and sanctions evasion services, helping cybercriminals and drug traffickers.

For example, if a Russian cybercrime group held $1 million US in cryptocurrency paid by the victim of a ransomware attack and a drug gang in the U.K. had a similar amount in cash that needed to be laundered, TGR would arrange for the U.K. drug gang to be paid in crypto in exchange for their cash. The cash would then be laundered through a network of international business accounts.

Investigators at the U.K.’s National Crime Agency (NCA) have seen similar exchanges where cash handovers were followed almost immediately by the movement of a similar denomination of crypto.

Both Carenoks and Maksakov are accused of playing major roles in the TGR network, according to authorities in the U.K. and U.S.

"TGR is massive. It's really, really huge," said Elise Thomas, senior open-source investigator at CIR and author of the OneGate report. "To have Carenoks’s name on the actual company documents [for Maple Digital Financial Solutions], I think it's some really strong connections to TGR."

Janis Zvigulis is the current director of Maple Finance and TGR Wealth Solutions in the U.K. TGR Wealth Solutions was sanctioned in 2024. (Instagram)

CBC tried reaching out to Maple Finance and The OneGate through email and phone but did not receive a response.

The registered Vancouver address on the Maple Finance website led to Canadian business law firm Osler, Hoskin & Harcourt LLP.

In a call, Osler lawyer and partner Matthew Burgoyne said, "the Law Society code of conduct doesn't let us disclose who our clients are and who they're not. So, unfortunately, I wouldn't even be able to tell you if we acted for them or not."

CBC followed up via email requesting that the lawyer ask Maple Finance for comment on this story. The firm wrote in an email, "we cannot help with your story."

"I think it sort of underscores that this is not a normal business. Because normally, when you call the business, they answer," said Thomas. "And when you try to contact them through the channels that they've given to be contacted by customers, they would respond."

'Silent director'

CBC News reached out to Careneks, Zvigulis and Maksakov but did not receive a response.

Attempts were also made to reach former directors of Maple Digital Financial Solutions.

One of those former directors, Elen Kazarian, is based in Ontario. In an email, she told CBC News she was appointed as a "silent director" because the “owner and CEO of this company are foreigners I was told by my cousin — who knew these owners to help them to register this Corporation."

She said she didn’t do anything during her tenure as a director and wasn't paid.

Maple Digital Financial Solutions is part of a group of companies connected to The OneGate.

The financial network offers products such as virtual and physical payment cards, and services such as cryptocurrency trading through shell companies spread across at least seven jurisdictions, from the U.S. to Switzerland to Hong Kong.

"OneGate seems to be presenting [itself as a] payments service company that provides a number of different financial products and services," Thomas said. "Under the hood, there are all these deep historical connections to TGR, which obviously is accused of being a transnational money-laundering ring."

The TGR network was disrupted in 2024 after a three-year international probe led by the NCA codenamed Operation Destabilise. It was a global effort to dismantle a multibillion-dollar shadow banking and cryptocurrency network that laundered proceeds for violent drug cartels, ransomware gangs and Russian intelligence operations.

It resulted in 128 arrests worldwide and the seizure of more than $44 million Cdn in cash and digital assets.

A screen cap from a web page promoting Operation Destablise on the website of the U.K.'s National Crime Agency. (U.K. National Crime Agency)

The OneGate network was operating in parallel to TGR and started with a virtual office in Vancouver when Maple Finance was still called Fexcool Payments.

The CIR report further detailed the digital forensic connections. When it changed its name to Maple Digital Financial Solutions, it registered a website: maplefinance.ca .

Andrejs Carenoks was the one who registered that domain.

CIR found website registration records for maplefinance.ca showing Andrejs Carenoks’s name. (Illustration: Froilan Untalasco/CBC)

At the same time, Carenoks was the director of a TGR entity later sanctioned by the U.S.

The overlap between Maple Finance and TGR went beyond Carenoks. Archived records of that website show that Maple Finance listed a Toronto-area phone number also used by TGR Partners.

CIR used digital clues to discover Maple Finance had the same number as TGR Partners, a sanctioned entity. (Illustration: Froilan Untalasco/CBC)

Maple Finance provided clients with a branded payment card issued by OneCard — a service in part operated by TGR at the time.

Maple Digital Financial Solutions is named in TGR-connected OneCard and The OneGate. TGR is sanctioned by the U.S. and accused of being a money-laundering network by the U.K.’s National Crime Agency. (Illustration: Froilan Untalasco/CBC)

In 2023, Maple Finance became the acting primary legal entity behind The OneGate. Its customer portal was fully merged into the main OneGate domain a short time after.

TGR Partners also actively recruited staff for Maple Finance online, including posting job listings for an IT project manager to work out of TGR's physical office in Podgorica, Montenegro, under a TGR human resources manager.

Job postings for Maple Digital Financial Solutions request applicants to contact someone on the social media site Telegram with TGR in its username. (Illustration: Froilan Untalasco/CBC)

PDF files created for Maple’s privacy agreements contained metadata listing the author as "Max Travel," a likely digital trace left by TGR leader Yury Maksakov, who uses the username "Max Traveller" on Facebook.

The digital clues and overlaps between Maple Finance and TGR are consistent with "illicit financial activities," said Peter Dent, a former forensic services lead for global professional services firm Deloitte who is also part of the Vancouver Anti-Corruption Institute.

"I'm certainly concerned," said Dent. "They share a common directorship, they share a phone number with another entity that has been alleged to be involved in illicit financial activity. They don't even have a phone number in Canada."

Metadata for OneGate, OneCard and OneRemit showed the author as Max Travel, a likely digital trace left by TGR leader Yury Maksakov, who uses the username "Max Traveller" on Facebook. (Illustration: Froilan Untalasco/CBC)

FINTRAC registration

Following the global crackdown on the TGR Network in December 2024, Maple Finance was scrubbed from the active provider list on The OneGate website, as its FINTRAC registration expired.

The FINTRAC registration has since been renewed and Maple Finance now advertises itself as an "innovative financial ecosystem for modern business owners to manage their finances on their own terms."

FINTRAC shows Maple Digital Financial Solutions registration. The address links to the law firm Osler, Hoskin & Harcourt LLP. (FINTRAC)

FINTRAC wrote in an email to CBC News that it is "prohibited from disclosing information on the compliance history of individual entities... except in the case of a public notice of an administrative monetary penalty imposed."

"If I was the government authority in charge of money-laundering enforcement, like FINTRAC here in Canada, I think I'd be looking at this report," said William Pellerin, international trade lawyer at McMillan LLP, who also reviewed the report and CBC’s findings.

"You have known actors that have been under investigation in other jurisdictions … in conjunction with everything else, maybe this is something we ought to dig into."

World.title: Hamilton NHL prospect Matthew Mayich 'needs a miracle' after training collapse, family lawyer says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hamilton-born NHL prospect Matthew Mayich "needs a miracle" after being hospitalized following a training incident at Arizona State University last month, his family's lawyer has said.

Attorney Rob Carey spoke to CBC Hamilton on behalf of Mayich's family on Friday, saying the 21-year-old's parents, who live in Hamilton's Stoney Creek area, are staying near the hospital to be with their son each day.

"They really appreciate the love and the prayers and the support they've received from their Canadian friends," the partner with U.S. law firm Hagens Berman Sobol Shapiro LLP said.

The St. Louis Blues draft pick collapsed following a morning workout at Arizona State University (ASU), Carey said. He said Mayich suffered exertional heatstroke causing a lack of oxygen to the brain.

A report in the journal BMJ Medicine describes exertional heatstroke as "the third leading cause of mortality in athletes during physical activity." It says data indicate mortality rates of about 27 per cent, with long-term negative health consequences for survivors.

University says senior vice-president reviewing incident

ASU confirmed a student on the hockey team collapsed during an Aug. 20 training session but has not named them, citing privacy obligations.

"The morning outdoor workout was a team event at which coaches and training staff were present along with a third party who had previously worked with the ASU Hockey team," the university said in a Sept. 3 statement.

ASU vice-president James Rund is leading a review, the school said, looking at "the workout and related university policies, procedures and training protocols."

The review will be conducted in a manner respectful of "the student-athlete, his family, his teammates and ASU’s privacy obligations," ASU said.

A St. Louis Blues player wears the team logo on his sweater in 2025. The team picked Mayich in the sixth round of the 2023 NHL Draft. (David Zalubowski/The Associated Press)

Mayich endured 'brutal' workout: lawyer

The university has been "tight-lipped" about what occurred, Carey said, but based on his own investigation, he believes Mayich endured a "military-style, brutal, grueling workout," with no breaks and no water for over an hour.

"You have an elite NHL-drafted athlete showing up on the first coach-led workout, the very first day the team could organize formally, and he left the field with no chance of recovery," Carey said. "Obviously there's something wrong."

When Mayich collapsed, the lawyer said that no one immediately immersed him in cool water, contrary to best practices for treating heat stroke.

It was about 31 C in Tempe, a college town just east of Phoenix, as of 7:51 a.m. on Aug. 20, according to Weather Underground . University police received a call about the hockey player's collapse around 8:30 a.m., ASU said.

CBC asked ASU to respond to Carey's allegations and to provide details about its own investigation.

A spokesperson said they had no further information beyond the Sept. 3 statement.

The university has guidelines for heat illness, as well as for for how third parties interact with ASU athletes, the statement said.

Questions about the workout are part of ASU's review, it added.

Family's questions unanswered

"The goal right now is just to get evidence about what happened," Carey said. "We don't know why [the workout] was set up, who set it up, what was really designed for the day, what safety precautions were taken, and who made a decision not to have safety precautions ready."

The family wants a fair and complete investigation, involving witness interviews, security video and digital communications, he said.

"If it's not happening, then either we need a proper police department to investigate it or we will do it when we have the ability with a civil lawsuit," Carey said.

CBC asked the University of Arizona Police Department if it's investigating but did not receive a response.

Mayich mentored younger players in Hamilton

Mayich played minor hockey with the Hamilton Huskies between 2016 and 2020 then with the Ottawa 67's before the St. Louis Blues drafted the defenceman in the sixth round of the 2023 NHL draft.

During his six seasons with the Huskies and one as a member of the Hamilton Jr. Bulldogs, Mayich established "himself as a tremendous hockey player and, more importantly, an outstanding person both on and off the ice," the Hamilton Steel Hockey Club, formerly the Huskies, said.

The statement was sent to CBC Hamilton on behalf of the organization, former Huskies president Mike Spadafora and former Huskies head coach Chris Travale. Spadafora is currently the councillor for Hamilton's Ward 14, running for re-election.

"Without fail, whenever [Mayich] is asked, he comes back every year to speak and skate with a new crop of young kids," Travale said. "His message is always about so much more than hockey — it’s about relationships, friendships, and the experiences you have along the hockey journey.

"From everyone at Hamilton Steel Hockey Club, the Hamilton Huskies family, Hamilton Jr. Bulldogs and the Hamilton hockey community — Matthew remains in our thoughts and prayers, and our hearts are with him and the entire Mayich family."

World.title: Survivor Greece contestant Stavros Floros sues producers after leg severed in accident
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A former contestant on the Greek edition of the hit competition show Survivor is suing the show's producers after a horrific boat accident that severed his leg.

Stavros Floros filed a lawsuit in a Florida court on Thursday, seeking $100 million US in damages.

Floros, now 22 years old, was competing in Season 13 of Survivor Greece when he went spearfishing with another contestant in the waters off the Dominican Republic on May 11.

According to court documents obtained by CBC News, a tourist boat accidentally struck Floros, severing his left leg above the knee and severely injuring his right leg.

Floros was taken ashore and transferred to a local medical clinic before being transferred to a hospital in Miami, where he underwent multiple surgeries and spent 61 days in recovery.

TMZ published graphic photos of Floros in the aftermath of the accident, showing the extent of his injuries.

Stavros Floros's photos, videos while recovering at Florida hospital:

Skai TV, which broadcasts Survivor Greece, said at the time that it immediately suspended the show, even though Turkish company AcunMedya is solely responsible for its production, and offered its support to Floros and to contribute to his treatment and rehabilitation.

But Floros alleges that wasn't the case.

“I went onto a reality show and ended up with only one leg at 22 years old, having felt like I was slowly dying,” Floros said in a statement to TheWrap on Thursday after filing the lawsuit.

“I want people to know that they didn’t look after us, that I haven’t received the proper support from the production company."

The lawsuit, filed in Miami-Dade Circuit Court, names AcunMedya, AcunMedya Global, Acun LLC and Turkish businessman Acun Ilicali as defendants, as well as the parent company of Skai TV.

WATCH | Why reality competition series Survivor became a cultural phenomenon: Reality TV show Survivor marks 50 seasons | Duration 7:30 The 50th season of the long-running competition reality show Survivor kicked off on Wednesday. Superfan and CBC associate producer Zach Orobko joined CBC's On The Coast alongside professor Hartley Jafine, who co-created a McMaster University course based on the show, to discuss Survivor's cultural significance.

Contestant's life changed 'for a game'

The court documents include statements from Floros and other cast members who described how the events unfolded.

Floros said the show's format meant he and other contestants were expected to fish for food in the open ocean while competing.

The lawsuit alleges that the production had not established any protections or deployed any safety vessels despite knowing there was "heavy, high-speed commercial and tourist boat traffic."

May 11 was not a "game" day, in which the contestants take part in challenges, but they were still to be filmed carrying out other "survival activities."

Floros and fellow contestant Emmanouil Malliaros swam out to spearfish around 7:30 a.m. The court documents state that the accident happened sometime between 8:00 a.m. and 9:30 a.m.

In his statement, Malliaros said "it was common for tourist boats to travel close to shore," and that Survivor Greece cast members were viewed as "entertainment."

LISTEN | Survivor gives viewers an extreme version of their own interpersonal relationships: Day 6 9:12 Why Survivor endures after 25 years and 50 seasons

Malliaros stated that Floros was swimming within 10 metres of a small inflatable dive marker, and within 100 metres of the shoreline, when the boat struck him, adding that he later learned of another contestant having a close call with a passing boat.

After Floros was struck, Malliaros said, the boat kept going and only turned back once tourists on board demanded the operator return to help.

Malliaros said that that a passenger on board applied a temporary tourniquet to Floros's leg. The severed part of his leg wasn't recovered, the documents state.

"My whole life has changed," Floros told the Miami Herald on Thursday. "My mind is like, 'All of this happened for a game?'"

Although the series shares a name with the hugely popular U.S. series Survivor, which remains a juggernaut after 50 seasons airing over 25 years, Survivor Greece is not affiliated with it.

The 50th season of the U.S. version of Survivor commenced on Feb. 25 and wrapped on May 20. It featured fan-favourite cast members who had participated in the reality competition series over its first 25 years. (Scott Duncan/CBS)

Floros's lawyers, with the firm Lipcon, Margulies & Winkleman, filed the lawsuit in Florida citing AcunMedya and Ilicali's ties to the state and claiming that the businessman made decisions — including those related to contestant safety — from his residence in Miami Beach.

Floros also said he was influenced to apply for Survivor Greece because of the show's past seasons being filmed in Florida and because the prize for being the "sole survivor" included a luxury trip to Miami.

He also stated that Ilicali visited him in the hospital. A photo of them together is included in the documents but is no longer on the businessman's Instagram account. Ilicali also purportedly offered Floros and his family a place to stay at his residence, according to Floros's statement.

CBC News reached out to AcunMedya for comment but did not receive a response in time for publication.

Aside from Survivor Greece, AcunMedya is behind several other international editions of the franchise, including Turkey, Mexico, Romania and Germany.

World.title: PQ leader says he's worried Ottawa is meddling in Quebec election
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says he's worried the Canadian government is meddling in the Quebec provincial election, saying there is a “possibility that we are facing the greatest federal interference in our affairs and our election since 1995.”

St-Pierre Plamondon says during the eight years the Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) government was in power, the federal government quietly rejected every request from the province, but “for the past few months, the federal government has been multiplying announcements.”

Speaking during a news conference Friday while on the campaign trail ahead of the Oct. 5 election, St-Pierre Plamondon cited examples such as the $11-billion investment in the Davie shipyard, unveiled a few days before the campaign, and the recent agreement between Newfoundland and Quebec on Churchill Falls.

Then, he added, there was Wednesday’s announcement of a $4.7-billion investment to construct train cars in La Pocatière.

The PQ leader also suggested co-ordination between CAQ Leader Christine Fréchette’s campaign and Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government on the issue of the tariff war between Canada and the United States as another example.

“The federal government and the CAQ are collaborating,” he said. “We cannot deny that the federal government is interested in the outcome of the Quebec election.”

He said the federal Liberal party doesn’t want a sovereigntist government taking shape, but the PQ has been leading in the polls. He said “you have to connect the dots” when you see the federal government taking sudden interest in files that have stagnated for years.

“I am worried, and I have the right to voice that worry,” said St-Pierre Plamondon.

Fréchette, Carney deny allegations

But the CAQ leader and province’s premier isn’t hearing it.

“Absolutely not,” Fréchette retorted when asked about possible interference from Ottawa in the campaign. She said the announcements over recent weeks are good for Quebec and would not have occurred under a Parti Québécois government.

“It is essential to have partnerships with the federal government when it is good for Quebec, and then to stand our ground when necessary.”

Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette responds to questions during a campaign stop outside a school in Gatineau, on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

Repeating a phrase she has used several times before, she said, “I don’t work for Ottawa. I don’t work against Ottawa. I work for Quebec.”

The Prime Minister's Office (PMO) said in a statement that Canada's new government "will always be ready to work with all premiers, across party lines, to build a stronger economy, protect our workers and businesses, and make life more affordable."

The federal government does not interfere in provincial elections, and will work with Quebec's government to achieve its goals no matter who wins on Oct. 5, the statement says.

While the PQ has asked Élections Québec to investigate, the province’s Liberal Leader Charles Milliard accused St-Pierre Plamondon of seeing a conspiracy.

“But I don’t think there is a grand scheme behind all of this. In any case, no matter how many consultants the CAQ buys, they aren’t federalists. They are opportunists,” Milliard said.

Group's involvement challenged

St-Pierre Plamondon also called attention to alleged ties between the CAQ campaign and Mission Leadership Québec.

The group describes itself as a non-profit organization whose objective is to promote citizen participation, democratic dialogue and political awareness. It promotes itself as a non-partisan group that advocates for strengthening Quebec's place within the Canadian federation.

St-Pierre Plamondon described the group as a covert organization hijacked by figures linked to the federal Liberal Party. As proof, he cited a recent Journal de Montréal report stating that Mission Leadership Québec, which advocates for Canadian unity, received contracts to run campaign events for Fréchette’s team.

The PQ asked Quebec’s chief electoral officer on Friday to investigate allegations of interference and illegal contributions by the group to benefit the CAQ campaign.

Asked Friday about her party’s ties to Mission Leadership Québec, Fréchette brushed off concerns, saying she doesn’t analyze how every group or company her party deals with runs its operations.

She said the CAQ has a contract with Mission Leadership Québec to organize two town halls and “that’s it. We don’t go beyond that."

World.title: Bond yields are soaring to multi-decade highs. What does that mean for Canadian consumers?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

With global bond yields surging to multi-decade highs, a previously mundane corner of the financial world is now a hot topic on Wall Street.

For the average Canadian, it means higher borrowing costs for some products, such as mortgages and auto loans, but also stronger returns on other products, such as other guaranteed investment certificates (GICs) and money market funds.

Let's start with the basics. When you buy a bond, you're effectively lending money for a predetermined amount of time to the issuer. That could be the federal government, provinces, municipalities or a private company. Investors are typically paid interest until the maturity date, when they get the face value of the bond back.

So, what's a bond yield? It's the annual return an investor earns from holding a bond, expressed as a percentage. After bonds are issued, they can be traded on the open market, causing their prices to shift. When bond prices drop, yields rise. This is because investors get the same interest payments for a lower buy-in price.

Until recently, the global bond market was pretty sleepy. That's because central bankers around the world kept interest rates at near-zero for more than a decade following the 2008 financial crisis. Now, a growing number of investors see rate hikes on the horizon as central banks look to tamp down sticky inflation.

When a central bank raises interest rates, newly issued bonds offer higher payouts, making existing lower-paying bonds less valuable.

Higher inflation puts pressure on central banks

Right now, the bond market is experiencing a steep, global sell-off. From the United States, to Germany, Japan and Canada, yields have jumped to multi-year or even multi-decade highs.

"What's going on there? Well, when you see a substantial movement, usually it's because there is more than one thing happening at once," Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem said on Wednesday, after the central bank's latest interest rate decision was announced.

Inflation fears and concerns about ballooning government debt are feeding expectations for the Bank of Canada and its global peers to raise their trend-setting interest rates.

"Central banks' tolerance for higher inflation is limited," said Macklem. "That is causing the market to build in the possibility of future interest rate hikes."

According to the latest Statistics Canada data, gas prices were a key driver of higher inflation in July. On Wednesday, the Bank of Canada said global oil prices are persistently high, with no end in sight for the U.S.-led war with Iran, which has disrupted seaborne crude traffic in the region. U.S. benchmark oil prices have soared nearly 60 per cent year-to-date.

At the same time, the bank sees the Canada-U.S. trade war pushing up costs for businesses, which could feed into consumer prices over time. Macklem noted the AI infrastructure buildout is stoking demand for new corporate bond issuance, lowering prices for previously issued bonds.

"All those things are tending to work in the same direction to boost global bond yields," Macklem said.

WATCH | The expected inflationary impact of counter-tariffs: Inflationary impact of counter-tariffs expected to be 'relatively modest': Bank of Canada governor | Duration 2:06 Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem says the central bank will update its estimates, but as of now officials assess the 'inflationary impact of those counter-tariffs is fairly modest,' adding that the situation in the Middle East remains the 'bigger issue' for inflation.

Canada's 10-year government bond yield hit a two-year high on Wednesday, after the Bank of Canada signalled inflation risks are rising.

Because Canadian banks can invest risk-free with the government, government bond yields set the floor for all other lending. Fixed-rate mortgages, auto loans and other forms of credit are linked to five-year and 10-year government bonds, meaning the higher the yields for those bonds are, the higher the banks set their interest rates for those loans.

For those looking to invest their savings, rising bond yields force banks to raise their GIC rates to stay competitive, boosting guaranteed returns.

WATCH | Why U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is setting off alarm bells for many investors and analysts: Will Bessent's bond market intervention make U.S. inflation worse? | About That | Duration 4:38 U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's recent intervention in the bond market is setting off alarm bells for many investors and analysts. Avneet Dhillon breaks down concerns that Bessent’s attempt to calm the markets and decrease the cost of borrowing may actually worsen inflation. (Photo credits: The Canadian Press, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images)

'A good time to lock in your mortgage'

True North Mortgage founder and CEO Dan Eisner says savvy borrowers are locking in rates.

"Fixed mortgage rates won't drop substantially until yields do. Yields aren't likely to enter a sustained downward trend unless signs of deeper economic softening gain momentum and inflation pressures ease," Eisner wrote in a blog post on Wednesday .

"It's a good time to lock in your mortgage rate if you're looking to buy a home or renew your mortgage, as fixed rate movement is likely to resemble a rollercoaster for the next while, or at least until we see some clarity on geopolitical activity and U.S. trade."

Google Trends data show Canadians are taking a keen interest in the ongoing bond market upheaval. The volume of inquiries about the bond market over the past month is up 5,000 per cent on a yearly basis, according to the search engine giant.

No 'dysfunction' in Canada's bond market

Macklem said while there has been some "spillover" from higher global yields into Canada's bond market, Canada's yield curve sits well below that of U.S. government bonds.

Speaking at Wednesday's press conference in Ottawa, Bank of Canada senior deputy governor Carolyn Rogers reassured investors that Canada's bond market, while affected by global trends, is not necessarily in dangerous territory.

"I think it's important to distinguish between volatility and dysfunction or instability when prices and yields are moving, because investors are repricing risk," she told reporters.

"The vulnerability that we have talked about in our previous financial stability reports really comes when you get leveraged investors unwinding their positions quickly, and liquidity starts to dry up," she added, referring to investors such as hedge funds and non-bank asset managers who use borrowed money to fund their investment strategies.

"That's the risk we worry about. We don't see that happening right now."

World.title: After 12 years of fried chicken and flirting, hit YouTube series Chicken Shop Date to end
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

After more than a decade of interviewing and flirting with movie stars, musicians and athletes while sharing some fried chicken, Amelia Dimoldenberg, the host of the popular YouTube talk show Chicken Shop Date, announced this week she's closing up shop.

"To me the show is my very own romcom and I have loved creating so many stories for you to watch. I am so grateful to everyone who has followed me on this journey and found some joy in these episodes," Dimoldenberg wrote in an Instagram post on Thursday.

"I never thought I'd stop Chicken Shop Date, I thought maybe it would be a part of me forever, and in some way it always will, but I feel like it's now time to move on from this adventure and onto a new one."

Dimoldenberg started the show 12 years ago, interviewing musicians in Britain's underground rap scene. Since then, she's gone on to chat with celebs, including Keke Palmer, Conan O'Brien, Paul McCartney and Jack Harlow and garnered close to 3.5 million subscribers to her YouTube channel.

WATCH | Her interview with Jack Harlow:

Chicken Shop Date follows a simple format: Dimoldenberg goes on a date of sorts with a celebrity at a fried chicken shop in London and asks them a blend of questions that are flirty, funny and sometimes awkward.

It produces the type of banter you'd more likely expect on a first date than a typical sit-down, talk show style interview. In some cases, like her 2024 sit-down with Andrew Garfield, it's led to what seemed to be some actual flirting.

"This is called flirting, Amelia, this is called flirting," Garfield says at one point.

WATCH | Her Andrew Garfield interview:

Dimoldenberg also has some Canadians among her dozens of interviews. That includes Ryan Reynolds, whom Dimoldenberg corrects when he gives the wrong name for the character his wife Blake Lively played on Gossip Girl.

"That is right, Brooke from Gossip Girl loves you," Reynolds tells Dimoldberg, hinting at Lively's fandom of her show. At that point, Dimoldenberg points out Lively's character was named Serena.

"I don't think there is a Brooke," Dimoldenberg says.

WATCH | Ryan Reynolds and Hugh Jackman on the show:

Shania Twain also sat down for a date with Dimoldenberg in 2023, where Twain revealed that she'd never actually met Brad Pitt (despite mentioning him in her hit song That Don't Impress Me Much).

WATCH | Shania Twain on the show:

The massive success of her YouTube channel has led to opportunities for Dimoldenberg outside the chicken shop, including working the red carpet at the Oscars this year, where she interviewed another Canadian, Hudson Williams.

WATCH | Dimoldenberg interviews Hudson Williams at 2026 Academy Awards:

It's unclear what Dimoldenberg's next move is after Chicken Shop Date, but it appears she has some irons in the fire. She's currently signed on to develop a young adult drama series for the BBC, according to Deadline.

But in her goodbye post on Instagram, Dimoldenberg also promised "a few final dates" before ending the show for good.

World.title: Vancouver police officer accused of defrauding 19 victims of $3M
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. Vancouver police say a high-profile officer who was arrested on Thursday allegedly defrauded at least 19 victims of a total of about $3 million. Kal Dosanjh, a 26-year veteran of the Vancouver Police Department (VPD) and the CEO of the KidsPlay Youth Foundation, is facing four counts of fraud over $5,000, four counts of theft over $5,000 and one count of breach of trust dating back to 2017. At a Friday news conference, Vancouver police Chief Steve Rai said Dosanjh had been suspended, and that he had recommended to the Vancouver Police Board that the suspension be served without pay. Kal Dosanjh is seen in this file image, speaking in his capacity as CEO of KidsPlay. (CBC) He added that investigators believe there may be additional victims who have yet to speak to police. "These allegations are deeply troubling not only because of their seriousness, but because they have the potential to undermine the trust that our members work very hard, very hard to build and maintain with the public," Rai said. "This officer had a profile in the community and internally, and officers are angry and disappointed." Dosanjh was arrested in Surrey in what police described as a "controlled" traffic stop. He has been released on conditions and relieved of his service weapon, police said. Rai said police began a large-scale, covert investigation in December 2023 after multiple alleged victims came forward. He said that after consulting with the RCMP, it was "determined with collective judgment" that the VPD would head the investigation because it was best equipped with the expertise and resources to handle the file. Police were seen taking items in boxes from Kal Dosanjh's place of residence after his arrest Thursday afternoon. (CBC News) Property developments targeted According to court documents, multiple charges relate to alleged fraud and theft from investors in the Azura, Queen's Park and Sahara development projects. Sarabjit Singh Gill, who police described as Dosanjh's business partner, is listed as a co-defendant in those charges. "It began over a series of years until such a point that victims then started to question the veracity of those things," said Supt. Mike Ritchie, who led the 2½ -year investigation. "We were not made aware internally until 2023." WATCH | Dosanjh faces multiple charges: High-profile VPD officer Kal Dosanjh faces fraud, theft charges | Duration 1:37 Dosanjh also faces two charges alleging fraud and theft from the KidsPlay Youth Foundation. Dosanjh founded the charity in 2015 with the stated aim of "keeping B.C. kids away from a life of crime." Ritchie confirmed police had searched KidsPlay's offices. Ritchie said the province's Civil Forfeiture Office has been engaged in a separate but parallel process for "quite some time," and added that police weren't ruling out additional criminal charges. Municipal election ripples Dosanjh's arrest has already had ripple effects in Surrey's upcoming municipal election, where his wife was running for council. On Friday, the Conservative Party of Surrey announced that Sandy Dosanjh was no longer one of its council candidates. Sandy Dosanjh is not named or accused in any of the charges or allegations her husband is facing. He has, however, participated in her campaign as a speaker and supported her campaign on social media. FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

Statement from the Conservative Party of Surrey:

Sandy Dosanjh is no longer a Conservative Party of Surrey candidate for Surrey City Council.

As Sandy is no longer a candidate for public office, we ask that her privacy be respected at this time so that… pic.twitter.com/ACuAfHxZry —blue_townhalls Richmond City Coun. Kash Heed, a former West Vancouver police chief and B.C. solicitor general, said the move was not a surprise given the election was just weeks away. "When you have something of this nature, your significant other under such a cloud, it's going to be difficult to maintain the credibility and confidence of the public that are going to elect you to serve in office," he said. "Certainly it will override anything that she is positively able to add as the individual running for municipal government." In a statement on Thursday, Dosanjh's law firm Alliance Lawyers said it was "inappropriate to draw conclusions" based on the reported arrest of their client. "Mr. Dosanjh has committed no crime and is innocent of any wrongdoing," the statement reads. "An arrest, or a report that an arrest has occurred, is not evidence of guilt, misconduct, or criminal responsibility." None of the charges have been tested in court. Anyone who believes they may be a victim can contact police at 604-717-2601.
