The real problem is not the exchange rate but the math of government finances.

Growth slows, inflation turns volatile

Kenya’s economy expanded 4.9 percent year-on-year in the third quarter of 2025, up from 4.2 percent in the same quarter of 2024.

The National Treasury projected 5.3 percent GDP growth for 2025, while the World Bank expected only a gradual medium-term recovery.

Headline inflation fell from 4.5 percent in December 2025 to 4.3 percent in February 2026.

It then climbed sharply, reaching 5.6 percent in April and 6.7 percent in May 2026.

The May rise reflected higher energy prices and transport costs during elevated global oil prices.

Core inflation rose to 3.2 percent in May 2026, while non-core inflation jumped to 16.0 percent.

This split exposes Kenya’s vulnerability to imported fuel and food shocks even when domestic demand stays soft.

The shilling’s tight trading band

The Kenyan shilling has been the quiet anchor of the macro story in 2026.

On December 31, 2025, it traded at KSh 129.01 per US dollar.

By July 23, 2026, it stood at KSh 129.53, after moving between KSh 128.99 and KSh 129.99 over the period.

On September 4, 2026, the Central Bank of Kenya’s own rate put the dollar at KSh 129.47, still inside that band.

The Central Bank of Kenya (CBK), the country’s monetary authority, repeatedly described the shilling as stable against major international and regional currencies.

Investors should read this as managed stability rather than a freely floating market outcome.

The current account deficit, estimated at 2.4 percent of GDP in 2025 and 2.2 percent in 2026, supports the balance.

However, about 59.7 percent of external debt was in US dollars as of June 2025. This keeps demand for hard currency alive.

Forex reserves provide a fragile cushion

Kenya’s foreign exchange reserves stood at US$12,394 million on December 31, 2025, equal to 5.3 months of import cover.

They rose to US$13,655.70 million by April 2, 2026, reaching 5.8 months of import cover.

By June 25, the reserve stock had eased to US$13,173 million, still covering 5.6 months of imports.

The Central Bank’s statutory requirement is at least four months of import cover, so the buffer remains compliant.

In the week ending July 23, 2026, reserves fell by about KSh 40 billion, equivalent to about US$309 million.

That one-week move shows how quickly cash can shift when dollar demand rises.

Reserves are adequate for now, but they are no substitute for reducing external debt pressure.

Policy rate cuts meet sticky available cash

The Central Bank cut its benchmark policy rate from 9.25 percent in November 2025 to 9.00 percent in December 2025. It cut further, to 8.75 percent, by August and September 2026.

The Kenya Shilling Overnight Interbank Average Rate, known as KESONIA, stood at 8.75 percent in May and June 2026.

Commercial banks’ excess reserves above the 3.25 percent cash reserve ratio averaged KSh 6 billion, about US$46 million. That was for the week ending May 21, 2026.

They had averaged KSh 18.0 billion, about US$140 million, above the requirement in the first week of January 2026.

The interbank rate indicates that available cash remains reasonably priced despite fiscal pressures.

Softer policy is meant to support credit growth, but private sector borrowing still faces crowding-out from government financing.

IMF programme and the next cheque

The International Monetary Fund, known as the IMF, is the global lender that helps countries manage balance-of-payments and debt problems.

The IMF disbursed about US$606 million to Kenya on October 30, 2024. That followed completion of the programme’s seventh and eighth reviews.

Kenya then missed the ninth and final review in early 2025, and the two sides agreed not to proceed with it.

That decision forfeited about US$850.9 million Kenya would otherwise have received, according to IMF and government statements at the time.

Kenya has since asked the IMF for an entirely new programme, and talks continued through 2026 without a finished deal.

Central Bank of Kenya Governor Kamau Thugge said in August 2026 that discussions on a fresh IMF-supported programme were still under way.

No new loan amount, staff-level agreement or board approval date had been confirmed as of September 2026.

IMF engagement still matters, because a completed deal would anchor the credibility of Kenya’s consolidation plans with other lenders.

Debt service eats into tax revenue

Kenya’s public and publicly guaranteed debt is estimated at 74.8 percent of GDP at the end of the 2025/26 fiscal year.

That is down slightly from a peak of 77.2 percent in the 2023/24 fiscal year.

The IMF has classified Kenya’s debt as at high risk of distress.

External debt service costs consume nearly 32 percent of tax revenues in the year ending June 2026.

Almost one in three shillings collected in tax goes to foreign creditors.

Kenya also bought back part of its Eurobond debt in February 2026, spending about KSh 64.4 billion, about US$500 million.

The buyback smoothed Kenya’s repayment schedule rather than adding fresh borrowing.

Fiscal deficit targets and the wage bill

The Treasury aims to cut the fiscal deficit to 3.5 percent of GDP in the 2026/27 budget.

That is down from 4.9 percent of GDP in the previous 2025/26 fiscal year.

Kenya’s tax-to-GDP ratio stands at 16.8 percent, below the sub-Saharan Africa average of 18.5 percent.

The IMF recommends improved compliance, digital tax administration and fewer VAT refund leakages.

Public wages absorb about 7.5 percent of GDP.

Treasury Cabinet Secretary John Mbadi has described the road ahead as demanding, highlighting constraints before the 2027 elections.

Tax protests remain a political brake

The 2024 finance bill sought to raise KES 346 billion, about US$2.68 billion at 2024 rates. The plan relied on VAT hikes and other tax measures.

Mass protests, led largely by young Kenyans known as the Gen Z protest movement, opposed the tax package.

President William Ruto eventually refused to sign the bill, effectively shelving the proposed tax increases.

The protests were driven by frustration over austerity measures and new taxation.

The government is now cautious about introducing levies perceived as regressive.

That political constraint directly limits how quickly Kenya can close its fiscal deficit before the 2027 vote.

Nairobi as an expat and tech hub

Nairobi remains East Africa’s main hub for expatriates and technology firms. Its edge is regional connectivity, a skilled English-speaking workforce and established financial services.

A stable shilling reduces expat and investor uncertainty on rental and salary costs. Rising fuel and transport costs, though, push up living expenses.

For investors, Nairobi offers regional market access, but also exposure to sovereign debt pressure and election-year politics.

What investors should watch into 2027

First, watch whether headline inflation eases below 5 percent after the May 2026 spike to 6.7 percent.

Second, monitor whether Kenya and the IMF reach a new staff-level agreement, since the last programme lapsed in 2025 without one.

Third, track the fiscal deficit path from 4.9 percent toward the 3.5 percent target in 2026/27.

Fourth, follow the shilling’s band; a break above KSh 130 could signal dollar scarcity or reserve stress.

Fifth, watch election-related spending promises as the 2027 campaign approaches.

The combination of high debt service, a wafer-thin tax base and political resistance to new levies remains Kenya’s central risk.

World.title: Rare Blue Octopus Returns to Galápagos as a Newly Identified Species
World.content:
The rare blue octopus that surprised scientists has returned to the Galápagos Islands. The specimen, about the size of a golf ball, will be preserved at the Charles Darwin Research Station, which houses an extensive collection representing the archipelago’s extraordinary biodiversity.

An expedition collected the first specimen of this species, distinguished by its small tentacles, in 2015 at a depth of more than 1,700 meters (5,600 feet) in the northern part of the Ecuadorian archipelago, known for its endemic flora and fauna. Only three specimens have been observed to date, but the other two were recorded only on video.

The octopus, which was already dead, was taken in 2022 to the Field Museum of Natural History in Chicago, United States. There, it was given the scientific name Microeledone galapagensis, classified and introduced to the world. On Monday, it returned to the Galápagos, although its tentacles had lost their intense blue color, its body had turned opaque and its head was completely pale.

Researchers at the Charles Darwin Research Station handled the specimen with extreme care after it arrived on the islands, located 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) off Ecuador’s coast, wrapped in alcohol-soaked gauze. The octopus has returned “with a name, and we have good news: it is an endemic species,” Miguel Pinto, the station’s senior curator of natural history collections, told AFP.

Since this week, the specimen has been preserved in a collection gallery, bearing a red label identifying it as the holotype, meaning the animal used as the reference specimen for the description of the new species. It will now be housed alongside another 140,000 specimens of marine organisms, vertebrates, terrestrial invertebrates and plants preserved by the research station.

For Paulina Sepa, who oversees the marine collections, the octopus’s return will help advance research into the vast biodiversity of the Galápagos, a UNESCO biosphere reserve and World Heritage Site. There is “so much more to discover, so many more questions,” even “a million questions,” Sepa said.

“We need to study it further,” Pinto said of the species. “More deep-sea exploration is also needed in the Galápagos to search for them and understand them a little better,” he added.

World.title: What a Costa Rican migratory alert actually does
World.content:
A judicial notice served on live television this week put an obscure piece of legal machinery in front of all of Costa Rica. Most of what was said about it afterward was wrong. Here is how it played out:

A judicial officer walked up to Pilar Cisneros Gallo outside Casa Presidencial on Thursday afternoon, handed her a document, and ended a two-day story about a measure almost nobody in Costa Rica had heard of a week ago. Earlier that day the Fiscalía General confirmed it had issued a migratory alert against Cisneros, a former legislator who now works without pay as a communications adviser to the Executive.

Prosecutors said they needed to summon her for a declaración indagatoria — the statement a person under investigation is entitled to give — in a case examining the alleged illegal receipt of private contributions during the 2022 presidential campaign. They said they had not been able to reach her. Within hours of the notice being served, the alert was cancelled. That sequence tells you most of what the document is for.

It is not an arrest warrant and it is not an exit ban

This is the part that got scrambled fastest. A migratory alert does not stop you leaving the country, and it does not authorise anyone to detain you. The Ministerio Público said plainly that the measure was neither an arrest order nor an exit impediment, and that it did not require the Dirección General de Migración y Extranjería to report each of Cisneros’s border crossings back to prosecutors. The alert existed to help locate her for a summons, nothing more.

An exit ban is a different instrument with a different weight. Under the Ley General de Migración y Extranjería, an authority ordering an exit impediment has to supply the person’s name, nationality, identity document type and number, date of birth and the reason for the restriction. Migración cannot record the impediment if any of that is missing, and cannot lift it without a written order from the authority that imposed it.

None of that applies to an alert. An alert is a flag in a system. An exit ban is a wall.

What happens if you hit one at the counter

The Sala Constitucional examined how these alerts operate in a 2024 ruling, working from the procedure Migración described to the court. When someone carrying an alert is detected at a border post, officers can verify their identity, establish which authority issued the alert, and contact that authority for instructions.

That is the whole mechanism. What happens next depends entirely on what the issuing authority says, and in a case like this one the answer would be that the person needs to be handed a summons. You would notice it as a delay at the counter while an officer makes a call. You would not be handcuffed, and you would not be turned around.

Why this one drew a formal complaint

The Ministerio Público described the request as normal and proportionate, the kind of step taken when a person cannot be located or served. Prosecutors laid out what they said they had tried during August: two attempts at her home and five calls to numbers registered in her name. At one of the home visits, they said, they were told she no longer lived there. On one of the calls, a man who identified himself as her husband said she was out of the country and supplied a second number, and a person answering that number said she was not available.

Cisneros rejected the account. She said she had lived at the same address for 17 years, had kept the same phone number for 25, and worked at Casa Presidencial every day. She called the alert a political attack and a score-settling move by Attorney General Carlo Díaz, and challenged prosecutors to come and serve her, noting the distance between Casa Presidencial and the Fiscalía is about 2.3 kilometres (1.4 miles). Asked by reporters whether she had evidence connecting the measure to the coming selection of a new attorney general and Supreme Court president, she said she had none, but had no doubt either.

Justice Minister Gabriel Aguilar then escalated it. In official document MJP-DM-822-2026, addressed to Supreme Court President Orlando Aguirre, he called the measure abusive and disproportionate and asked that the Judicial Inspection, the full Court and the anti-corruption prosecutor’s office examine the conduct of adjunct prosecutor Edith Morera and of the Attorney General in his supervisory capacity. Aguilar argued it was serious to reach for a migratory alert to accomplish something as routine as a notification.

Where it stands

Cisneros was served during a press conference on Thursday afternoon and summoned to appear at 8 a.m. Friday with defense counsel. The Fiscalía emailed Migración the same day to void the alert as she has not been charged. A declaración indagatoria is the stage at which the Código Procesal Penal requires that a person suspected of involvement in a crime be given the chance to speak, and it carries no obligation to answer questions or testify against oneself.

Cisneros lost parliamentary immunity when the 2022–2026 constitutional term ended, which is why the case is no longer handled under the special rules that apply to members of the supreme powers. The Fiscalía said the file is not directed by the Attorney General personally, precisely because nobody currently named in it holds immunity, and that the others under investigation had already given their statements.

The measure at the center of all this lasted less than a day and never restricted anyone’s movement. Whether reaching for it was proportionate is now a question for the Court, and the answer will matter well beyond this one file.

World.title: Watch Spider Monkeys Return to Costa Rica’s Nicoya Peninsula
World.content:
Costa Rica is famous for its biodiversity. There’s an incredible amount of life packed into this tiny country. However, this diversity of species isn’t uniformly present throughout the nation. Many factors, including habitat type and the impact of human beings, affect the presence of a certain species present in a given area.

I’ve spent the last 8 years or so using camera traps to sample the level of species diversity around the country, but I’ve mostly focused on a specific part of the country, Guanacaste. After many camera revisions from locations throughout Guanacaste, I’ve come up with an informal gradient of species diversity that’s based on the animals that my cameras are best at recording, mammals.

Areas with the very highest levels of species diversity are still home to Costa Rica’s largest mammals, the white-lipped peccary, the jaguar, and Baird’s tapir. As the level of species diversity begins to drop, the white-lipped peccaries are the first to disappear, followed by the jaguars and tapirs. In my experience, the first primate species to disappear when dropping down a level of diversity are Central American spider monkeys.

These levels of diversity are nothing official, just patterns I’ve noticed while carrying out camera trap projects throughout Guanacaste. At this point, when I begin a new project, I have a pretty solid idea of what species are going to be missing from the environment based on results from work I’ve done in that general area.

This year, when I had the opportunity to work with a coalition of organizations including the Fondo de Biodiversidad Sostenible and FONAFIFO on a wildlife monitoring project in the Nicoya Peninsula, I thought I knew what species were going to present on the properties. The project is still ongoing, but my assumptions were proven incorrect during the revision of the very first camera.

As I scrolled through species that I knew were going to be present, agoutis, ocelots, nine-banded armadillos, one video stopped me in tracks. It featured two Central American spider monkeys fleeing from the ground up into the trees, either frightened by the presence of my camera or something else nearby.

I was shocked. The nearest property where I had recorded or seen spider monkeys was in northern Guanacaste some 100 kilometers from the place I was sitting. On top of that, I had done some internet sleuthing in the past about locally extinct species on the peninsula and had read that spider monkeys were amongst the species, like jaguars and Baird’s tapirs, that had disappeared decades ago.

Obviously delighted to be wrong, I did some more research when I got home and found that Rescate Wildlife Rescue Center (formerly Zoo Ave) had a reintroduction program that had done some work in the Nicoya Peninsula and one of the species that they had focused on was spider monkeys. Excited about learning more, I reached out to Rescate Program Director Amy van Esch to tell her about my camera trap video and learn more about the program. Amy confirmed that they had been working on wildlife reintroductions for years and even offered to share some more information about their work. Here’s what she had to say –

“Rescate Wildlife has been working in the Nicoya region for over 35 years. Within the foundation we have a large protected area of over 800 hectares (about 2,000 acres) that we use as a release site for many different species.The spider monkey was completely extinct in this region at that time.

In the year 2000 we released a group of 44 spider monkeys, 31 former pets (who came to our rescue center through the pet trade), and 13 born onsite through our endangered species breeding program. Fast forward 26 years and we now have various wild troops with over 100 individuals! It’s pretty amazing to think, this population has all come out of animals that were formerly pets, now living wild, reproducing and dispersing into other areas.

This last year we also started something completely new: we built one of the world’s largest pre-release enclosures, over 4 hectares in size. We currently have a troop of 12 individuals preparing for release (all former pets, some even arriving dressed in baby clothes). This will be the first time we release new spider monkeys in over 15 years.

This enclosure is unique in its size, which is full of large growth trees, allowing them to learn “to fly” between trees and gain real agility before being released into the wild. It’s something we are really looking forward to in the coming year: finally seeing them fully wild!“

How cool is that? Check out the ten second video below that proves that all of their hard work has resulted in spider monkeys once again living wild on the Nicoya Peninsula.

About the Author

Vincent Losasso, founder of Guanacaste Wildlife Monitoring, is a biologist who works with camera traps throughout Costa Rica.

World.title: Costa Rica Renters Face Major Barriers to Buying a Home
World.content:
More than eight out of every 10 Costa Rican households that rent would face serious income barriers if they tried to finance even a relatively modest home, according to a new study showing how far property prices have moved beyond many local salaries. The report, Balance and Trends in the Housing Sector 2025, estimates that 81.4% of renter households face either complete exclusion from formal home financing or significant restrictions because of their income. That represents approximately 279,890 families.

The study was produced by the University of Costa Rica’s Graduate Program in Architecture, the Federated College of Engineers and Architects and the organization Gestionando Hábitat. It was released on August 20 but keep in mind the figure does not mean banks have rejected mortgage applications from 81.4% of renters.

Instead, researchers compared household incomes with the financial requirements for purchasing a model home priced at ₡76.5 million, or approximately $170,000. That amount corresponds to the maximum price used in the study for a property classified as social-interest housing.Researchers reviewed financing conditions offered by 26 institutions authorized under Costa Rica’s national housing finance system. They then compared those conditions with the average incomes of households currently renting.

The first major obstacle is the down payment. Depending on the lender, buyers could be asked to provide between 5% and 20% of the purchase price. For the model property, that would mean finding between ₡3.8 million and ₡15.3 million, or roughly $8,500 to $34,000.

Legal fees, property valuations, bank commissions and other closing expenses could add another ₡1.5 million to ₡3.1 million, approximately $3,300 to $6,900. Even buyers who qualify for financing covering 95% of the property could still need between ₡6 million and ₡7.3 million, or $13,300 to $16,200, before completing the purchase.

Monthly payments create another hurdle. Financing about ₡72.7 million over 30 years would produce estimated payments ranging from nearly ₡393,000 to ₡585,000 a month, or approximately $870 to $1,300, depending on the interest rate. Under the study’s most flexible calculation, households would need monthly incomes ranging from approximately ₡786,000 to ₡1.17 million to keep the mortgage payment below half of their income.

Using a more cautious limit of 35%, the required income increases to between ₡1.12 million and ₡1.67 million, or about $2,500 to $3,700 a month. Households in Costa Rica’s two lowest income groups fall below those requirements. Families in the middle group might qualify only under the lowest interest rate and most flexible debt limit. Even households in the fourth income group would not automatically qualify under the more cautious calculation.

Previous debts can make the situation worse since banks consider credit card balances, vehicle loans, personal loans and other obligations when deciding how much a household can borrow. Independent and informal workers may face an additional obstacle if they cannot document their income through tax returns, bank records or official payment receipts.

The problem is not limited to obtaining a mortgage. The study also found a large gap between local incomes and the prices being asked for homes in the Greater Metropolitan Area. Researchers examined 4,338 houses and apartments offered for sale and 1,824 rental properties, using listings collected by the UCR Real Estate Observatory in late June 2026.

They found that 47% of the properties for sale were priced beyond the estimated purchasing ability even of households in the country’s highest income group. For rentals, 56% of the properties in the sample exceeded the estimated spending limit for that same group. Among the lowest 60% of households, only 17% of the homes for sale and 6% of the rentals analyzed were considered financially accessible.

The researchers cautioned that cheaper homes advertised through informal channels or without real estate agents were probably underrepresented. The percentages therefore describe the properties in the study’s sample, not every home available across the region. Even with that limitation, the findings point to a widening mismatch between property prices, household earnings and the amount banks are willing to lend.

For many Costa Rican families, renting is no longer simply a lifestyle choice. It is the only realistic option. Foreign residents may have different incomes, savings or access to financing, particularly if they buy with cash. However, the report helps explain why property prices that appear reasonable to some international buyers remain out of reach for much of the local population.

World.title: Why is Daniel Ortega Shutting Nicaragua’s Opposition Out of Elections?
World.content:
Nicaragua approved a constitutional reform that bars the opposition from participating in elections and extends Daniel Ortega’s term in office, a measure aimed at securing a presidential succession within the family of the octogenarian former guerrilla leader.

Ortega and his wife and co-president, Rosario Murillo, tightened their grip further by pushing through the amendment, which closes the door to a political transition after two decades of rule marked by the concentration of power and harsh repression.

What was approved?

The National Assembly, controlled by the Sandinista National Liberation Front (FSLN), voted Tuesday to prohibit “traitors to the homeland,” people linked to attempted coups, or those who call for “military intervention” or “economic blockades” from participating in elections. The couple routinely levels those accusations against all their opponents.

Lawmakers also extended the terms of current elected officials and the heads of the Armed Forces from six to seven years. The reform also granted new powers to electoral authorities to dissolve political parties and sanction candidates. If reelected in late 2028, Ortega and Murillo could remain in power until 2036.

The reform must be ratified during a second legislative session in January 2027. In practice, it would pave the way for a one-party system controlled by the FSLN.

What is the objective?

Ortega, 80, and Murillo, 75, tightened their control over society following the 2018 protests, whose repression left more than 300 people dead, according to the United Nations. The co-presidents describe the demonstrations as an attempted coup sponsored by the United States.

Thousands of people went into exile following the protests, including opposition leaders, intellectuals, journalists and members of the clergy who were stripped of their nationality after being accused of “treason.” During the 2021 election campaign, Ortega’s main rivals were imprisoned before the vote, leaving virtually no domestic opposition today.

Ortega suffers from lupus and kidney problems and has difficulty walking. Most of his children hold key government positions, while opposition figures warn that an internal purge is underway to secure a family succession. Rebecca Bill, president of the Inter-American Dialogue, said Ortega and Murillo do not need tougher measures to win elections because the opposition “has already been crushed and democratic institutions destroyed.”

“The objective is to ensure there is as little uncertainty as possible about what happens after Ortega. Elections create uncertainty, as do independent institutions and a genuine opposition, which is why they have eliminated all three,” Bill said. Extending their terms would also allow the co-presidents to outlast the current period of pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump and postpone any possible negotiations over electoral conditions, according to former Nicaraguan lawmaker Eliseo Núñez.

What could the consequences be?

The United States on Wednesday urged its partners to sever ties with Nicaragua, arguing that “dictatorships” should not enjoy the political and economic benefits afforded to democracies. Washington, Nicaragua’s largest trading partner, has already imposed sanctions on government figures and is pushing for a meeting of foreign ministers from the Organization of American States (OAS) to consider measures against Managua.

The European Union also condemned the amendment before it was approved. “The international community needs to coordinate more effectively and raise the cost of repression in a targeted manner, while avoiding measures that primarily punish ordinary Nicaraguans,” Bill said.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Whale and Dolphin Festival Returns This Weekend
World.content:
If you have been waiting for the right weekend to see humpback whales in Costa Rica, this is it. The 16th Whale and Dolphin Festival takes place this weekend, September 4, 5 and 6 in Costa Ballena in the South Pacific, timed to the peak of the season when humpbacks fill the warm water off Uvita.

The whales are the reason the festival exists. Adults reach nearly 16 meters (52 feet) and weigh up to 36 metric tons (about 40 short tons), and they arrive here after one of the longest migrations any mammal makes. Whales reaching Costa Rican waters can cover between 5,000 and 8,000 kilometers (3,100 to 5,000 miles) from cold-water feeding grounds, some as far south as the waters near the Antarctic Peninsula.

They come to breed, give birth, and raise their calves where the water is warm and sheltered. Mothers spend these weeks teaching their young to feed, socialize, and move through open ocean. Bahía Ballena, next to Marino Ballena National Park, is one of the best-documented breeding areas in the country. It is also home to the tombolo that gives the park its nickname, a sandbar that takes the shape of a whale’s tail when the tide drops and you see it from above.

Festival organizer Karol Monge said Bahía Ballena belongs on every Costa Rican’s list, describing it as a destination known not only for whale watching but for its beaches, mountains, rivers and waterfalls. Programming runs across all three days and mixes cultural, sporting and nature activities with whale-watching tours sold at special rates for Costa Ricans.

You will also find kite-making workshops, free surf lessons, a food court, a craft fair built around nature themes, concerts, and a communal ceviche event. A whale sculpture several meters tall, built from recycled material including plastic bottles, is on display. To check schedules and prices or reserve a tour, organizers are directing people to the festival’s Facebook page, Festival de Ballenas y Delfines Costa Rica, and to the phone number 8729-3624. Tours book out fast during festival weekend, so calling ahead matters more than usual.

Marcos V. Borges, executive president of the Costa Rican Tourism Institute, said whale watching in the southern Pacific during breeding and calving season is one of the experiences that sets Costa Rica apart. He encouraged domestic travelers to come for the weekend and to choose sustainable tour operators.

That last point is worth taking seriously as Costa Rica regulates how close boats may approach whales and how long they can stay near mothers with calves, and those rules exist because a boat that crowds a nursing calf can separate it from its mother. Ask an operator whether they are licensed and whether a naturalist guide is aboard. Smaller boats carrying eight to twelve passengers generally give you a better view than large catamarans, and morning departures usually mean calmer water and more active animals.

Book a morning tour if you can since most run three to four hours and leave by boat from Bahía Uvita inside the park. If you are driving from San José, you have two routes. Route 34, the Costanera Sur, runs down the coast. The alternative is Route 2 south to San Isidro, then Route 234 toward Dominical. Either way, allow more time than a map suggests on a festival weekend.

The land section of Marino Ballena National Park is open daily and charges a small entrance fee, lower for nationals and residents than for foreign visitors. There are no shops or facilities inside, and the beach at the Uvita sector has almost no shade, so bring water and sun cover. Walking out onto the whale’s tail only works at low tide, so check a tide table before you plan the day around it.

The southern humpback season runs roughly from July into November and peaks between August and October, which means the whales will still be here after the festival packs up. What the weekend adds is the rest of it, the crowds and the music and the ceviche, and the reminder that in Uvita and Bahía Ballena the arrival of these animals is not just an ecological event but the thing that keeps hotels, restaurants, guides and small businesses running through the green season.

World.title: ‘I nuh juck nobody’: Dalla van driver angry as sex assault charge upgraded to rape of a child over 15-year-old’s allegations
World.content:
‘I nuh juck nobody’: Dalla van driver angry as sex assault charge upgraded to rape of a child over 15-year-old’s allegations

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City “dalla van” taxi driver who has been on bail since last year on a sexual assault charge was sent to prison on Friday after prosecutors withdrew that charge and replaced it with the considerably more serious offence of rape of a child.

Wenseslao Garrido-Veilz, 43, a Guatemalan national, appeared unrepresented before a Senior Magistrate in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where prosecutors informed the court that his previous charge of sexual assault was being withdrawn.

He was then read a single charge of rape of a child stemming from the same alleged incident involving a girl who was 15 years and 10 months old at the time.

The allegation is that on November 22, 2025, Garrido-Veilz had sexual intercourse with the minor without her consent.

Because of the nature of the new charge, the Magistrate explained that the lower court could not take a plea from Garrido-Veilz and could not grant him bail.

Garrido-Veilz repeatedly attempted to address the allegation, telling the court that he lives in Guatemala, has three children and has evidence in his defence.

“I have the evidence,” he told the court before being cautioned not to discuss the facts of the case at that stage of the proceedings.

An interpreter was eventually provided for Garrido-Veilz, who speaks Spanish, and he responded, “Bueno,” after the court explained the process to him.

He was denied bail and remanded to the Belize Central Prison until September 28, 2026.

Garrido-Veilz appeared visibly angry as he was escorted away to begin his remand. While being taken to prison, he was heard protesting in Kriol: “I nuh juck nobody.”

Breaking Belize News first reported on Garrido-Veilz’s case following his November 25, 2025 arraignment. At the time, police alleged that a 15-year-old girl boarded his grey dollar van near New 2 U on Cemetery Road and that, after the other passengers had exited, he drove her to a feeder road between Miles 2 and 3 on the George Price Highway and allegedly touched her inappropriately.

During that first court appearance, Garrido-Veilz pleaded not guilty to sexual assault. BBN reported that he was a Guatemalan national with Belizean residency and that prosecutors objected to bail on the grounds that he could be a flight risk. He told the court then that he had three Belizean sons and family ties in Belize. He was nevertheless granted bail with strict conditions, including that he not leave Belize, contact the minor or her family, or go within 200 yards of her.

That arraignment also produced a memorable courtroom moment when Garrido-Veilz, who had initially communicated through a Spanish interpreter, suddenly exclaimed in English after learning he would receive bail, denying that he had touched the girl.

BBN subsequently reported in August that the sexual assault case had been delayed while the court awaited CCTV footage from law enforcement.

The case took a dramatic turn on Friday, however, after prosecutors withdrew the sexual assault charge and substituted the charge of rape of a child.

The more serious allegation reportedly follows a further statement given by the minor concerning what she alleges occurred during the November 2025 incident.

Garrido-Veilz will now have to seek bail at the High Court if he wishes to be released while the case proceeds.

World.title: The door that slammed in your face this week may have saved your life
World.content:
The door that slammed in your face this week may have saved your life

By Horace Palacio:

It is Friday, the day Belize passes judgment on its week. The deal that died Tuesday. The call that never came. The door that closed Wednesday afternoon. By Friday evening we have the verdicts stamped, good week, bad week, and we carry them into the weekend like sentences.

So Friday is exactly the right day for a line from the American novelist Cormac McCarthy that has been drifting across Belizean timelines.

“You never know what worse luck your bad luck has saved you from.”

For once, the internet attributed correctly. The line is truly his, from No Country for Old Men. But the meme leaves out the detail that gives the sentence its license. In the novel, the words are spoken by an old lawman named Ellis, shot years earlier, living out his days in a wheelchair, as he comforts a sheriff drowning in despair. Hear that clearly. This is not a comfortable man’s philosophy. It is a crippled man’s. From a healthy mouth the line is a greeting card. From his, it is a verdict earned in blood.

Unpack the logic, because it is sturdier than it looks. Every time misfortune strikes, we grade it against an invisible alternative, the week where the bad thing did not happen. But that alternative is pure imagination, and notice how we always imagine it. Perfect. The job we lost would have flourished. The person who left would have loved us forever. The deal that died would have made us rich. We compare our real, wounded week against a fantasy week with the flaws airbrushed out, and of course reality loses. McCarthy’s old man simply points at the fraud. You never saw the real alternative. It might have been worse. It might have been fatal.

History keeps receipts on this. Milton Hershey, the chocolate king, had paid his deposit for passage on a magnificent new ocean liner in 1912, and business forced him to cancel. The ship was the Titanic. Nearly a century later, a young writer named Seth MacFarlane overslept, missed his morning flight, and cursed his luck at the gate. The flight was American 11, the first plane into the towers on September 11. Both men had bad mornings. Both bad mornings were rescues wearing disguises. And here is the humbling part, for every famous case there are millions of invisible ones, because the accident that never happened calls no witnesses. The truck you never met has no headline. The unseen ledger of your life is full of mercies filed under inconvenience.

The old world knew this. There is an ancient Chinese story about a farmer whose horse ran away, and the neighbors cried, what bad luck. Maybe, said the farmer. The horse returned leading wild horses, what good luck. Maybe. His son broke a leg taming one, what bad luck. Maybe. The army came conscripting young men for a doomed war and passed over the boy with the broken leg. The farmer’s entire philosophy was one word, maybe, the discipline of the unfinished verdict. Life, he understood, is graded in pencil, and every Friday we grab the ink.

Now bring it home, because Belize has lived this line at national scale, and some of our luckiest breaks arrived dressed as disasters.

We never struck the great oil gusher, and we cursed those dry wells for decades. Then look at the nations that did strike it, and count how many the black gold made more corrupt, more divided, more broken. Our dry wells may be the luckiest holes we ever drilled. We spent the Cold War decades feeling small and overlooked, while that very smallness was camouflage, the proxy wars that drowned Guatemala, El Salvador and Nicaragua in blood found nothing here worth fighting over, and we held peaceful elections through it all. The superbond years were agony, and that agony was the schoolhouse where this country learned the fiscal discipline that later cut our debt nearly in half. And when 2020 shut the airport and we called it catastrophe, the collapse ran the great sorting this column wrote about, separating the waiting from the working, and forced lessons no boom would ever have taught. You never know what worse luck your bad luck has saved you from. Neither does a nation.

Now, the guardrails, because this column never sells a sedative, and this beautiful line can be abused into one.

Guardrail one. The line is for the rearview mirror, never the windshield. It is medicine for what you cannot change, the grief, the closed door, the hindsight, and it must never anesthetize what you can. Do not bless the blackout, it was negligence, not providence. Do not thank fate for the stolen millions. A wound you can still treat is not a mystery to accept, it is a job to do. Comfort belongs to the past. Effort belongs to Monday. Confusing the two is how the old ghost of resignation sneaks back in wearing philosophy’s coat.

Guardrail two. The symmetry cuts both ways, and this is where the line turns from comfort into wisdom. You also never know what worse luck your good luck is steering you toward. The lottery winners broke by year five. The promotion that fed the pride that caused the fall. So the mature conclusion is not that bad luck is secretly good. It is that all verdicts on fortune are premature. Hold your celebrations loosely and your despair looser. Maybe, says the farmer, about everything.

So here is your practical instruction for this evening, Belize, and it costs nothing. Before you stamp this week’s verdict, take the worst thing that happened, write it down with the date, file it, and reopen the file in two years. You will be astonished how many entries have quietly converted from disaster to rescue. And tonight, spend one minute on the unseen ledger, the crashes that never happened, the wrong turns not taken, the worse luck your ordinary, complaining, imperfect week quietly saved you from. Gratitude for the visible blessings is easy. Gratitude for the invisible ones is faith, and even an old country song figured it out, thanking God for the prayers He declined.

Somewhere behind you, my friend, is a door that shut in your face this very week and saved your life. You will never see the room. You will never meet the truck.

Say thank you anyway.

Then put down the gavel, pick up the pencil, and go enjoy your weekend.

Monday, we build.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: What the $200 electricity GST exemption means for Belizeans
World.content:
What the $200 electricity GST exemption means for Belizeans

By Zoila Palma: Belizean households could see savings on their monthly electricity bills following Cabinet’s decision to double the GST exemption threshold for residential electricity consumption from $100 to $200, effective September 1, 2026.

Under the new measure, residential customers with electricity bills of $200 or less will have GST removed from the applicable electricity consumption, providing direct relief to household budgets.

For example, if a residential electricity bill is $200 before GST, the 12.5 percent GST would amount to $25. With the new exemption, that $25 would no longer be charged, meaning the customer would pay $200 instead of $225.

The change is expected to benefit more than 91,000 residential customers, representing approximately 96 percent of all residential electricity customers in Belize.

The previous $100 threshold had been in place since April 1, 2017, meaning the new measure significantly increases the portion of residential electricity consumption that can qualify for GST relief.

The measure is intended to provide immediate financial relief to families by reducing the tax burden associated with residential electricity costs.

World.title: Cabinet approves Digital Register and new Licensing system for electrical workers
World.content:
Cabinet approves Digital Register and new Licensing system for electrical workers

By Zoila Palma: Cabinet met on September 2, 2026, and approved the introduction of regulations to establish a digital Electrical Workers Register and a searchable public verification system.

The new framework will introduce a class-based licensing system for electrical workers, along with clear application procedures designed to ensure that workers maintain the required level of competence in the field.

The regulations will also provide for supervised apprenticeships, continuing competency requirements and public electronic verification, allowing members of the public to verify the status of licensed electrical workers.

Cabinet said the framework will also establish clearer administrative and disciplinary procedures while providing transitional measures to ensure continuity for existing electrical workers as the new system is implemented.

World.title: Cabinet approves measures to strengthen electricity security
World.content:
Cabinet approves measures to strengthen electricity security

By Zoila Palma: Cabinet has approved a series of measures aimed at strengthening Belize’s electricity security while providing additional relief to residential consumers.

An Emergency Declaration will allow Belize Electricity Limited (BEL) to begin procuring additional generation capacity ahead of a projected electricity supply shortfall in 2027.

Government says the move is intended to ensure Belize has sufficient electricity to meet growing demand and maintain a reliable supply. The procurement of additional generation capacity is being described as a proactive step toward safeguarding the country’s energy security.

Cabinet has also supported an expansion of the Social Rate, increasing eligibility from 60 kWh to 80 kWh per month.

The change is expected to extend the preferential electricity tariff to approximately 17,000 residential customers.

Together, the measures combine immediate assistance for households with longer-term investment in Belize’s electricity supply. Government says the approach is intended to provide relief to consumers today while strengthening the country’s energy security for the years ahead.

World.title: 91,000 households to benefit as Electricity GST exemption doubles to $200
World.content:
91,000 households to benefit as Electricity GST exemption doubles to $200

By Zoila Palma: Cabinet has approved an increase in the GST exemption threshold for residential electricity customers, raising the monthly threshold from $100 to $200, effective September 1, 2026.

The measure is expected to provide direct relief to more than 91,000 residential customers, representing approximately 96 percent of all residential electricity customers in Belize.

The $100 exemption threshold had been in place since April 1, 2017, when it was lowered by the then United Democratic Party administration.

Cabinet’s latest decision effectively doubles the amount of residential electricity consumption covered by the GST exemption.

World.title: New U.S. Ambassador André Bauer confronted by press over infamous ‘stray animals’ remarks as he arrives in Belize
World.content:
New U.S. Ambassador André Bauer confronted by press over infamous ‘stray animals’ remarks as he arrives in Belize

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Newly arrived U.S. Ambassador to Belize André Bauer has again defended controversial remarks he made more than 16 years ago comparing government assistance for poor people to feeding stray animals, arguing that his comments were about breaking generational dependency rather than denying assistance to people in need.

Bauer was confronted about the remarks during his first press encounter in Belize on Friday.

“If I didn’t know the background and the way the press tried to present it, I would feel the same way they did,” Bauer said.

The controversy dates back to January 2010, when Bauer was lieutenant governor of South Carolina and campaigning for governor.

During a town hall discussion about government benefits, Bauer invoked advice from his grandmother about not feeding stray animals “because they breed” while arguing that public assistance programs should include greater personal responsibility requirements. The comparison generated national controversy in the United States.

Bauer later said at the time that he had not meant to call recipients of public assistance animals and argued that the metaphor had been taken out of context.

On Friday, Bauer said the discussion was not about healthcare, as one question suggested, but about whether government programs merely maintain poverty rather than helping people escape it.

He also revealed that his own family had qualified for free school lunches when he was growing up in what he described as a broken home.

“I believe in doing all we can instead of just giveaways,” Bauer said, pointing to healthcare, transportation, childcare and education as examples of assistance that can help people become self-sufficient.

“I’m all about opportunity, access, and lifting people up,” he added.

Bauer argued that public officials sometimes have to engage in politically difficult conversations rather than simply support programs that sound compassionate.

“If you really want to help people, sometimes you have to have very difficult conversations,” he said.

World.title: ‘Judge me by my actions’: New Ambassador responds to concerns over U.S. Embassy influence in Belize
World.content:
‘Judge me by my actions’: New Ambassador responds to concerns over U.S. Embassy influence in Belize

By Breaking Belize News Staff: New United States Ambassador André Bauer says Belizeans should judge him and the U.S. Embassy by their actions after he was questioned about perceptions that Washington sometimes acts as a disciplinary or oversight force over Belizean public officials.

Bauer was questioned Friday about the U.S. Embassy’s role in governance, including the perception among some Belizeans that U.S. visa restrictions, revocations and other diplomatic measures can be used to exert pressure on elected and government officials.

“Everybody… we all have opinions and different perspectives based on life experiences,” Bauer responded.

He said most people he has spoken with appear comfortable with the relationship between Belize and the United States but acknowledged that others may see it differently.

“They’ll be able to judge me by my actions and the actions of what the United States tries to do to work together,” Bauer said.

Pressed specifically on what oversight role he believes the United States should play in Belizean governance, Bauer said he did not have a direct answer.

Instead, he described diplomacy as a process through which countries discuss both shared interests and areas of disagreement.

“We have certain things that are important to our country, and you have certain things that are important in your country,” Bauer said.

He suggested informal and formal engagement with Belizean leaders could help each side better understand the other’s position.

“If leaders in your country break bread with me or we spend time together, I think we’ll get a mutual understanding of places that maybe we don’t agree, and places that we do agree,” he said.

Bauer said he intends to take that approach beyond government officials and meet ordinary Belizeans around the country.

“We don’t have to agree,” he said, adding that a well-made argument has changed his own mind in the past.

Bauer said his objective is for Belizeans to ultimately feel better about the bilateral relationship and see the United States as a partner rather than simply an outside power exercising influence over the country.

World.title: Market Bag: Sweet pepper hits $600, lettuce $1k as drought sends prices higher
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — Shoppers at local markets could see higher prices over the next few weeks as vendors report growing shortages of agricultural produce due to drought conditions affecting the island.

According to vendors, several items have become increasingly difficult to source, including Irish potatoes, now selling for $350 per pound; sweet potatoes at $250; pumpkins at $300; and lettuce at $1,000. Carrots, priced at $400 per pound, and sweet peppers ($600) are being imported to help meet demand.

Vendors say the reduced supply has also pushed up the prices of onions ($250) and other produce, with consumers expected to feel the impact.

One vendor told Market Bag host Carlysia Ramdeen that the lack of rainfall has made it difficult for some crops to survive, particularly water-dependent produce such as pumpkins and sweet peppers.

“Pumpkins cannot withstand the heat because pumpkins need water so because of the drought, we don’t have pumpkins. Peppers can’t grow without water. Sweet peppers cannot grow without water. So, the drought is really affecting the market,” she said.

Catch the latest episode of Market Bag on all Jamaica Observer digital platforms.

World.title: UPDATE: Mistrial ruling upheld in case of US mother who killed her children
World.content:
Kevin Reddington, defense attorney for Lindsay Clancy, and Lindsay Clancy look on as Judge William Sullivan (out of frame) instructs the jury to continue deliberating, during Lindsay Clancy's murder trial at the Plymouth County Superior Court in Plymouth, Massachusetts, on September 4, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

PLYMOUTH, United States (AFP) — A judge declared a mistrial on Friday in the high-profile case of an American woman who killed her three young children.

Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict in the case of Lindsay Clancy, and an appeals court rejected a last-minute bid by the defence to have a juror replaced.

The jury was deadlocked 11-1, with the majority apparently leaning to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity.
