World.title: Fewer kids open books for fun, prompting calls for national reading strategy
World.content:
From a last-minute Where's Wally to a classic Harry Potter, kids across Australia dressed up as their favourite literary characters to celebrate Book Week in August.

But literacy and library organisations across Australia are concerned that kids are more interested in their costumes for Book Week, than actually reading the books that inspired them.

A new declaration released to coincide with Book Week says more needs to be done to encourage reading, improve literacy, and boost library funding across Australian schools.

The Statement on School Libraries and Reading for Pleasure was produced by the Australian Library and Information Association, the Australian Coalition for School Libraries, and literacy not-for-profit Australia Reads.

The declaration calls on the federal government to make school libraries mandatory, and ensure they are properly resourced and staffed.

Australia Reads chief executive Anna Burkey said the statement was part of her organisation's call for a national reading strategy.

Anna Burkey is calling for a national reading strategy. (Supplied: Anna Burkey)

"Things like Book Week happen because of volunteer organisations like the Children's Book Council and the hearts and souls of parents, teachers and librarians making it happen," Ms Burkey said.

"But we want more support and investment in reading as an infrastructure.

"We need a national plan."

She said it was often children in lower economic regions that did not have sufficient access to books.

"It becomes a postcode lottery," she said.

" I was at a private school yesterday and it had five librarians but you go five miles down the road and there's a school that has no library or librarians. "

What the stats say

A 2025 study from the University of South Australia found that children and teenagers were reading less than in previous years, if at all.

The study into post-pandemic after-school activities found that fewer young people were reading for pleasure.

Sarah Mayor Cox says people should prioritise the joy of reading. (Supplied: Mark Leonardi)

In 2019, 10.8 per cent of children never read for fun; in 2022, the figure had climbed to 52.5 per cent.

By comparison, daily social media use had increased from 26 per cent in 2019 to 85.4 per cent in 2022.

The study's results are reflected in the nation's NAPLAN results from recent years.

During 2023, NAPLAN reading results showed that 74.5 per cent of year 5 students were reading at a strong or exceeding level, compared to 2026 where that figure has decreased to 71 per cent.

Ms Burkey said the drop in reading was not just in children, but adults too, with 30 per cent of all Australians not picking up a book in the last year.

"We have more choices than ever before for entertainment," she said.

Ms Burkey said there were plenty of positives as well.

"Even if a third of people in Australia is not reading, that still means the vast majority are," she said.

" The other good news story is that half of Australians want to read more often. "

How to get kids reading

Literary consultant and Bendigo-based author Sarah Mayor Cox said literacy skills often fell off the list for struggling families, which is why programs such as the late Dolly Parton's Imagination Library were so important.

"A child can have their own mini library by the time they age out of the program," Ms Mayor Cox said of the Imagination Library.

"It gives them such a head start before they start school or kindergarten."

According to the Grattan Institute, one in three children can not read proficiently at their grade level.

Sarah Mayor Cox says literacy skills often fall off the list for struggling families. (Supplied: Sarah Mayor Cox)

Ms Mayor Cox said prioritising the joy of reading over the technical skills was foundational for getting children to read for fun, and eventually their literacy skills would improve.

"There is this obsession with technical reading, such as phonics," she said.

" People should prioritise the joy of reading over competency. "

Ms Burkey agreed, saying the relationship between literacy skills and reading for leisure was critical and the benefits were "life-changing".

She said often people could feel overwhelmed with the choices of books, and it could be an obstacle for those wanting to read more.

But she said the best way to encourage kids to read more was to support their choices.

"Supporting them to test and trial, finding out what they like is really important [as is] validating what they choose," Ms Burkey said.

"It doesn't really matter what they choose.

"If they are excited by that, amazing, lean in."

World.title: Aussie star Myers beats Olympic champions to win Diamond League Final
World.content:
Australia's Cameon Myers has recorded the most significant win of his young career by taking out the men's 1,500 metres at the Diamond League Final in Brussels.

Myers became only the eighth Australian to win a Diamond League Final title when he clocked a time of three minutes and 30.14 seconds at the King Baudouin Stadium.

The 20-year-old beat home a stacked field featuring the two most recent Olympic champions in the event, the USA's Cole Hocker and Norwegian Jakob Ingebrigtsen.

"I wouldn't say this victory comes as a surprise to me," Myers said after the race.

"It's more a relief to finally showcase what I've been building toward over the last couple of years.

"It feels surreal, even though I always believed I had it in me. But it's so different to actually do it and actually execute it when it matters.

"This is going to be a fun memory to look back on."

Cameron Myers (right) pipped Kenya's Phanuel Koech to claim victory. (Getty Images: Tim Clayton)

Myers timed his final sprint in the home straight to perfection, narrowly edging out Kenyan teenager Phanuel Koech (3:30.18) and American Ethan Strand (3:30.50).

Ingebrigtsen, who was the Tokyo Olympic gold medallist, posted a time of 3:30.52 to finish in fourth place, with Hocker seventh in 3:30.80.

Coached by Dick Telford, Myers is the best Australian prospect in the men's 1,500m since 1960 Olympic champion Herb Elliott.

The Brussels victory is the latest chapter in the Canberran's stellar season.

Myers set a national record of 3:28.00 in winning the 1,500m at the Paris Diamond League meet in June.

The time is the second-fastest run in the world this year.

Myers won the mile (3:46.06) at another Diamond League meet, Eugene's Prefontaine Classic, in July and finished second to Scottish world-record holder Josh Kerr in the same event at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games.

Less than a week ago, Myers triumphed in the 1,500m (3:30.96) at Berlin's prestigious ISTAF meet.

Kurtis Marschall finished third in the men's pole vault. (Getty Images: Richard Heathcote)

Among other Australian results in Brussels, Kurtis Marschall was third on countback in the men's pole vault.

Marschall and second-placed Sondre Guttormsen of Norway both cleared 5.82m, with Greece's Emmanouil Karalis winning with a meet record of 6.12m.

Sweden's Olympic and world champion, Mondo Duplantis, was a late withdrawal due to leg tightness.

Lachlan Kennedy ran under 10 seconds for the fifth time this season in the men's 100m, posting 9.99 to be fourth behind winner and reigning world champion, Jamaica's Oblique Seville (9.90).

Matthew Denny was also fourth in the men's discus with a best throw of 68.04m.

Slovenian Kristjan Čeh produced a meet record of 71.29m to claim victory.

Two-time Commonwealth Games champion Rose Davies also just missed the podium in the women's 5,000m, finishing fourth in 14:37.47 behind Ethiopian victor Freweyni Hailu (14:35.20).

Fellow Australians Georgia Griffith (14:38.69) and Linden Hall (14:40.62) were sixth and 10th respectively.

World.title: Broome disappears into thick fog as WA wet season nears
World.content:
A thick blanket of fog engulfed Broome, in Western Australia's far north, this week with visibility limited to less than 50 metres.

The weather bureau said it was a sign the tropical dry season had come to an end, and the hot semi-arid Broome climate was on the precipice of entering the wet season.

Residents heading about their morning activities on Wednesday described the "eerie" magical feeling of being surrounded by dense fog.

Fog is a common occurrence during September in Broome. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

Cable Beach blanketed

Broome resident Hilary Wilkins described a strange scene on Wednesday morning.

"When I woke up, it was suspiciously quiet out there; normally you can hear aircraft taking off where I live," she said.

"So I got in the car to go to the beach with the dog and it was absolutely thick fog, dripping off the roof."

Once Ms Wilkins was on the beach, she saw yacht masts "sticking out of the fog" as the sun was rising, catching glints of light.

"As I walked down the beach there was this really cool, what I call a fog bow, it's literally like a rainbow, but with the blue sky coming through the fog," she said.

"I thought, 'This will be a cracking shot if I can get the dog in the middle of the bow.'"

Jane Meade was also walking her dogs on the beach and said her visibility was as little as 30 metres.

Jane Meade driving through the fog in Broome. (Supplied: Jane Meade)

"It's really eerie because with the fog being so thick, you can stand on the beach and not actually see anything," she said.

"It reminds me of my travels overseas being in the USA and waking up in the morning listening to the foghorns in Santa Barbara."

What causes fog?

BOM senior forecaster Jonathan How said fog formed due to the amount of moisture in the air and when night temperatures fell.

At the weather bureau, fog is measured if visibility falls below 300 metres, with anything above that considered mist.

The visibility on Wednesday got below 50 metres at Broome Airport and persisted for nine hours, soaking Broome up to the Dampier Peninsula.

Jonathan How says the foggy mornings indicate the dry season is coming to an end. (Supplied: BOM)

Mr How said it was typical this time of year, as Broome headed towards the wetter months.

"So certainly people might be noticing a bit more fog on the forecast over the next few days and weeks," he said.

" Hopefully everyone enjoyed the dry season because the humidity is really starting to pick up. "

Mr How said safety concerns on the road should be considered and advised people to drive to conditions and take precautions.

He said seeing how fog affected different parts of WA's vast state was interesting, reaffirming it was indeed the "Kimberley's turn" for this weather occurrence.

"Western Australia spans tropical climates in the north and then cool Mediterranean South," he said.

"So not surprisingly, we do see quite a variation in climate across the state, not just month-to-month, but also day-to-day."

Yawuru seasons

Broome's traditional owners, the Yawuru people, have six different seasons relating to the changes in climate.

These are Man-gala, Marrul, Wirralburu, Barrgana, Wirlburu and Laja.

The current season is Wirlburu, aligning with the re-emergence of foggy morning as the weather slowly starts to warm up.

Coco Yu is a Yawuru language specialist, teacher, mentor, and translator, working at the Mabu Yawuru Ngan-ga Language Centre. (Supplied)

Coco Yu from the Yawuru Language Centre said Wirlburu was a short transition season.

"The two big seasons for us are wet season, which is Man-gala, and the cold season was just Barrgana, and then we have these little ones in between usually connected to wind," she said.

"Wirlburu could last for one or two weeks, it's just one of those little things when sea breeze starts to blow and the day starts to warm up a bit."

Ms Yu said she felt awareness around Yawuru seasons was growing in the community.

Wirlburu was everyone's favourite season, according to Ms Yu, because the combination of sun and breezes were a relief before it got too hot.

World.title: Blood-sucking, eel-like fish another possible casualty of algal bloom
World.content:
The disappearance of a blood-sucking, eel-like fish could be welcome news for those who are fearful of the toothy creature, but scientists say they are concerned lampreys may be the latest casualty of South Australia's devastating algal bloom.

Every winter the South Australian Research and Development Institute (SARDI) uses fishway traps to monitor for lampreys as they swim from the ocean through the barrages into the Murray River.

Senior researcher Chris Bice said the team usually caught about 20 to 100 lampreys, but the last two monitoring periods had left them empty-handed.

In conjunction with SA Water, SARDI uses large cages to catch and count lampreys during their migration period. (Supplied: South Australian Research and Development Institute)

"This year, unfortunately, we haven't caught any despite trying reasonably hard," he said.

While the "incredibly cryptic" fish could be hard to catch, Dr Bice said he was concerned about what may have led to their absence.

"On the weight of evidence, I think it's pretty fair to say that the algal bloom may have had an impact on the upstream migration of these fish," he said.

Beginning in March 2025, South Australia's harmful algal bloom stretched across more than 20,000 square kilometres and resulted in the death of approximately 1 million marine animals of more than 600 species, according to the Australian Marine Conservation Society.

Floodwater, a coastal upwelling and a marine heatwave all contributed to the harmful algal bloom along South Australia's coast. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Older than dinosaurs, but still relatively unknown

Lampreys are part of an ancient vertebrate group and resemble an eel, although they bear no relation.

The species can be traced back hundreds of millions of years and are related to "an ancient family known as the jawless fishes", according to Dr Bice.

Estuarine ecologist Faith Coleman said while the algal bloom could be a contributing factor to the lack of sightings in the River Murray, there could be several reasons that SARDI was unable to catch them.

Lamprey range in size from 10cm to 120cm. (Supplied: South Australian Research and Development Institute)

"Most farmers will tell you there's been some really weird things around climate and that may have also changed how the lampreys migrate," she said.

Dr Coleman also said dead lampreys could have gone undetected due to their biological makeup.

"There is a question of whether they float when they die or whether they sink," she said.

Faith Coleman says there could be any number of reasons why lampreys have not been spotted over the past two monitoring periods. (ABC News: Stephen Opie)

" We've found a lot of species have been badly impacted [by the algal bloom], but because of how their biology works, they have sunk rather than floated and they've not come into shore. "

Why are we monitoring them?

SARDI has been undertaking targeted monitoring of lampreys for about a decade but only keep tabs on their movement as they migrate to freshwater to spawn during winter.

Chris Bice is optimistic the lampreys will return as the algal bloom subsides. (Supplied: South Australian Research and Development Institute)

Dr Bice said they only had a short window to research the relatively unknown species each year.

"They move vast distances when they're out in the ocean when they're attached to large fishes and feeding on them," he said.

" Right now we know almost nothing about the marine part of their life cycle. "

Despite their alarming appearance, Dr Bice assured people they had nothing to worry about if they were lucky enough to come across a lamprey.

Despite their scary exterior, scientists have assured the public the fish are not a threat in freshwater environments. (Supplied: David Moffatt)

"When they're on their freshwater upstream migrations, they actually stop feeding," he said.

"As soon as they enter freshwater, they're no danger to humans at all.

Dr Bice said he hoped the absence of lampreys could be short-lived as the impact of the algal bloom continues to subside.

"I am optimistic they will turn up again in future years and hopefully next year," he said.

World.title: Stephanie Akehurst sentenced to home detention after deadly crash
World.content:
The family members of a man who was struck by a car and killed at a busy intersection while riding his motorbike home from work have said they are "ropeable" after a judge sentenced the woman behind the wheel to two months home detention and 180 hours of community service.

Stephanie Akehurst pleaded guilty in the Darwin Local Court in July to careless driving (which carries a maximum penalty of two years jail), failing to give way, and driving with a drug in her system.

It was daytime, the road was dry and Ms Akehurst, who was 28 at the time, was driving north on Chung Wah Terrace towards a busy intersection in Palmerston at 30 kilometres an hour.

Stephanie Akehurst (far left) earlier pleaded guilty to careless driving, failing to give way, and driving with a drug in her system. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

In handing down his sentence on Friday afternoon, Judge Steven Ledek said it was a moment of careless inattention on the road in 2024 that resulted in the tragic loss of 56-year-old Anthony Hobden, a beloved father and husband and well-known member of the Northern Territory's motorsport community.

He said Ms Akehurst turned right and failed to give way before colliding with Mr Hobden, throwing him into the air "before coming to rest on the road".

He died at the scene.

"This was not anticipated. This was not planned. This was not something that anyone wanted to happen," the judge said.

"Every single day there are close calls but on this occasion that inattention led to a death.

"She was not speeding, she was not grossly intoxicated … she had no criminal history whatsoever."

Steven Ledek handed down his sentence in Darwin Local Court on Friday. (Supplied: DPP)

Judge Ledek made particular note of the fact that Mr Hobden's family wanted Ms Akehurst to face jail time.

"I go back to what [Mr Hobden's partner] Gabrielle had to say in terms of what she wanted as an outcome for today," he told the court.

"She said [she] would like to see her go to jail, not for the rest of her life, but there has to be a consequence for killing someone.

"In my view, in my mind … I think Stephanie is in a jail already.

" This is a person that has well and truly suffered as a natural consequence of her criminal conduct. "

Gabrielle Johnson says she is disappointed in the sentence handed down to Stephanie Akehurst. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Outside court, Mr Hobden's family members were visibly emotional and incensed by what they described as an inadequate sentence.

"I'm ropeable … it's an absolute insult," Mr Hobden's partner, Gabrielle Johnson, said.

"[Two months at home is] disgraceful.

"Anthony's life was worth more than two months to go home and watch DVDs."

Anthony Hobden was riding a motorbike when he was killed in the road accident in 2024. (Supplied)

According to agreed facts tendered in court, Ms Akehurst admitted to smoking cannabis the night before the collision but returned a negative roadside drug and alcohol test.

Subsequent blood tests detected a small amount of cannabis in her system, which prosecutors said had a minor adverse effect on her driving.

The court heard Mr Hobden's blood contained a cannabis concentration about three times higher, though there was no evidence it contributed to the crash.

'I'm profoundly sorry,' Ms Akehurst says

On Friday, Judge Ledek read aloud Ms Akehurst's apology letter to the family, in which she said she was "profoundly sorry" and recognised her mistake had devastating consequences.

She said she had not been able to drive since the incident and had spent countless hours replaying the moment before the collision.

"This tragedy has changed me completely," the court heard.

" It's taught me how a single moment can alter countless lives forever, and I think about Mr Hobden and those who loved him every day. "

The court heard Ms Akehurst had been using cannabis to self-medicate after she injured her back moving heavy objects to help her pregnant friend two years ago.

Ms Akehurst told the court she had not been able to drive since the accident in 2024. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

In handing down his sentence, Judge Ledek acknowledged that no sentence could compensate for the loss of a life, but he believed it was "appropriate in all circumstances".

"This is the lesson for everybody in our community who's driving … you must drive like your life is depending on it because everybody else's is too," he said.

Ms Akehurst was also ordered to pay the family $7,770 in restitution, to wear an ankle monitor and to continue her current psychological treatment.

World.title: Record regional road toll hits 1,000 due to complacency, report finds
World.content:
The crash that nearly ended Peter Kalbfell's life happened on a long, deserted highway in outback Queensland.

"There is a lot of nothing out there, you know," he said.

"Miles and miles and miles of nothing."

In January 2000, Mr Kalbfell was driving back home to Alice Springs after a "whirlwind" Christmas holiday with family and friends in Maryborough, three hours north of Brisbane.

Peter Kalbfell is president and head coach of the Fraser Coasters Wheelchair Basketball Club. (ABC Wide Bay: James C Taylor)

It was a trip he and his then-girlfriend had made countless times before, which, he conceded, led them to "be a bit more complacent" about driving while fatigued.

" We were pushing pretty hard to get back and I'd driven through the night. "

With his girlfriend behind the wheel, Mr Kalbfell undid his seatbelt to get more comfortable.

Peter Kalbfell was injured in a serious crash near Kynuna in outback Queensland. (ABC News: Lucy Cooper)

He does not remember what happened next.

Police later told him the car had veered off the road and rolled seven or eight times, crushing him underneath.

The crash rendered him an incomplete quadriplegic: paralysed from the neck down except for minimal movement in his arms and legs.

Mr Kalbfell's girlfriend sustained minor injuries.

Rural road deaths increasing

While the pair survived, a new report has identified an increasing number of fatal crashes on rural and regional roads.

An analysis by the Australian Road Safety Foundation (ARSF) found 906 people died on roads outside the capital cities in 2025, a 10.5 per cent increase on 2024.

According to the ARSF report, 906 lives were lost on rural, regional and remote roads in 2025. (Supplied: Police Media)

The ARSF understands this to be the highest number of regional fatalities since 2020.

Deaths on rural, regional and remote roads made up nearly 70 per cent of the national road toll in 2025, despite only about 25 per cent of the population living in those locations.

The study released last month found complacency was one of the main causes of risk-taking on regional roads, with many drivers saying they broke road rules because they believed it was safe to do so on familiar roads.

ARSF president Russell White said drivers needed to take more responsibility for their own safety.

"We've somehow outsourced that responsibility; whether it's to government, or it's to police, or it's to road builders or car manufacturers," he said.

Mr White said some simple techniques could help to disrupt complacency and improve driver awareness and responsiveness on the road.

Tips for safe driving on rural and regional roads Be situationally aware: look as far ahead as possible and scan for obstacles.

Consciously bring yourself back to the present: don't drive on autopilot.

Be prepared: give yourself time and space to take evasive action. Source: Australian Road Safety Foundation

Ioni Lewis is an expert in driver psychology at the Queensland University of Technology.

She said the ARSF findings correlated with a "longstanding overrepresentation" of road trauma in regional and remote areas.

The overrepresentation of regional fatalities became evident when the federal government began breaking down road crash data by urban and regional areas in 2017

This triggered 2017's Saving Lives on Country Roads throughout New South Wales, which targeted the role of complacency in rural and regional crashes.

Ioni Lewis says safety campaigns need to be targeted at regional audiences. (Supplied)

"There is that perception that the crashes are because of people who are unfamiliar, they haven't travelled here before," Professor Lewis said.

"But the data certainly doesn't suggest that's the case."

Professor Lewis said the fact that Mr Kalbfell was not wearing a seatbelt prior to his crash was an example of the way safety campaigns need to be targeted at regional audiences.

Ioni Lewis says city drivers are more likely to be wearing the seatbelt incorrectly, whereas regional drivers tend not to wear one at all. (ABC News)

Professor Lewis said city drivers are more likely to be wearing the seatbelt incorrectly, whereas regional drivers tend not to wear one at all.

"So, if they're saying they're not wearing their seatbelt because there's no-one else on the road, then we need to sort of challenge that idea that it's just you on the road," she said.

"We have to keep up those efforts with really developing resources, developing initiatives that focus on regional and remote Australians and what matters to them."

'It is a trauma that can be stopped'

Fatalities in Mr Kalbfell's home region of the Wide Bay have led Queensland's road toll for the past five years.

Detective Senior Sergeant Wade Lee said he had attended more than 100 crashes in his 35-year career in Wide Bay.

The officer himself was the victim of a head-on collision while on duty on a rainy day in 2021.

Wade Lee has attended more than 100 crashes in his 35-year career as a police officer. (ABC Wide Bay: James C Taylor)

Senior Sergeant Lee said the other vehicle lost control in the wet conditions and collided with his unmarked police car, which was then rear-ended by a semi-trailer.

While he is no longer a first responder, he says his officers attend crashes daily, often delivering heartbreaking news to families.

"It is a trauma that [can] be stopped, if we could change that driver behaviour," he said.

Echoing the ARSF study, Senior Sergeant Lee said complacency was a factor in most crashes in his region.

Passengers played a role in helping to keep the driver present and aware, even when driving on familiar roads, he said.

"Having the courage to say, 'Hey mate, slow down … it's raining,' or 'Mate, there's roadworks up ahead.'

"That in itself is a pretty easy conversation to have."

Peter Kalbfell speaks about road safety at a Rotary young driver's course. (ABC Wide Bay: James C Taylor)

Senior Sergeant Lee now helps to organise a Rotary young driver's course instructed by Mr Kalbfell.

"We don't want to see anybody go through what I've been through, or what [Wade] has seen on the roads, the carnage," Mr Kalbfell said.

"The message we try and get across is making smart choices, especially in the area that we live in."

World.title: What Labor's safe seat loss to One Nation means for Australian politics
World.content:
After a decade of dominance in Western Australia, Labor's dramatic defeat in its heartland seat of Secret Harbour has prompted plenty of self-reflection.

The loss to One Nation wasn't a surprise.

Luke Herdegen celebrates after his party claimed victory in the Secret Harbour by-election. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

The ABC understands in the weeks before veteran minister Paul Papalia resigned from his safe seat, internal party polling showed One Nation was on track to win the by-election.

Voters were frustrated with politicians, the cost of living, housing pressures and their future prospects.

One Nation supporters celebrate the party's win. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Labor paid the price at the ballot box, shedding 23 per cent of its primary vote to suffer a huge 19 per cent swing.

"When you have underlying issues that the government find difficult to resolve, you can campaign all you like but you can't necessarily make housing cheaper, you can't necessarily make the cost of living more affordable overnight," Notre Dame University politics professor Martin Drum said.

One Nation supporters watch Pauline Hanson on News24 on the evening of the by-election. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

A coastal, outer-suburban electorate which has changed name and shape over the years, Secret Harbour had been held by Labor since at least 1989.

Hanson thanks Liberals for by-election win One Nation leader Pauline Hanson says she is grateful to WA Liberal leader Basil Zempilas after his party preferenced hers at the weekend's Secret Harbour by-election.

Its population includes many young, working families. Residents are more likely to have vocational qualifications than a university degree and it's less multicultural than the rest of the state.

It recorded the eighth-highest vote for One Nation at the last state election.

Some Labor figures dubbed the Secret Harbour by-election "the worst seat to contest at the worst time".

It was a test of what a Labor-One Nation contest looks like and gives another data point for the major parties ahead of statewide polls in Victoria and New South Wales.

The One Nation alternative

Voters in Secret Harbour wanted change. What kind of change wasn't always clear.

One Nation supporters said they wanted change. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

One theory was that people have come to believe the government can fix their problems. It's created a reflexive response to pain.

The common sentiment amongst voters the ABC spoke to this week was that they were "sending a message to government".

Gabriel Vandermerwe, who put One Nation second after the Australian Christians, said he was "happy with the result".

Gabriel Vandermerwe welcomed One Nation's win. (ABC News: Courtney Withers )

"People want change, they're not happy with the current situation," he said.

Hank Vandenbelt, who is married to an Australian citizen but couldn't vote himself, said he was worried about what the change meant for him personally.

Hank Vandenbelt lives in the Secret Harbour electorate but couldn't vote because he is not a citizen. (ABC News: Courtney Withers )

"I'm a little bit concerned about the rise of One Nation … I'm an immigrant myself, I'm not even a citizen but there's some mood against immigrants," he said.

Close friends David Mackney and Leslie Simmons are on opposite ends of the political spectrum but were able to find some common ground.

"Policies are really non-existent I think … or they're irrelevant [from] One Nation so we'll wait and see," Mr Simmons said.

David Mackney (l) and Leslie Simmons (r) discuss the by-election over a drink at the Port Kennedy RSL. (ABC News: Courtney Withers )

Mr Mackney, traditionally a Liberal voter, put One Nation second but agreed there was "little substance on policy" from the minor party.

"I knew the Liberals wouldn't be able to get in because of the way they are at the moment … it's a protest to let people know that central government needs to sort itself out."

Several women the ABC spoke to, who didn't want to be photographed, said they were pleased by the "expected" One Nation win.

One Nation presents as a sympathetic ear and a chance to try something different.

Its popularity has baffled both major parties, in part because of how quickly it's come about.

These results from three successive DemosAU polls show how Western Australians intend to vote at a federal level.

With federal issues influencing both One Nation's support and the by-election in particular, it shows the trend Labor is up against.

Labor's campaign

The red campaign, which Labor says cost hundreds of thousands of dollars, was an experiment in fighting that wave, with the usual caveats that come from extrapolating too much from a by-election result.

The party maintains that despite some missteps and miscalculations, its campaign was technically strong.

That includes 19,000 doors knocked on, 8,000 voters spoken to and more than 210,000 pieces of mail sent into the electorate.

And yet it wasn't enough.

Labor candidate Georgia Tree joined Premier Roger at a number of press conferences during the campaign. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

It's understood a "frank and fearless" review led by three experienced figures will soon begin to unpack what went wrong.

Two senior Labor figures said they had been surprised by the impact of their candidate living 60 kilometres from Secret Harbour and being silenced at two consecutive press conferences.

Georgia Tree had grown up in the area and lived there for a long time, but had moved to the city for work. And, they pointed out, she spoke at more press conferences than her opponents.

Georgia Tree, pictured with Roger Cook, lived 60km away from the seat. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

One possibility is that she was perceived as disconnected and unable to speak up. It's the opposite of what One Nation seeks to appeal to.

"The people have had enough. They definitely felt neglected in the outer-southern suburbs," MP-elect Luke Herdegen said the day after his victory.

Connecting with voters

One immediate lesson which both sides appear to have taken from the result is that people’s sense of disconnection from their representatives should be countered by politicians spending more time with voters.

Social media, which was once thought to provide a more direct connection to constituents, has instead become "contaminated", Deputy Premier Rita Saffioti said on Thursday.

"People want to know you, they want to see you, they want to talk to you, and they want to make sure that you've got their priorities top of mind," she said.

Saffioti suggested that was difficult to achieve in the frenetic pace of a by-election but would be more feasible in the lead up to a state election.

Rita Saffioti said voters expect more connection from politicians. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

It's a view shared by another outer-suburban MP, Liberal Adam Hort.

He holds the seat of Kalamunda, which takes in the Perth hills, on just 82 votes. On paper, it would be prime One Nation territory.

"One of the clearest lessons from the recent by-election is that people expect their local member to be part of their community, to listen and to work hard for them," he told the ABC.

"That means being out there every week — doorknocking, meeting community groups, taking my mobile electorate office across the hills, visiting schools and listening to local residents."

Adam Hort says it's important to connect with constituents. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Challenging One Nation

Labor moved swiftly to show it is listening to voter concerns, with a housing announcement on Monday promising to boost the supply of rentals in nearby Mandurah.

Political observers sense voters have outsized expectations of their governments' ability to solve the often complex pressures they're facing.

But Labor is best placed to relieve that pressure, if it can work out how. It still holds 45 of 59 lower house seats and controls a government with plenty of money to direct in the right ways.

The Liberals have the easier job of pointing out the government's flaws from opposition, but have little room for error with just six lower house seats.

"While we are now the opposition in residence, One Nation is the opposition in waiting," one senior Liberal said.

Luke Herdegen will be the new member for Secret Harbour. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

The WA branches of the major parties have three years until the next state election to work out how to challenge One Nation, if the orange wave lasts that long.

If the solution is deep, meaningful engagement with their community though, the time to act is now.

World.title: Handcrafted violins take six months to make, but bring timeless joy
World.content:
Richard Hall sits tapping his foot and plucking a banjo in the front window of his music store on the main street of South Gippsland's Korumburra.

Out the back is his workshop — a warm space covered in pots of glue, wood shavings, planes of all sizes and stringed instruments at various stages of completion.

When he's not noodling on his banjo and making another instrument, Mr Hall is normally fielding sales from punters off the street, or shooting the breeze with musicians who drift in through the front door.

But for the past six months, the 59-year-old has been hard at work on a new project, handcrafting a bespoke violin using Australian hardwood.

And he's just about ready to hand it over to its new owner.

The violin has been hand crafted over the course of months, using traditional woodworking techniques. (ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery)

'I just liked making things'

Salted throughout Mr Hall's life is a love of music and guitars: he learnt first how to build guitars fresh out of school, aged 19.

Then came the music lessons, which would put him on the path to becoming a workshop owner decades later.

Interspersed among it all was a myriad of jobs, including teaching woodworking at a high school.

Just like his instruments, it all came together in the end.

"All along in the background, I had a little workshop, and I just liked making things using my cabinet-making skills that I learned all those years ago," Mr Hall said.

Richard Hall owns a music shop in a country Victorian town. (ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery)

When his son, Tony, started playing the violin, the call of the workshop proved too strong to resist.

He would mend and repair Tony's violins in the shed, scratching an itch to create.

Tony went on to learn to play viola, and now plays in a Finnish chamber orchestra.

"All the while I was tinkering away in the shed, trying to make instruments that would keep up with his level," Mr Hall said.

"I still haven't got there yet."

The lure of the luthier

Local fiddle player Ellen Hubble walked through the doors of Mr Hall's shop, Black Creek Music Merchants, on its opening day.

She immediately commissioned a violin from Mr Hall, and has waited months for it to be ready to play.

"We were pretty excited there was a music store, particularly a luthier," Ms Hubble said.

"And certainly from my point of view, a violin maker, so close in the area."

Ms Hubble's connection to the violin runs deep.

Her opa was a German-Jewish refugee who arrived with his wife and daughter with minimal possessions.

He did, however, have a violin.

It wasn't until she was in her late 40s that she first started learning to play the instrument.

Ellen Hubble ordered a bespoke violin from Black Creek Music Merchants the first day the store was open. (ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery)

Ms Hubble and her husband are now regulars on the local music scene, and are key organisers of the recent Wonthaggi Accoustic Music Festival.

"The music that is played at country dance was accessible to us," she said.

" We thought, if other people can play these tunes, then it must be accessible music. "

Having a bespoke instrument made using Australian timber was a "once-in-a-lifetime experience", Ms Hubble said.

"These instruments are personal, and they're handed down through generations."

Once in a lifetime

Mr Hall was nervous on the day he was due to hand over Ms Hubble's new violin.

He was worried about how his custom piece would be received.

"I took it home [when it was finished] to wait for my son, who is a good player," he said.

Handcrafted using Australian hardwood, Ellen Hubble's custom violin is now complete. (ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery)

"He was about four hours later than I expected, and I was just pacing the floor. Eventually he came home, and I handed him the violin. He played it, and we were happy," he said.

Holding her new violin for the first time brought tears to Ms Hubble's eyes and a sense of responsibility.

"I hope I do it justice in playing it," she said.

"It's beautiful. It's hard to believe it's Australian. What a beautiful mixture of Australian materials and European style.

"I can't believe how much skill and expertise has gone into it. It's beautiful."

From having photos of the timber selected for her instrument texted to her, to being invited to view the building process, Mr Hall and Ms Hubble have walked in step throughout the violin-making process.

Ms Hubble said the process reflected the open, generous spirit of Mr Hall's music merchant store.

"The fact that people can come in here, to a live, living music shop, is really lovely. Musicians come here, and it's an amazing, unique place to be," she said.

"Everyone who walks in here is incredibly welcomed. It's a treat to come up and visit Mr Hall and the shop."

World.title: Annie and Jim wanted an undercover pool. They ended up with the Australian House of the Year
World.content:
NationalQueenslandArchitecture Annie and Jim wanted an undercover pool. They ended up with the Australian House of the Year Nick Dent September 5, 2026 — 10:36am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Brisbane couple Annie and Jim bought their 1920s timber cottage in 2008, but 10 years later, it was too small for their growing family with three small kids. They also wanted a swimming pool. “We knew we wanted the pool to be undercover so we didn’t have to mess about with sunscreen and rashies every time the kids wanted a swim,” the couple told this masthead via email. Built around the pool, the Half Light House extension embraces views to the west. Toby Scott The extension’s glass walls open the back of the house to sunsets and hill views. Toby Scott “We also didn’t want to expand the house’s footprint much, as we didn’t want to reduce the green space.”



They ended up with an extension built around a pool that uses transparent walls to open the back of the house up to views of hills to the west. Now “Half Light House”, in the northern Brisbane suburb of Clayfield, has been named Australian House of the Year, as well as winning for best House Alteration and Addition Over 200 Square Metres, in the Houses Awards 2026. The house comes alive during golden hour. Toby Scott Brisbane architect John Ellway has taken the awards’ top accolade for the second time, having won in 2021. Toby Scott Organised by Houses magazine, the awards celebrate the creativity of Australian architects and designers in shaping the future of residential design.



They are judged by a panel of top architects chaired by the magazine’s editor, Alexa Kempton. Related Article Architecture Peter designed a Brisbane house that breaks all the rules. Now it’s an award winner “Rather than building homes that are much larger than occupants need or building to the extremities of the block, architects have instead embraced the surrounding landscapes and minimised the impact of the home on the site,” Kempton said. “What we really enjoy observing in Brisbane houses is when architects and designers preserve the qualities already there and then update them for modern life without just building more.” Brisbane architect John Ellway has taken the awards’ top accolade for the second time, having won in 2021 for a Paddington house built on three platforms.



Ellway said the Half Light House design hinged on the pool. “People are safety conscious with pools, and the clients wanted to be able to overlook and see their kids from nearly every room,” he said. The original house remains white and the extension is dark, in keeping with the name Half Light House. Toby Scott The carport nods to undercroft spaces familiar in older Queensland homes. Toby Scott A covered outdoor patio provides a space for entertaining, and a void above the pool is open to the sky.



“There’s this beautiful, dappled reflection on most of the ceilings at different times of the day,” Ellway said. Management of the intense afternoon sun was another consideration. The original house was designed to be closed off at the back; Ellway’s extension controls the light with a simple system of blinds. The western outlook is visible even from the front door of the original cottage. Toby Scott “It’s a beautiful outlook to the west, and they get this amazing light around dusk,” he said. Annie and Jim said now that the rear of the house was open, they could enjoy the sunset from almost everywhere in the house, “even as you’re walking through the front gate”.



“When we wake up in the morning and open the sliding glass doors above the pool, with the sun shining in and the trees just outside, it feels like we’re on holiday.” Related Article Arts ‘We thought it might go straight in the bin’: The design rule the architects of GOMA ignored Kempton said the house replicated a backyard pool experience without sacrificing green space. Ellway collaborated with garden designer Andrew Coates to incorporate a native verge garden, a shady undercroft garden, hard-wearing planting in the driveway that can handle being driven over, and a backyard miniature forest. “Often we can get caught up thinking that the garden is an afterthought or something that happens once the house is designed, and John’s approach is very different,” Kempton said.



“Excellent architecture in Brisbane at the moment is thinking about how you can live outdoors and enjoy the climate, rather than feeling that you need to build a fortress.” Other Houses Awards 2026 winners came from New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania. Awards were given to houses, apartments, renovations, small projects, heritage projects, and an emerging architectural practice. World.title: ‘It was quite humbling’: The moment Roosters-Rabbitohs rivalry was put aside
World.content:
After sharing a few moments with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on Friday night, Jai Arrow spent time with a very different rugby league powerbroker. In a departure from the usual state of affairs between the foundation clubs, retiring Rabbitoh Arrow made his way into the opposing sheds. There he mingled with the Roosters players and staff, including Roosters chairman Nick Politis, who became one of Arrow’s main benefactors after learning of his Motor Neurone Disease diagnosis earlier this year. Loading “We were stranded in LAX a few years ago together, that’s how we first met,” Politis said. “That was the first and last time until last night.



“I read what happened and I wanted to help him. “It was very nice that he found his way to our dressing room, it was quite humbling. Robbo [Roosters coach Trent Robinson] and some of the players spent some time with him. It was good to see him.” Nick Politis and Jai Arrow in the Roosters’ sheds. Politis helped pay for Arrow to attend a wellness retreat in Spain earlier this year to help with his MND after it emerged the Queensland Origin representative had been forced to medically retire. Politis also made sure the Roosters bought a table for an Arrow fundraiser later this month. Earlier on Friday night, Arrow brought up his 100th and last game for the Rabbitohs. It was a milestone made possible after the NRL and the players’ association granted Arrow special dispensation to “play” following his diagnosis.



After full-time, Albanese visited the Rabbitohs sheds to acknowledge the milestone man. “I think there wasn’t a dry eye in the house,” Albanese told this masthead. The Roosters welcomed Jai Arrow into their dressing sheds. “Jai’s courage ... he is an inspiring person. He shows the strength of his character. He came a few weeks ago to Kirribilli House, and I’ve had the opportunity to get to know him. “I just think the occasion tonight was rugby league at its best. Rugby league is about tribalism, but it’s also about something bigger. It’s about looking after each other. Tonight, whether they were Souths supporters, Roosters supporters, or just human beings, it was really uplifting. A great moment.”



A packed house at Allianz Stadium, much like the man of the moment, struggled to contain its emotions. They came for what preceded the match as much as for what occurred during it. “His character is extraordinary,” Albanese added. “He’s much loved by his teammates and by everyone who comes into contact with him.” Nick Politis donated generously to Jai Arrow’s cause. Arrow stepped onto the pitch wearing jersey No.23. He was replaced by his great mate Cody Walker before the game began in earnest, with coach Wayne Bennett holding the interchange card. “Anytime I’ve handled any of this, it’s with a bit of humour,” Walker said. “He was walking off, flipping me the bird, which made me laugh. Look, emotional scenes. It was hard to put into words what was going through my head at that point in time, given how close we are.



Related Article NRL 2026 The night two tribes put 120 years of feuding aside to honour Jai Arrow “On the surface, it’s all banter and giving each other a hard time, but deep down, we’ve got a deep care for one another. We have a strong relationship that goes beyond footy, which is nice. “I know for a fact that on the surface, he’d be burning, giving me raps and things like that, and I’m pretty much the same. It’s actually nice to hear each other talk nicely about one another. He deserves every moment that he’s had this year, given everything that he’s gone through and how he’s dealt with it. It’s been phenomenal - the strength he’s shown and the courage he’s shown.” Walker said Arrow would be a source of inspiration for the Rabbitohs’ finals campaign. “I don’t think there’s anyone that has been a current player diagnosed with this sort of cruel disease,” Walker said.



“It’s just really difficult to witness one of your good mates go through that sort of stuff. It’s been a bit of a journey for him, but you can’t fault the guy for how he’s handled everything that’s been thrown in front of him. “He’s an inspiration to each and every one of us.”

World.title: Dawdlers to dynamos: Dolphins the new comeback kings
World.content:
NationalQueenslandMatch report Dawdlers to dynamos: Dolphins the new comeback kings Joel Gould September 5, 2026 — 10:02am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Dolphins have established themselves as both the starting snails and the comeback kings of the NRL ahead of their maiden finals appearance. After trailing 14-0 and ultimately winning 24-20 in the final-round game against Gold Coast in Robina on Friday night, coach Kristian Woolf was not concerned. He basically has the philosophy that winning covers a multitude of sins. This season the third-placed Dolphins have won a club record 17 games, 11 of which came after conceding the first try. Loading On six occasions they have trailed 10-0 or worse, with their biggest comeback a 40-32 win over Brisbane after falling behind 24-0.



Whether they play Penrith or the Warriors in a qualifying match next week will not be known until the Panthers play Wests Tigers in the final-round game on Sunday afternoon. There are aspects of the Dolphins’ play that need addressing, in particular poor discipline in the opening exchanges of matches. Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow scored two tries against the Titans at Cbus Super Stadium on Friday night. Getty Images They recorded their first win of the year in round two at Suncorp Stadium after trailing 14-0 against Gold Coast, prevailing 18-14 with a late surge, so it was fitting that their final victory of the regular season was against the same club after also falling 14-0 behind. “I am not too worried about it, to be honest,” Woolf said of the slow starts.



“I think tonight was a hard game for us in a lot of ways. “It’s hard when other teams have rested players and you know you are playing for something a lot more next week. Loading “Blokes don’t want to get injured and don’t want to get suspended. We were a little bit tentative at the start in different areas but got ourselves into gear.” Woolf identified yardage errors and penalties as an issue against the Titans.



Related Article NRL 2026 The Roosters put 82 points on the Cowboys. What Todd Payten did next saved their season In the first half, the Dolphins gave away 10 penalties – either general play infractions, ruck infringements, or inside 10 metres – while also making four errors. “I’ve got no dramas,” Woolf said of the uneven display. “The two most important things are that we won, and we got no injuries.” In their last five outings, the Dolphins have not scored in the opening 20 minutes, but they have won all of those matches while conceding just four tries in the final 60 minutes of those games and piling on 146 points overall.



A relentless forward pack led by Tom Gilbert wears teams down as the game goes on, and a skilled backline led by half Isaiya Katoa, centre Herbie Farnworth and fullback Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow can score points quickly. The bench includes linchpin utility Kurt Donoghoe and wild and woolly Ray Stone, who both terrorise opponents in their own unique style. The Dolphins’ Tom Gilbert and Arama Hau embroiled in a heated exchange. Getty Images They will have to be a lot better to prevail against the Warriors or Penrith, but Woolf knows what his team is capable of in the finals after seven consecutive wins. “I am very confident in the group and what I think we can do,” he said. “We have just got to be at our best and we will be hard to beat.” AAP

World.title: Judge declares mistrial in Lindsay Clancy murder case that gripped America
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaCourts Judge declares mistrial in Lindsay Clancy murder case that gripped America Michael Koziol Updated September 5, 2026 — 9:52am ,first published 4:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: The judge in the triple murder trial of Massachusetts woman Lindsay Clancy has declared a mistrial after the jury was unable to reach a unanimous verdict after nearly a week of deliberations. Clancy strangled her three children in 2023 in a case that has generated intense interest across the US and divided the country over mental illness and the 36-year-old’s criminal culpability. Loading That Clancy killed her children – the youngest of whom was just eight months old – was not in doubt. But her lawyers argued she was suffering a rare and dangerous condition called postpartum psychosis, which can afflict new mothers, and was overmedicated. The jury in Plymouth, Massachusetts had previously advised they were struggling to reach a unanimous verdict. Judge William Sullivan had instructed them to keep deliberating.



But on Friday morning (US time), the jury returned a note to the judge: “It is with a heavy heart that we report we are unable to come to a unanimous decision and will not be able to.” Related Article Analysis

Courts The Lindsay Clancy army, from mums in pink to right-wing podcasters Sullivan said he had no option but to declare a mistrial, which was also the position of the prosecution. Clancy’s lawyer Kevin Reddington initially argued the jury should be sent back to deliberate further, and then requested a poll of the jury to see whether they had formed a unanimous verdict on any charges. That would lay the groundwork for a claim of double jeopardy on those charges. When that was denied, Reddington asked for – and was granted – an extra hour to lodge an emergency appeal for a stay from the Massachusetts Supreme Court. That court denied the request.



Confirming the mistrial, Sullivan thanked the jury and invoked Winston Churchill’s famous Their Finest Hour speech, in which the wartime leader asked Britons to “brace ourselves to our duties”. The Clancy case will return to court on September 29. A mistrial means the case can be retried with a different jury. Lindsay Clancy and lawyer Kevin Reddington look at jurors as Judge William Sullivan instructs them to continue deliberations during Clancy’s murder trial on Friday. Greg Derr/Pool The Patriot Ledger via AP Prosecutors argued Clancy knew what she was doing. They contended the then-mother-of-three deliberately sent her then-husband on errands to get him out of the house before killing her children, and questioned the seriousness of her subsequent suicide attempt. But it appeared the jury was deadlocked from early on. On Thursday, the foreman told the judge there was one juror who would not follow the court’s instructions about reasonable doubt. It raised the prospect of a single juror standing in the way of a verdict.



Reddington argued the court had the authority to intervene in circumstances where a juror was “holding out”, not acting in good faith and “refusing to apply the law” – asserting the juror was refusing to join their peers in acquitting Clancy. But the judge again denied that request. The jury consisted of nine women and three men. During a back-and-forth with the judge, Reddington indicated the holdout juror was male. Judge William Sullivan has declared a mistrial. Greg Derr/Pool The Patriot Ledger via AP Despite her actions, many women across America have expressed sympathy for Clancy. Hundreds have shown up to the courthouse dressed in pink and calling for compassion. In online forums, some Clancy supporters trade conspiracy theories about the children’s deaths. “Team Lindsay!” T-shirts are available. In that sense, the case is not unlike that of accused New York murderer Luigi Mangione, who last month pleaded guilty to charges of stalking and killing healthcare executive Brian Thompson on Manhattan street in December 2024.



Related Article Opinion

Women's health It’s the terrifying case that’s gripping America. But is this mother a murderer or a victim? Julia Baird Journalist, broadcaster, historian and author Outside court after the mistrial was declared, Reddington confirmed the 11 other jurors voted to acquit, and said they had been “robbed” by one man, “for whatever his agenda was”. “I hope that guy can sleep well tonight,” he said. Massachusetts law requires a 12-0 unanimous decision in criminal cases. Clancy was prepared for a retrial in the coming months, Reddington said. Plymouth District Attorney Timothy Cruz said it had been “an emotional trial for everyone”. “This was and has always been about getting justice for those three little babies,” he said.



Cruz said there would not be an immediate decision about a second trial. “I have never been swayed to act a certain way or make certain decisions based upon public sentiment,” he said.
