World.title: Latrell produces hit of the year as Rabbitohs crush Roosters in Arrow’s finale
World.content:
For one brutal, bone-crunching moment, all of rugby league held their breath. Except for poor old Toby Rodwell. He was trying to find it.

Latrell Mitchell, undisputed king of the NRL jungle, hit the rookie Roosters halfback with the most exquisite, most monstrous assault you could ever dish out without having to front court afterwards.

Loading

And as poor old Rodwell, 84 kilos, two games into his career, lay prone wondering what had hit him, all of rugby league wondered if Mitchell had hit him high.

Had the game’s most magnetic, single most-watchable player, just hit the kid in the head and rubbed himself out of the finals?

Nope, the replays showed. Mitchell had hit him square in the chest.

Wayne Bennett put it succinctly when asked about how he felt watching said replays and realising that Mitchell’s contact was nice and legal.

“Good”, was Bennett’s summation of that emotional rollercoaster.

Thank the big man above. Especially because Rodwell was showing signs of life. He was soon on his feet too, slowly making his way to the sideline, where Spencer Leniu had the crowd in raptures as well.

Leniu had, an hour earlier, goaded and growled at Souths fans sitting behind the Roosters bench on his way from the field. He had clashed with opposite number Keaon Koloamatangi from a kick-off, and twice again shortly afterwards, with the Rabbitohs prop winning the exchange, baiting Leniu into blowing up and a penalty being blown.

Spencer Leniu clashes with South Sydney’s Keaon Koloamatangi. NRL Photos

As the big screen cut between shots of Mitchell and Leniu, cheers rang out for the Rabbitoh, jeers for the Rooster. Leniu lapped it up, grinning with a touch of the madness that all the good front-rowers possess.

Despite the 50-20 scoreline, the Roosters had held their gloves up. In Leniu’s case, with eyes spinning like poker machines, he did so literally. Rodwell had his moments too.

And the Rabbitohs, with Jai Arrow leaving the Prime Minister emotional, along with 39,999 others at Allianz Stadium, they put their old enemy to the sword.

Before a ball was even kicked, the Dolphins’ narrow win over the Gold Coast meant the Roosters had to win or they would be locked into fourth place. Whether they head across the ditch to face New Zealand or west to take on Penrith won’t be confirmed until the final whistle of the regular season.

Loading

Barring a 41-point loss from fifth-placed Cronulla to Melbourne, the Rabbitohs will now finish sixth and host Newcastle in week one of the finals. Moments from Mitchell – even before Latrell’s scene-stealing 77th-minute shot – and David Fifita again spelled out the impact both men can have in the post-season.

“[Mitchell] needed to get some time behind him tonight and get involved in the game,” Bennet said.

“He didn’t do a great deal last week, which is understandable.

“I took a risk, I could have played him less time. A few people were trying to tell me on the bench to get him off.

“But he was enjoying himself. He wasn’t under stress out there into that second half, and he had that bit of a swagger that he has back.

“He did some really good things. I was really pleased with the outcome.”

And when Fifita took on four defenders from dummy-half in the fifth minute, there was only going to be one winner, and the bullocking back-rower had Souths’ first try.

Tries to Bud Sullivan, Alex Johnston and Campbell Graham ensured the Rabbitohs had plenty of breathing room and a 20-4 half-time lead, before the Roosters found fortune giving the ball air.

Rex Bassingthwaighthe finished off an excellent long-range right-side shift in the 50th minute, before Butcher did the same when the Bunnies were busted up the middle a few tackles later.

But with Cody Walker pulling the strings, the veteran No.6 ensured Souths weren’t ever truly threatened. He helped himself to a try with some light stepping before Adam Elliott, Graham again, Mitchell and Brandon Smith all joined him on the scoreboard.

And Mitchell, he proved once more why he’s the biggest show in town. Just ask poor old Toby Rodwell.

World.title: The Roosters put 82 points on the Cowboys. What Todd Payten did next saved their season
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 The Roosters put 82 points on the Cowboys. What Todd Payten did next saved their season Christian Nicolussi September 5, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Key points North Queensland lost 82-12 to the Sydney Roosters, but are playing finals football

The Dolphins lost 66-0 to the Sharks, and 52-18 to Manly, but have sealed a top-fourth berth

The last NRL team to concede more than 66 points in the regular season and play finals is Manly, who lost 68-6 to Cronulla in 2005

It’s oft-quoted fact that no team has won the NRL premiership after conceding 50 points during the regular season. What about simply reaching the finals after conceding 82? Never happened. Until now. That’s in Queensland: How did these men bounce back from horror scorelines to get their teams playing finals football? Matt Willis/SMH North Queensland coach Todd Payten described the round 22 horror show when the Sydney Roosters thumped the Cowboys 82-12 in their own backyard as “one of our darkest days, if not the darkest day”. “That night was also the first time in my career I was unsure what to say at half-time,” Payten said.



Yet here we are, just over a month later, and the Cowboys are in the finals. Saturday’s final round clash against Canberra is a chance to fine-tune things before a likely elimination final against Cronulla next Sunday. So how did Payten stop things capitulating after the Roosters? A marathon lock-in at the Mad Cow? Extra sessions charging up Castle Hill? Cowboys players react after conceding 82 points to the Roosters. Getty Images What he did next went a long way to salvaging their campaign. Yeeee-haaaaaw. Only half the playing group were required back at Cowboys Leagues Club after the loss, but Payten changed his mind and ordered every player and staff member to front the crowd of cranky fans.



“I told them we were all about to cop a pizzling, but everything that was coming our way was going to be warranted, and we’d have to wear it,” Payten said. “Our supporters are pretty honest. They stand behind us when they see effort, and let us know when we don’t. They pay their hard-earned cash, they’re an important part of the community, and we let them down that night.” Scott Drinkwater can’t hide his dejection. Getty Images Payten was aghast at what he witnessed against the Roosters, but saw enough to keep him from losing heart entirely. “In hindsight, I made some public comments about the Broncos a week earlier, I spoke to our players about our history and the history against the Broncos, and maybe I revved them up too much,” Payten said. “I knew we’d be flat, but in no way did I see that performance [coming].



“I felt like our leaders were unsure what to say at times behind the sticks, and there were moments we went super quiet. It was important we put in place a plan if there was any uncertainty about what to say moving forward. “There was no need to cut the game up and watch it again. I told them one game was not going to define our season, and nothing had changed in terms of us trying to make the finals. “I can’t remember which try it was the Roosters scored, but they had made a lengthy linebreak, and Heilum Luki chased from the other side of the field along with Jaxon Purdue, and we had about four or five guys around the ball running back. “We were still showing care and effort. If I didn’t see that, I would have been questioning what we were doing.” Payten returned home to watch the replay. His wife, Julie, to whom he refers as “Gus Gould”, chimed in with some free advice, as she usually does, and “gave me her rundown of what happened or what should have happened”.



“We showed a lot of resolve the following week, beat the Titans after having a man in the bin, and bounced back quickly,” Payten said. When the Cowboys had the bye a few weeks later, Payten drove four hours south to Mackay and spent time with the Australian cricket team, who were playing the second Test against Bangladesh. Herbie Farnworth tries to deny Cronulla during the 66-0 loss at home. Getty Images Payten wanted to know was how a group responded after a such a heavy defeat, and sought the counsel of the cricketers who had just gone down to a shock loss to the tourists Bangladesh in Darwin. “I spoke with several of the senior guys about taking emotion away from things; there was no over-reaction from them, no under-reaction from them after Darwin, just a need to stay calm and connected, which was refreshing to hear,” he said.



Related Article NRL 2026 What Benji Marshall really thinks about Jarome Luai’s two years at Wests Tigers Similarly, Dolphins coach Kristian Woolf has watched his side lose 66-0 to Cronulla as well as 52-18 to Manly this season. But, like the Cowboys, the Dolphins have recovered to reach the finals – and in it up to their eyeballs with a top-four berth. Manly was the last team to concede 68 points during the regular season and go on to make the finals, in 2005. Unlike 20 years ago, fatigue and momentum from set restarts mean lop-sided scorelines are the new norm. History is about to change. Woolf blamed the Manly loss on fatigue, while the Sharks defeat was a simple bludger of a performance. He knocked over that review the next day at recovery.



Woolf blamed himself for the preparation. The NRL newcomers have been on the end of several blowouts, but more often than not bounced back quickly to ensure there is no mental scarring. The unlikely campaigns continue.

World.title: Of God, Dolly and Gloria Steinem ... and the women who keep the faith
World.content:
NationalGender equality Opinion Of God, Dolly and Gloria Steinem ... and the women who keep the faith Julia Baird Journalist, broadcaster, historian and author September 5, 2026 — 9:30am

September 5, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The sun was shining in a clear blue sky last weekend in Adelaide when about 100 Anglican women gathered at St Peter’s Cathedral for a clergy conference. There was no fanfare, no media coverage, no razzle or dazzle, no influencer poses, just comfortable shoes and a series of workshops and talks. When I walked into one of the sessions on Saturday, I was struck by the cheer. Dolly Parton had died that week, and the women had toasted her at dinner the night before. Parton, as was pointed out in these pages, told Andy Warhol (whom she described as the only person she’d ever met who was weirder than her) that she saw herself as a preacher. Who might not have been allowed at a Southern Baptist pulpit, but who created her own platform, and united vast swathes of America – the world, really – as few others could. While Dolly Parton regarded herself as a preacher, feminists such as Gloria Steinmen worried that religion is used to oppress women. Artwork by Michael Howard. Photos: Netflix, AP Interviewed last year, Dolly said: “I like trying to make people happy and lift people up and glorifying God. That’s my mission in life, so I just hope to get to do more of that.” Her faith was rooted in love, tolerance and inclusion, though myriad news reports skipped over it entirely. Can you imagine the many thousands of conservative evangelical men who bop to her songs, who believe women should submit to men and shouldn’t vote, and who were at times so distracted by her glamour that they didn’t clock – or want to clock – that she was one of the most influential faith leaders in their country?



Thinking of Parton reminds me of the bald truth that women have long had authority from God, if not permission from the church. And of the fact that the enduring struggles inside the church are rarely aired. Some progress has been made, but many places still don’t ordain women as priests (most notably Sydney), and in some dioceses they struggle to maintain a foothold, as a recent report into Canberra-Goulburn revealed. Related Article Opinion

Domestic violence The church stripped bare: high rate of domestic abuse among Anglicans exposed Julia Baird Journalist, broadcaster, historian and author Women clergy are often ignored by mainstream feminists, whether from a belief that the church is intractable, concern about religion being used to oppress women (Gloria Steinem, who died this week, called it “politics in the sky”), or an impatience with faith. But as I looked around the room at these decent, caring women, who still face enormous opposition, who are not fully recognised in places like Sydney, whose authority and ministry is constantly questioned, whose work is often considered secondary, who report rising numbers of blokes who’d like them to submit to men, who have to grit their teeth during debates about the basic worth of women, I realised that this fight that they are still, quietly, engaged in is arguably the longest fight for emancipation and basic equality in Western feminism. Hear me out here. I know in many ways, on many fronts, as Steinem said, we have just started. But, happily, most obvious, basic barriers to equal participation were removed decades ago – even though backsliding is evident in many places. Think of the Seneca Falls Convention in 1848, the first national American women’s rights conference which produced the Declaration of Sentiments, listing 12 resolutions demanding equal social, civil and religious rights for women.



Their core demands were: the right to vote. Tick. Legal equality, especially for married women who wished to own property, manage their own wages and have independent legal standing. Tick. Family and divorce rights, especially over child custody. Tick. Equal access to higher education, universities, professional trades. Tick. And finally, religion – an equal voice and participation in religious institutions and the abandoning of the idea of a “separate sphere” for women. Womp-womp. In the 1890s, after she was elected president of the National American Woman Suffrage Association, Elizabeth Cady Stanton pulled together a group of women to edit and publish The Woman’s Bible, which caused a scandal – including among other suffragists who thought it was a distraction. This bestselling tome laid out an argument against the subservience of women to men that the church claimed to be an immutable truth, an argument that still needs to be heard today. When we talk about the manosphere, instead of blaming a “feminised curriculum” for the toxic sludge online, as Nationals leader Matt Canavan did, we need to stop and look in other directions. It’s significant that women were campaigning for the right to vote and the right to be equal in the church at the same time – and that now it is fundamentalist evangelical pastors in the US who are saying women should not vote. Back then, Stanton wrote to her critics: “The only difference between us is, we say that these degrading ideas of woman emanated from the brain of man, while the church says that they came from God.” Quite. Our parliaments are heavily populated with people of faith, many of whom have not ever been exposed to women in positions of authority in their upbringings, schools or congregations. We routinely forget or underestimate this, yet it is my belief that the reason the pushback from religious men has been so sustained and ferocious is because this is about the bedrock belief that women do not possess authority in the same way men do.



And this leaks into more cultural pockets than we recognise. Related Article Opinion

Religion Kay Goldsworthy is flying to Sydney. She won’t be an archbishop when she lands. Argh, men Julia Baird Journalist, broadcaster, historian and author It also means Christianity is more likely to be associated with a strongly male, American nationalism in the public imagination than a quiet, forceful compassion. So, when we talk about the manosphere, instead of blaming a “feminised curriculum” for the toxic sludge online, as Nationals leader Matt Canavan did this week, we need to stop and look in other directions. Where are women equal, upheld and respected? Where are women speaking? Where are they prevented from speaking? Why does this matter? The organiser of the Adelaide conference, the whip-smart Bishop Sophie Relf-Christopher, told me the mood of the conference – where the governor of South Australia, Frances Adamson spoke along with the Archbishop of Perth, Kay Goldsworthy, was “jubilant”.



“We persevere,” she said, “because we are unwilling to cede the Holy Church of God to people who do not support the full and equal worth of women when Jesus did. We are unwilling to leave the church a place that girls and women are coerced and controlled.” Relf-Christopher wants women who have left the church to return “to work with us in a new reformation”. She said: “If what you believe about God requires women to remain permanently grateful, un-ordained, quiet, or endlessly available, it is not a theology that is compatible with the message of Jesus Christ. Patriarchy is not synonymous with Jesus’ ideas, but more the Roman Empire that wanted to suppress them.” As Billy Bragg said last week, “at a time when followers of Jesus Christ are talking about ‘the sin of empathy’ and claiming that loving thy neighbour as thyself will lead to the end of Western civilisation, Dolly’s faith led her to embrace everyone”. Julia Baird is a journalist, author and regular columnist. Her latest book is Bright Shining: how grace changes everything.

World.title: A Super title and 25,000 crowds: How Reds plan to make Queensland a powerhouse
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Opinion A Super title and 25,000 crowds: How Reds plan to make Queensland a powerhouse Paul Cully Rugby columnist September 5, 2026 — 9:15am

September 5, 2026 — 9:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Queensland Reds chief executive David Hanham and general manager of high-performance Sam Cordingley are basking in the warmer relationship between Rugby Australia and New Zealand Rugby. Talking to the Herald from their offices in Brisbane, they expressed confidence that RA heavies Phil Waugh and Dan Herbert, and New Zealand counterparts Steve Lancaster and David Kirk have provided the stable platform that rugby needs at Test and Super Rugby level. Reds star Carter Gordon celebrates a try against the Brumbies. Queensland have big ambitions for the future. Getty Images There is a Bledisloe Cup Test coming to Brisbane on Anzac Day, a conviction among Super Rugby executives that 10 teams is the right number and confidence that the competition’s best team, the Hurricanes, would stack up well against any club side in the world. “Some of the best players in the world are playing in Super Rugby,” said Cordingley, who played a key role in the recruitment of new Reds coach Vern Cotter.



“If you put the Hurricanes up against any teams in the north, that would most likely be a really good result ... I don’t think it’s a question of talent [in Super Rugby], it’s a question of consistency.” But those more favourable bigger-picture conditions are only one reason why the Reds are, in cricketing parlance, determined to play on the front foot. The Hurricanes claim the 2026 Super Rugby final in Wellington. Their best is as good as any club side in the world. Getty Images Unlike their Super Rugby peers in Australia and New Zealand, the Reds have recorded a series of operating profits, participation numbers in the state are strong and 12 Reds were named in the Wallabies squad to face Argentina this weekend. As a result, Queensland have unambiguously set their sights high.



“We’ve set a five-year vision for the QRU [Queensland Rugby Union] to build ourselves and build Queensland back to being one of the best rugby provinces in the world,” Hanham said. “And part of that is making sure that we’ve got a winning team and a successful football program. Obviously, you can’t be a strong rugby province without winning on the field. Isaac Henry celebrates after scoring a try against the Waratahs. The Reds know success on the field is the most important thing. Getty Images “Keeping in mind when we talk about a rugby province, that’s the community game and the professional game that we’re responsible for. “In five years, we want to grow the game. We’re about 90,000 players [in Queensland]; we want to get to 100,000.



“We want the Reds to be a consistent top-three team, and in that period of time to be winning a title. We want our crowds at Suncorp to get from averaging 15,000 back up to 25,000. “A big part of that is maintaining financial sustainability as a business, and getting the Ballymore development under way. If someone said, ‘What does the best rugby province look like?’ That’s how we define success.” QRU chief executive David Hanham at the soon-to-be-redeveloped Ballymore. Brendan Hertel/QRU Media There are many layers to a project of such ambition, especially in a complex sporting landscape such as Australian rugby. While the New Zealanders are well into the National Provincial Championship, their domestic rugby competition that runs for 10 rounds before three weeks of play-offs, Australian clubs are about to embark on the four-week Super Rugby AUS.



Cordingley, who played for the Ballymore Tornadoes in the short-lived, eight-team Australian Rugby Championship in 2007, acknowledges that lack of exposure for the next tier of players remains a challenge. “I can only speculate on where we [Australian rugby] may have been if we’d retained that competition [ARC] relative to the New Zealand NPC ... or what the Currie Cup has delivered in South Africa,” he said. “Credit to Rugby Australia in terms of being able to invest in that product [Super Rugby AUS] ... but I still think we’re short of where we need to be.” That has forced the Reds to be creative, in high performance and commercially. After Super Rugby AUS, they will embark on a four-game tour of Japan and Italy, courtesy of their partnerships with Saitama Panasonic Wild Knights and Benetton Rugby in Treviso.



Hanham says the Reds have found a way to make these tours “cost neutral”, and Cordingley has been the driving force behind them as a way to accelerate the development of the Reds’ non-Wallabies. In echoes of former Wallaby Ben Darwin’s theories on cohesion, Cordingley says the tour games are not solely about accumulating playing minutes, but increasing what the Reds call “shared experience matches”. “It’s not just playing games of rugby,” Cordingley said. “We have created these partnership opportunities with Benetton and Panasonic to be able to provide experiences for our players and staff collectively to get to what we target – around 30 shared experiences matches a year to be competing with the French Top 14 clubs and the English Premiership.” The Reds are confident Cotter’s arrival will also be step towards their title ambitions, but they also hold firm views about Super Rugby’s structure. There is near-constant chatter about change or expansion, with Japan often mentioned as a possible entrant.



Hanham, however, urged caution. Related Article Australian rugby ‘Cheat code’: Wilson cleared to play in Shute Shield decider after Wallabies standby call “There is a very strong view – I believe shared by the clubs and unions – that we’ve got the right number of teams,” he said. “How do we improve the quality of the competition, in the sense of not only the onfield product, but how we market and promote it? “We’ve now got an Anzac Bledisloe, which I think is a great tent-pole event, like State of Origin is to NRL. We’ve got Super Round, which was a great success in Christchurch ... I feel like we’ve created a product that’s going to be successful. “My personal view is we don’t want to be messing with the integrity of that. However, there is an avenue to enable other competitions to join the Super Rugby Pacific competition at the appropriate times, where you’re not changing the number of teams every year.



“That’s probably been one of Super Rugby’s challenges – it’s constantly changed, too often, over a long period of time. “So, maintain integrity, keep the competition strong and then an opportunity to bring the Japanese competition in at the appropriate time – that will be down the track at some point, I assume, if all the stars align.”

World.title: A contempt of privilege: Parliament's Clerk explains
World.content:
Parliament's finding that officials from MBIE had committed a contempt of Parliament's privilege received a lot of news coverage, but in the aftermath, confusion may remain as to what the privilege was that they contravened, how the contempt was decided and what the possible punishments even were.

And why did they go down in flames when politicians seem to get away with similar behaviours?

The House put those and other questions to the Clerk of the House of Representatives, Dr David Wilson. Part of his role is to act as a specialist advisor to Parliament on its rules.

A contempt of privilege: Parliament’s Clerk explains The House Download MP3 13m

Broadly speaking, what is privilege?

"Well, it's perhaps an unfortunate term because it suggests some sort of entitlements or wealth or something like that.

It's none of those things.

"It is really just the rules and protections that are available to Parliament collectively, to the House of Representatives, not to individual members, but to them as a collective, that enable them to do their jobs thoroughly and honestly and without fear.

"And so I guess the best-known privilege that Members of Parliament (MPs) have is freedom of speech-that they're free to say almost anything they like in the House and there can be no legal consequence.

"In fact, the only consequences can be ones imposed by the House itself."

And there are also other privileges that help MPs do their job, including the one at the centre of this, which is different?

"It is. Really.

"It is a fundamental principle that Parliament is entitled to receive truthful answers to its questions.

"That is because it exists to hold the government to account. One of Parliament's primary roles, apart from making laws, is to scrutinise the government, and it can only do that if it can be sure that the government (both ministers and public servants) will tell the truth when they answer those questions.

"When we talk about the government, we're not just talking about the ministers, but also the whole machinery behind them, the senior public servants who also have to turn up to Parliament to answer questions.

"Generally, they do it twice a year. One is the Estimates process, where the government is setting out its budget and asking Parliament to agree to fund it, and the other is the Annual Reviews, where the performance of departments is scrutinised, usually by questioning the chief executive and other senior officials."

So, they may be in a room for half an hour or some hours with a select committee, who will have sent them hundreds of questions beforehand, will ask dozens of questions in the room, and then follow up with lots of questions afterwards - all of which they are expected to answer truthfully?

"Yeah, that's exactly how it works. And, [the] questioning of officials has got longer over recent years, as Parliaments have put more time and attention on that. But the obligation to tell the truth is always the same. The whole system falls down if people don't.

"Regardless of whether an answer might be embarrassing or might paint the government or a minister in a poor light, or the department itself, they're still required to give a truthful answer to the question.

"And that's where it kind of fell down earlier this year when, after a select committee hearing, the committee felt that they hadn't been told everything that they should have been told (in response to questions), so they did the next thing you'd do, which is… To raise a 'matter of privilege' with the Speaker."

The Speaker is the gatekeeper on these things - what does he do, and how does that work?

"So any member (and only members) can raise matters of privilege with the Speaker, and that's effectively making a complaint by saying 'I think one of the rules of Parliament have been infringed'."

"The Speaker's role is to look at that and [ask whether] on the face of it - does there appear to be an issue here that warrants investigation?

"They don't make any judgement about whether someone has done something wrong, for example, but on the face of it, if the allegations here could be true, then is this something that should be investigated?

"And they also give some weight to the seriousness of the matter, because there are lots of minor technical breaches that happen from time to time, particularly in the heat of Question Time.

"But where it appears to be a serious one, then the Speaker refers the matter to the Privileges Committee.

"And they do that by saying so in the House, so that all members and the public can hear what's happened. Applications, as I say, are also turned down, and that's just done in private between the Speaker and the member who complained."

So, the Speaker doesn't tell the rest of us that someone complained, but he decided not to do anything about it?

"That's right, and that's been the invariable practice of Speakers over the years."

If the Speaker decides that there may be a case to answer, then the Privileges Committee is convened?

"That's right.

"So it doesn't meet routinely because (unlike a lot of other select committees), it doesn't have a routine workload.

"Mostly, it just meets to consider these privilege matters, and there might be a handful of them in a Parliament.

"Sometimes there are none, but perhaps three or four would be normal. The committee has senior MPs on it and, by convention, is chaired by the Attorney General, and although it often has a government majority, generally it operates on a consensus basis."

It's quite fun to watch, and anyone can go along and observe.… It almost feels like a court, doesn't it?

"Yeah, it does have some similarities, and that may be one of the reasons the Attorney General chairs it.

"Of course, it isn't a court of any kind. I know that Parliament is sometimes referred to as the 'highest court', but it isn't a court; it is the supreme lawmaking body.

"The Privileges Committee does carry out a quasi-judicial function, which is why it has some powers that other committees don't have.

"For example, it can compel people to attend and answer questions. Other committees can't do that - they can only ask the Speaker to do it for them.

"It doesn't really have to use that (in the same way that other committees don't need to), because generally just the force of the expectation to be there is sufficient.

"But it is a committee that will quite often make adverse findings and therefore needs to put them to the people the findings are about before they're released. So those are some of the ways its practice is a little bit different to other committees.

And then whatever its findings are, it writes a report, and it returns that to the House, and then the House (as it has this week) debates that report?

"That's right. Like all committees, the Privileges Committee can make some findings and recommendations, but it is actually up to the House what happens.

"So if there's some sort of sanction that is proposed, it is the House that decides whether to uphold that.

"In this particular case, the House was simply asked to 'note the report' and the sanction was found to be the finding of contempt. No further sanction was proposed.

Apart from anything else, it must be pretty awful to have your name discussed in Parliament [in this way].

"No doubt it is, and members are generally pretty careful about that because they know that the people they are speaking about can't speak back.

"So they're pretty restrained in talking about public servants, or members of the public, as a general rule.

"But part of their role in scrutinising the government might sometimes be to critique the work that departments do, and particularly the chief executives.

In terms of the kind of recommendations the committee can make, despite what some people say, it cannot imprison anybody. That's been ruled out in legislation. It doesn't have a lot of options, does it?

"When you're talking about making recommendations about people who are not Members of Parliament. Really, it is a matter of telling the person off, reprimanding them, maybe having them apologise.

"There have, over the years, been a few unique penalties proposed.

"There was once a courier firm that was said to have transported some confidential committee documents, I think, to a journalist.

"They wouldn't say who had given them the documents to provide, and so that courier firm was banned from deliveries to Parliament for a period of time. But that's an unusual case.

"Most of these privileges cases have involved Members of Parliament.

"In the past, they used to involve journalists quite often because of the conflict between confidential Parliamentary information and journalists' duty to report on interesting news stories.

"That's not so common these days, and with members of the Press Gallery, I guess, there is an additional sanction available because they're only in the Press Gallery for as long as the Speaker will allow them to have access to Parliament.

"But for general members of the public or public servants, yeah, there are a smaller range of sanctions available.

"Technically, it is possible to find people up to $1,000. That's only been done once. That was against TVNZ some years ago, and it's really a symbolic punishment. It's highly unlikely to ever be levied against an individual."

A Privileges Committee hearing aimed at a government agency is quite rare, isn't it?

"Yeah, it is. It's very unusual. In preparing for this particular case (because I go along and advise the Privileges Committee each time), I looked back at other times that public sector agencies had been in front of the committee, and I could only find three.

"New Zealand Post in 2003 for a somewhat similar issue. They were accused of having deliberately misled a committee, but ultimately found not to have because it was probably more of a misunderstanding.

"TVNZ in 2006, which was found guilty of contempt and was actually fined. And then Maritime New Zealand in 2015, and in that instance, the committee found there was no case to answer. So it is pretty unusual.

For anyone who watches Question Time and who regularly shouts at the television in response to ministers from any government not quite answering questions properly, not quite telling the full truth, or even potentially full-on lying. Why don't they get brought before the Privileges Committee, or why aren't complaints made that 'minister so-and-so said something patently not true, and he's misleading the House'?

"I think there's a few reasons.

"One is: often answers to questions reflect different opinions, and the Speaker is not there to choose whose [opinion] is right and whose is wrong.

"The Speaker has got no way of knowing that. And there are different interpretations of answers. So sometimes those issues do get raised with the Speaker.

"I think the other thing is that Speakers really - over the whole time the Parliament has existed - have said that in order to be found to have deliberately misled the House (it's quite a high bar), there needs to be knowledge that what you're saying is incorrect and that you're setting out to be misleading.

"And often [for things said] in the heat of debate, Speakers have found it's difficult to sustain both those [requirements]. People might be wrong, but not have given much preparation to answers, particularly to supplementary questions.

"I suppose they're a bit lenient on it, but it is actually the same rule that applies in the case we're talking about now that has just been in front of the Privileges Committee, and Members of Parliament have occasionally been held to account for that.

"There was one in the last Parliament where a minister gave an incorrect answer and then didn't come back to the House to correct it for a period of time. And the committee was critical of that, although they in that case didn't find that contempt had occurred."

I suppose in order to successfully bring a case, you also need to have the majority support of the Committee, and that must be quite difficult to achieve when the committee numbers are somewhat split?

"The Committee, as I say, often has a government majority, but it's very rare for it to vote on anything. It does try to reach a consensus, and I think that reflects the function it's carrying out, which is sitting in judgement on other people's conduct.

"I think the Privileges Committee isn't inherently a particularly political environment, although of course the members are politicians, and you can never entirely separate those things, and nor should you try. But that is one of the barriers, I suppose.

"The other one is - some member has actually got to raise a complaint, and the Speaker does have that gatekeeping role of thinking, well, on the face of it, is there an issue here, and is it a serious enough one to warrant going to the Privileges Committee?"

Related Links:

The Privileges Committee's page, with links to this and previous cases.
